Section Eleven: The Six Recollections (Ṣaḍ-anusmṛti).
Regarding the first point of knowledge, the method for knowing the size of the moon and sun is as follows:

if it is the waxing moon (śuklapakṣa), one should say, "Today is the first day of the great waxing moon," and so on up to the fifteenth day; because the waxing moon is consistently large, there is no need to mention it being small.
If it is the waning moon (kṛṣṇapakṣa), it applies to both large and small phases; when it is the great waning moon, one should say, "Today is the first day of the great waning moon."
"Up to the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight when it is a short month, today is the first day of the dark fortnight's short month,

up to the fourteenth day"— this refers to the distance, near or far, between the time of consciousness-departure and the *poṣadha* day. Furthermore, to prevent inquiries from laypeople, it is explained that if one enters a village,
one should first know the number of days of the month and so forth.
Regarding the second method of mindfulness concerning the place of eating: one who entirely declines an invitation should say, "I now decline this invitation;
I shall eat my own food," or say, "I shall eat the regular food of the Saṃgha and do not accept this invitation," or say, "I shall go for alms and do not accept this invitation.
If one accepts an invitation but there is no offering, one should say, "I now eat on my own as there is no place of invitation," or say, "I now..."
When eating the regular food of the Sangha where there is no formal invitation, one may say, "I am begging for food where there is no invitation.
If one has accepted an invitation but does not go against it, one should say, "There is an invitation today; I shall go of my own accord.

If one has accepted an invitation but has a reason to go against it, one should say, "Today I have a certain reason (a 'reason' refers to occasions such as the distribution of robes during the *kārttika* month) that allows me to go against the invitation. If one has accepted many invitations, one should relinquish them in the presence of another person.

It is said that if one has many invitations today, one may accept one invitation for oneself and give the remainder to a Great Sister (mahallikā) at such-and-such a place (this relinquishment is accomplished by facing five classes of renunciants).
If there is no one present, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, one relies on a nun residing in one’s own kinship circle and performs a mental relinquishment (*manasikāra-parityāga*), saying:
"I, [Name], this morning, have been given five kinds of formal meals by a donor; I now transfer them as a gift to the bhikṣuṇī [Name]."
The donor [Name] does not consider me to have received a meal at will (three times).
Regarding the third mindfulness, one who knows the rules for the length of the summer retreat (*varṣa*), or one who has newly received the precepts, should say:
"In the year..., in the month..., on the day..., at the time when the shadow of the sun was such-and-such units on a one-foot measuring stick, I received full ordination (*upasampadā*); I now..."

Regarding the summer retreat: if there was no retreat, or if there was one, refer to its duration in days. (In the Western lands, after the ordination is completed, the length of the retreat is determined by comparing the shadow of a wooden gnomon.

Fourth, the method for mindfulness regarding robes and alms bowls: if one has received the full set of robes and bowl, one should say, "I have received and maintain the five robes and the bowl in their entirety.
(If they are incomplete, refer to the number actually possessed. If one seeks to speak of extra robes, bowls, medicine, and so forth, one should simply be mindful.
When performing the *śuddhi-vyavahāra* (declaration of purity) regarding surplus goods, the elder should say: "I now have surplus wealth; I shall perform the declaration of purity.

Fifth, as for the method of being mindful of eating in a separate group (*pṛthaggaṇa-bhojana*): if there is a reason for eating in a separate group—such as illness or during the month of Kārttika—one should say:
"Due to such-and-such a cause, I am permitted to eat in a separate group. If there is no such cause, one should say: "I am mindful that I shall not eat in a separate group."
The sixth [reflection] concerns being mindful of whether illness exists or not: if one has an illness, one should contemplate its treatment;
if one is free of it, one should say, "I shall follow the community in practicing the Path.
Section Twelve: Receiving Robes.
This chapter has seventy-one main sections: 1. Regulations and permissions; 2. Functional efficacy; 3. Explanation of the name; 4. Substance;
5. Material; 6. Color; 7. Measurement; 8. Number of strips; 9. Hemmed borders; 10. Number of layers; 11. Method of making; 12. Method of receiving; 13.
Method of relinquishing; 14. Gains and losses; 15. Repairing and washing.
Reverently observing the seventeen types of sitting mats:
first, regarding those that are "prescribed" (*niyata*), this means that for the five robes and six requisites, the Buddha prescribed that they be kept; to violate this constitutes an offense.
Regarding those that are "permitted" (*anujñāta*), this refers to all extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*) and the one hundred and one articles for the body's sustenance, and so forth.
According to their respective karmic retributions, they are permitted to hear [the Dharma], and there is no fault whether they comply or oppose it.
Regarding the second function, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Because he wishes to manifest unprecedented dharmas, all ninety-six types of non-Buddhist outsiders lack this robe;
therefore, they are called 'heterodox outsiders' (*tīrthika*). Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The noble disciples of the Buddha abide..."

Because it follows the Middle Way, the wearing of the three robes (*tricīvara*) was established to differ from the shameless nakedness of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and the excessive greed of the white-robed laity, for whom multiple layers were worn.
The *Pinjizhigongde lun* (Treatise on the Analysis of Merit) states that the three robes were established for the sake of the three seasons:
heavy robes are worn in winter, light robes in summer, and medium robes in spring; furthermore, they serve to protect against insects. This Vinaya prescribes them because of the cold.
Wearing the three robes (tricīvara) also signifies that one wears such garments for the sake of all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time;
the meaning is that the three robes were established as a causal condition for subduing the three poisons. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Those who wear the kāṣāya abandon the three poisons.
The *Mahākaruṇā Sūtra* states: "Provided that one's nature is that of a śramaṇa, even if one defiles the conduct of a śramaṇa, if one is a śramaṇa in form, one is clothed in the kāṣāya."
Those who [practice] shall attain *nirvāṇa* without remainder from the time of Maitreya Buddha until the time of Ruci Buddha.
The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "When the Tathāgata made his vow for Buddhahood in the presence of Ratnagarbha Buddha, he said: 'My *kāṣāya* shall possess five merits.
First, among the fourfold assembly—whether they have committed grave offenses or hold wrong views—who enter into my Dharma, in a single thought-moment..."
First, those who honor him with a respectful mind will certainly receive the prediction of enlightenment in one of the three vehicles.
Second, if devas, nāgas, humans, or ghosts can show reverence toward even a small portion of this person’s *kāṣāya*, they shall attain non-retrogression from the three vehicles.

Third, there are spirits and various people who, upon obtaining even four inches of *kāṣāya*, will have their food and drink sufficiently provided. Fourth, if sentient beings harbor mutual animosity or resentment, [they shall be pacified].

The power of the *kāṣāya* immediately gives rise to compassion. Fifth, if one is in the midst of battle, by maintaining even a small measure of reverence and respect for it, one will always prevail over others.
If my *kāṣāya* lacked these five powers, I would be deceiving the Buddhas and the Saṃgha of the ten directions. The *Saṃghīti-sūtra* states:
"If laypeople seek a piece of a *kāṣāya* from monks or nuns who possess the virtue of the precepts, wishing to ward off calamities, they may give them a small portion."
If a monk or nun destroys the three robes or the alms bowl, they commit a *stūlātyaya* of the essential nature (*svabhāva*).

However, regarding the robes and bowl themselves—whether they have been formally accepted or not—they must not be destroyed or ruined; nor should one tear them, sell them, or use them for miscellaneous purposes, as all such acts constitute the aforementioned offense.

Third, regarding the explanation of the name "robe" (*cīvara*): this Vinaya states that it is permitted to cut and tear [the cloth] with a knife to create the robes of a śramaṇa, so that they cannot be plundered by enemies or thieves.
One wears the *antarvāsa* as an undergarment against the body; one wears the *uttarāsaṅga* and the *saṃghāṭī* when entering the assembly.

Although there is no direct translation for these names across the various schools, if we infer them through their meaning, we can roughly understand their essential import. *Note: The term "慧" (hui) at the end of the passage appears to be a scribal error or a signature mark; it has been omitted from the translation.*
The aforementioned sutra states: "The five-strip robe is called the middle-layered robe; the seven-strip robe is called the upper-layered robe;
and the *saṃghāṭī* is called the 'robe for congregating. The meaning is that the *saṃghāṭī* is called the 'variegated robe' because its strips are numerous.

If named according to its function, it is the 'robe for entering royal palaces and villages. The seven-strip robe is called the 'robe of middle value,' being named from its function as the [robe] for entering..."
Regarding the five-fold robe (*pañcaka-cīvara*), it is called the "undergarment" (*antaravāsaka*) by way of its function; it is the robe for traveling on the road and for performing work.

Regarding the fourth point, "wealth is not as it should be": this means that wealth obtained through the four wrong livelihoods, or acquired by one's own hand through production, lending, or trade, is all unrighteous;
because such acceptance is invalid, the Vinaya states: "One does not obtain [wealth] through wrong livelihood, nor by inciting others, nor by manifesting signs."
If one obtains robes subject to forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) or similar items, they may not be used as the three formal robes (*tricīvara*).
Regarding the fifth point, "the substance must be suitable," the meaning is that they must be thick and heavy to qualify;

if they are fine, thin, coarse, or transparent enough to reveal the body—even if they are made of silk, brocade, embroidery, or ornate fabrics—they do not constitute valid acceptance. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "All [robes] made of raw [unprocessed] materials..."
Regarding items such as coarse hair, tree bark, and grass garments, they do not constitute [valid] robes. The *Wubai wen* (Five Hundred Questions) states:
"If one uses raw silk (*jǐngjiàn*) to make the three robes, and does not manifest them [upon the body], one incurs an offense.
Regarding the sixth point, "proper color": this Vinaya states that one must not keep robes dyed with superior colors; they should be destroyed and made into *kāṣāya*.

Regarding the color of the robe (the term *kāṣāya* refers here to "improper colors"): the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that one must not wear robes of any of the five pure primary colors—blue, yellow, red, white, or black—with the exception of the *nāṃgaliptaka* (patchwork) robe.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states that robes made from these five primary colors do not constitute the three formal robes (*tricīvara*).
Furthermore, dyes derived from purple grass, *kṣaṇa* bark, turmeric, vermilion, madder, and the wood of *dhātakī* are all considered improper.
If one has five types of primary colors, one may perform the *trimaṇḍala-śuddhi* (purification by three dots) on a robe and wear it as another garment;

that is, dark blue, black, and indigo are permitted, and all [colors] such as saffron and madder may be accepted. Pure blue, light blue, azure, and so forth, when purified by the three dots, may be used for the lining of a robe.
If they are not pure primary colors—such as red, white, or yellow—one may also do so. If the color is not according to the Dharma, once it has been dyed, one should further [apply the purification].

Regarding the requirement for robes to be covered by the proper color (*dharmaranga*), the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states: "The color of the robe should not be too red, too yellow, too black, or too white;
it should be pure and according to the Dharma. This applies to the three types of religious robes (*tricīvara*) as well as other garments; they must all be of this color.
Regarding the ritual for making them pure (*pariśuddhi-karma*), one uses the aforementioned dark blue, black, or green at each of the four corners, applying it as desired.
The *Saṃghīti* states that [the size] is at its largest like four fingers and at its smallest like a pea; the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* says it is as large as a sesame seed.
The *Saṃghīti* further states that one must not sew them together, nor should one use one, three, five, seven, or nine [patches]; they must not be made in the shape of a flower.

If a robe worn for bathing becomes soiled with mud, it is then considered "clean" (pure). If it is a new *saṃghāṭī*, one should proceed by making [patches] starting from one corner... up to [the end].
It is the same for all new garments. If many pieces of torn cloth are joined together in one place to be patched, purification (*kappiya*) is performed in that single spot.
"Blue" refers to copper-blue; "black" refers to various clays and the like; "madder" (*māñjiṣṭha*) refers to fruit juices and the like.
The meaning is that in the land of Shu there is the *māndārava* tree; its bark is reddish-black yet bright and vivid, and it may be used [for dye].

It is used for dyeing and possesses a slight fragrance; there are also *mulan* trees in Bingzhou to the east of the Pass, whose seeds are suitable for making rosaries and can also be used for dyeing, though the resulting color is somewhat black.
There are those within the capital who seek them from the various mountains, but they are rare.
Seventh, regarding the proportions: this Vinaya states that for the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṭika*), the length is four cubits and the width is two cubits;
for the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) of seven strips, each is five cubits long and three cubits wide. Even the smallest permissible size is four cubits long and two and a half cubits wide;

these are all termed "in accordance with the Dharma" (*yathādharma*). If they exceed these dimensions, they may still be accepted and worn because they can be cut down. However, if they exceed the maximum limit, [they are not permitted].

Regarding whether one should perform the *śuddhika* (purification) or not, the meaning of the offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*) is as follows: at the time of speaking [the formal declaration], it should be after the robe has been accepted, because the Dharma robe is considered "extra" (*atireka*) beyond that.
As for the number of strips in the eighth rule: according to this Vinaya, the *saṃghāṭī* (outer robe) consists of nine strips up to nineteen strips; if it exceeds these, [it constitutes an offense].

Regarding these numbers, one should also maintain the seven-strip and five-strip robes; this is termed the "Self-Regulation" (zì kǎidìng). The *Pó lùn* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra) states: "The saṃghāṭī has three grades:
the nine-strip, eleven-strip, and thirteen-strip are the lower grade; the fifteen-strip, seventeen-strip, and nineteen-strip are the middle grade;
and the twenty-one-strip, twenty-three-strip, and twenty-five-strip are the upper grade."

Regarding the ninth point concerning measurements: this Vinaya text is not definitive; following the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it states that for the outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*), the lower grade consists of two lengths and one short unit, while the upper grade consists of four lengths and one short unit;

both are termed "in accordance with the Dharma. If there is mutual increase or decrease in these measurements, although the formal acceptance (*parigraha*) may be established, wearing or using such a robe constitutes a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*).
Regarding the tenth point, the number of layers: this Vinaya states that for a new *saṃghāṭī*, there must be two layers; for the other two robes, one layer each;
as for old ones, they may be made with as many or few layers as desired.
Regarding the eleventh point, the method of construction: this Vinaya states that for a *saṃghāṭī* of seven strips, it must necessarily be cut (in patches); for a five-strip robe, it is permissible.

Regarding the folding of leaves into five parts, it is said: if one dyes a plain robe (*maṇḍala-cīvara*) and makes stripes, or sews leaves onto the robe, or folds them to form leaf-patterns on the robe—whether the leaves are half facing upward and half facing downward—all such acts constitute a *dukkaṭa* offense.

Ānanda, following these instructions, made robes with the left stripes slanting to the left and the right stripes slanting to the right; as for the central stripes and leaves, they were slanted in both directions. If one obtains a robe [in this manner], it is not [an offense].
If the cloth is insufficient even when one side is made longer and the other shorter, it is permitted to patch it with leaves of cloth;

if it is still insufficient, it is permitted to make it into a *maṇḍala-anta* (a rectangular robe). The *Saṃghāṭi-sūtra* states: "The leaves [of the patch] may be at most four finger-widths wide and at least as thin as a grain of barley;

they must not be sewn horizontally across the middle. When sewing the robe later, one should use a 'horse-tooth' stitch (*aśvadaṃṣṭrā*), and the upper and lower parts of the robe should be joined so that they do not fray."

One should secure the border by folding back the edge; the *Śāriputra-vinaya* states: "The Buddha taught that when a bhikṣu gives leather for a sandal, the front border should be folded back four finger-widths and the rear border eight finger-widths.
When providing the straps, one should follow this method. Furthermore, 'folding back the edge' is what the Buddha permitted as a lawful way to possess and use [the leather];
sewing it straight is not permitted, as this would differ from the clothing of worldly people."
Furthermore, to prevent the influence of non-Buddhists (tīrthika), this Vinaya merely mentions sewing the *saṃghāṭī* and does not discuss the removal of thorns;
however, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is more appropriate on this point. The *Sāhasrika-vidhi* states that the three robes should have their four corners reinforced with patches.
According to this Vinaya, one should attach leather ties (*guṇa*) to the shoulders to cover areas prone to dirt and grease.

Regarding the twelfth matter, the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) of the Dharma: this Vinaya merely states that "the three robes should be accepted and maintained," yet it lacks the specific text for the ritual of acceptance.
Now, following the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, I shall clarify the method for its acceptance. As for the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*), one should refer to it by the number of its strips;
here, we shall first provide the text for accepting the fifteen-strip robe, and the other cases may be understood by analogy with this explanation.
Sister, attend with one-pointed mind: I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], receive this saṃghāṭī robe consisting of fifteen strips, three long and one short, a robe of cut-and-sewn patches.
(Recite three times. I receive the seven-strip robe.
Sister, listen with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], receive this seven-strip uttarāsaṅga robe, consisting of two long pieces and one short piece, as a cut-and-sewn garment (to be worn).
(Recite three times. Receiving the five-strip [saṃghāṭī].
"Venerable Sister, attend with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [name], receive this five-piece *antarvāsa* robe, consisting of one long and one short patchwork garment, for keeping.
(Recite three times. The text for receiving the *sāṃghāṭī* robe states:
Sister, attend with one-pointed mind: I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], receive and maintain this mañji-saṃghāṭī (recite three times;
the other two robes may be understood accordingly).
Regarding these five types of robes permitted by this Vinaya, if they are made with folded leaves (*kuṭaka-patta*), one should say "I possess the folded-leaf robe" (*kuṭaka-patta-cīvara*);

if they are made with sewn leaves (*sīvana-patta*), one should say "I possess the sewn-leaf robe" (*sīvana-patta-cīvara*). When sewing, one may leave one side unsewn so that it resembles a robe of cut-and-sewn pieces (*khaṇḍa-cīvara*);
however, if both sides are sewn, it is simply treated according to the rules for a seamless robe (*saṃghāṭī*).
The Text for Receiving the Saṃkakṣikā:
"Sister, attend with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], am receiving this saṃkakṣikā robe;
it is four cubits in length and two and a half cubits in width. This is a saṃkakṣikā robe which I shall wear. (Recite three times.)

Regarding the *saṃkakṣikā*: its length is four spans (*vitasti*) and its width is two and a half spans. If the measurements are mutually deficient or mutually excessive, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
The principle for the *aṃśuka* (shoulder-covering garment) is likewise. The commentary states: "The term *saṃkakṣikā* refers here to a garment that is narrow at the top and wide at the bottom.
As for the term *kūrmāsaka*, because the dialects of the Western Regions differ, there are two translations; if both are cited interchangeably, [it refers to the same garment]."

The text does not contradict the underlying principle: one may fashion it according to the size of one's own body; when receiving it, one simply says, "This saṃkakṣikā has been made to measure and is fit for formal acceptance.

(This too should be valid. Originally, because nuns were criticized and looked down upon by the world for exposing their chests and shoulders, the Buddha established the rule that they should keep the saṃkakṣikā and the uttarāsaṅga—these two garments—to cover them.
The Text for Receiving the Shoulder-Covering Robe (Saṃkakṣikā).
Sister, attend with single-mindedness: I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], this is a shoulder-covering robe, made according to the Dharma;
I now receive and maintain it. (Recite three times.)
Regarding the thirteenth method for relinquishing robes: as there is no text on this in the *Mūla-vinaya*, I shall now provide it according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
[The formula for relinquishment is: "Sister, attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], this saṃghāṭī robe is counted among my five robes."
Having previously accepted [the robe], I now relinquish it (one recitation; the other two categories may be understood by analogy).
If one accepts and relinquishes at the same time, it constitutes a violation of the Vinaya.
Sister, attend with a single mind: I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], this *kūrcāra* robe has been made according to the Dharma. Previously...
"I now relinquish that which I previously undertook (one recitation).
Sister, attend with single-mindedness: I, the bhikṣuṇī [name], this shoulder-covering robe, having been made according to the Dharma, was previously undertaken;
I now relinquish it."
Furthermore, according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*:
"I, the bhikṣuṇī [name], now relinquish this saṃghāṭī robe consisting of [number] strips" (recited once).
The subsequent two types of robes should be understood by analogy with this recitation. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one goes to another's home and forgets to take the three robes along..."

Upon arriving there and having recalled [the transgression], one should discard it from afar. Having discarded it, one should temporarily borrow the robes and clothing of a layperson to perform the ritual of purification (*śuddhi*) by attaching hooks and fasteners.
The meaning of "receiving" is that it is especially virtuous for a monk to know that a member of the Saṃgha or a nun possesses an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*) and to borrow and receive it.

When intending to return it, one should discard it; once back at the original location, one may receive the old robe again without committing the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one borrows a robe and stays overnight separated from it..."
However, one need only repent for the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (the forfeiture offense) and does not need to relinquish the items again.

Regarding the fourteenth point, "Gain and Loss," the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If various bhikṣus receive other robes without relinquishing those they previously possessed, the previous three robes are still considered received;
likewise, if one has performed the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification) on them, that remains valid because they were not relinquished. One merely commits a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*)."
Regarding the offense in this Vinaya: if one has the perception that the robes have been lost, burned, stolen by thieves, or swept away by water, then the formal undertaking (*samādāna*) is lost;

in such a case, the recipient must receive them again because they were forgotten. However, there is no offense of relinquishment (*pratyākhyāna*). If, due to encountering difficult circumstances on the road, one is unable to reunite with the robes, the formal undertaking is not lost.

The *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya* (or *Po-lun*) states: "If the three robes are not formally undertaken, there are two faults: the impairment of dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) and the deficiency of the robes."

If the original *śuddhi* (purification) of a robe has already been performed, then by making it into the three robes (*tricīvara*), one loses that original *śuddhi*. Furthermore, if one discards this robe and accepts another robe, must the previous robe be purified again?
Regarding the offense of keeping an extra robe (*atireka*) for more than ten days, the *Pōlùn* (婆論) states:

"If the three robes are torn, regardless of the size of the holes, as long as the seams (*pratyanta*) are not severed, the formal possession (*dhāraṇa*) is not lost; [the same applies to] the *nivāsana* and the *saṃkakṣikā*."
The meaning of the shoulder-cloth (*aṃśuka*) is explained according to this principle.

Regarding the fifteenth [offense], "patching and washing": the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that if one patches a garment with small pieces of material and sews them back in place, it is not necessary to perform the ritual of purification (*śuddhi-vidhi*).
However, if one sews them directly [without patching], one must perform the ritual of purification for each piece; otherwise, for each piece, one incurs two offenses.
This means that one does not declare it pure nor mark it as pure. The *Śāstra* (Treatise) states:

"If a robe is about to tear but has not yet been pierced or damaged, whether it be a single strip or two strips, one should first patch it with material and later cut away the old [material]. Thus, the acceptance of the three robes is not lost.
If the back of a robe is about to tear, one should turn it so that both edges meet first; then, having joined them together, one cuts them apart with a knife, and afterwards [rejoins them]."
If one mends the edges with stitches without losing the integrity of the robe, whether by cutting away excess fabric or patching with small pieces, the formal acceptance (*parigraha*) is not lost.

Even if the color deepens through washing, the acceptance is not lost. According to this Vinaya, when the three robes are worn out, they should be repaired by patching according to the size and shape—square or round—of each hole (the same applies to the two lower robes).
Sixteenth, regarding "Veneration and Protection": The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that one should protect the three robes as one would one's own skin and the alms bowl as one would one's own eyes.
One who wears the outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) must not carry wood, stones, soil, grass, or sweepings;

nor may they step upon bedding or sitting mats with their feet, nor sit or lie upon them, nor wear them as an undergarment. If one enters a village or a layperson’s dwelling without wearing the three robes, one commits an offense.
The *Jiluo yijiao sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Bequeathed Teachings of Kātyāyana) states: "When a bhikṣu travels, his saṃghāṭī, kāṣāya, bowl, and mendicant’s staff must accompany him;
they must not be separated from his person by more than six feet. The *Wubai wenshi* (Five Hundred Questions) states:

"If one is unable to wear the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) when entering a village, it is no offense provided that one carries it on the shoulder while walking. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Revere the three robes as [one would revere the Buddha]."

When entering a village, a stūpa attendant must wear the robe with the ties fastened. If there are no ties, one should sew them on with a needle; if there is no needle, one must at least hold it by hand.
If there are ties but one enters house after house without wearing them, one incurs a *vyatikrama* offense of mental regret (*cittāpatti*).

Even if the ties are present, not wearing them also constitutes a *vinayātikrama*. When putting it on, one should cover both shoulders evenly; when holding it with the left hand, it must not remain in the hand.

The corners [of the robe] protrude like the ears of a sheep. According to the Vinaya, when one reaches the presence of the Buddha or the position of the Elder (upādhyāya), one must always bare the right shoulder;
the Sūtras state that one should wear the robe covering both shoulders. For five hundred lifetimes, one enters the Iron Armor Hell (*ayomukhāra-śastra-niraya*).

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that one obtains a four-layered great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) to use as a pillow. There are numerous passages in the *Āgama-sūtras* regarding this; it is permitted to use the great robe as a pillow while lying down on a seven-strip robe (*saptaka-cīvara*).
The *Sahasra-īryāpatha-sūtra* states: "One shall not wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* without wearing the *saṃkakṣikā*; thus, proceeding in successive layers up to the uppermost, one wears the *saṃghāṭī*.
Therefore, it is known that the three robes may be worn in layers, both above and below. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If one goes out of the village and the robe is torn by being caught on grass or wood, or if dust enters the folds, one is permitted [to wear an inner layer] for the sake of protecting the robe."

Outside the village, one should wear the robe with the folds turned outward; it is permitted to wear it with the folds turned inward when returning [to the monastery]. Hooks, buttons, and belts should be attached at the top and bottom. During rain, one should not wear it with the folds turned inward.

According to this Vinaya, a *bhikṣuṇī* commits a *pāyattika* offense if she enters the house of a layperson without wearing a *saṃkakṣikā* (breast-covering garment); [the rule for] covering the shoulders should be the same.

Furthermore, according to the *Vinayamātṛkā* and this Vinaya, one must not let the *kaṣāya* hang over a bed or step on its legs. The *Sānqiānwēiyí jīng* (Sūtra on the Three Thousand Dignified Manners) states: [same as above].

Regarding the rule that one wearing the three robes (*tricīvara*) on the lower ground may not sit upon a high seat, the *Jueding erbu vinilu* (Decisive Treatise on the Vinaya of the Two Schools) states:
"If one wears the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) when entering a village, one must not perform prostrations to teachers, monks, or elders. The *Wubai wenshi* (Five Hundred Questions) states:

"When the middle robe (*antaravāsaka*) is absent, it is permissible to wear the great robe while ascending the lecture hall; one should prostrate with the small robe (*nivasana*) not touching the body, provided it is clean."

If one does not possess a seven-strip robe, a five-strip robe may also be worn when entering the assembly for meals or performing prostrations; however, it is an offense not to wear the three robes at mealtime.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) is likewise.

Seventeenth: The Rules for the Sitting Mat (*niṣīdana*). According to this Vinaya, its length is two spans (*vitasti*) of the Buddha’s hand, and its width is one and a half spans. Its width and length [are as specified].
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* further adds that each [side] is increased by half a *vitasti* (span) and five *aṅgulas*. It states that one Buddha-span is two feet long;

according to this interpretation, the total length of the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) is five feet and its width is four feet. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that if the dimensions are mutually reduced beyond these limits, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that the four corners must be reinforced with patches; otherwise, it is permissible. This Vinaya [text] specifies that if it is made smaller than the prescribed measure, or if it is made in two layers, both cases are likewise [prohibited].
The *Dapilun* (Treatise on Obtaining) states: "Now, when using [the cloth] to spread as a bedding, the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing) says: 'One must receive and hold it;
it is not permitted to perform the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification), as the text for receiving it has not been set forth.
The present meaning is derived from this. Sister, attend with one-pointed mind: I, the Bhikṣuṇī [Name], have made this *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) according to the prescribed measure. I now receive it."
[Recite] three times. [The text for relinquishing:
Sister, attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], this niṣīdana, which I previously accepted and maintained, now relinquish.
(Recite once.)
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that one should not accept a single *niṣīdana*; to do so constitutes a *pāyattika*, and to remain separated from it overnight constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.

The *Gā-lùn* says that there is no need for forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*) nor for remaining separated overnight. The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* says that one should protect the *niṣīdana* as one protects one's own body.

The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* says that Śāriputra placed his *niṣīdana* upon his left shoulder when entering the assembly to subdue those on heterodox paths. The *Vinaya-naiḥsargika* [also records this].
The Sūtra says: "Also place it upon the shoulder. Regarding the meaning of entering the assembly to sit in meditation, it is said: "In the present day, many people place it on the left arm;
according to what is appropriate for each individual, there is no fault in this visualization.
○ Section Thirteen: Receiving the Alms Bowl.
This chapter has seven main sections: 1. The Intent of the Regulation; 2. The Substance; 3. The Color; 4.
The Measurement; 5. Receiving and Discarding; 6. Losing the Dharma; 7. Protecting the Dharma.
Regarding the first, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The alms bowl is the vessel of those who have left the household life; it is not suitable for worldly people. 10.

The recitation states: "The alms bowl is the emblem of the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; it must not be used for evil purposes. The *Zhonghan jing* (Sutra of the Middle Containment) states:

"The name 'alms bowl' (*pātra*) means 'appropriate vessel' (*saṃbhoga-bhājana*). The *Pó lùn* (Treatise on the Dharma) states: "Seeing an excellent alms bowl in a shop—perfectly round and lovely—the Vinaya Master said:

'When the Buddha first appeared in the world, the monastic community had no alms bowls. The Buddha commanded Śakra to have celestial artisans fashion one hundred thousand bowls for use in the world.'"
Regarding the bowl mentioned above, the "heavenly bowl" is not something made by humans.
Second, as for its substance, the general meaning of this Vinaya is twofold: first, clay; second, iron. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"To use a bowl of white copper or a wooden bowl such as those of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) is the practice of non-Buddhists; if one keeps such a bowl, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense."

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that one may not even make a bowl out of stone; the commentary explains that in the present day, monks and nuns also possess bowls made of porcelain, which is judged to be equivalent to stone.
Furthermore, possessing bowls made of lacquered cloth (*nāgapuṭa*) or bowls polished with oil and glazed with clay is both contrary to the Dharma;
there is no offense in breaking them.

Third, regarding the similarity of color: this Vinaya states that it should be colored by fumigation; according to the Mahāsāṃghika school, fumigating it to produce the color of a peacock’s throat or the color of a pigeon is in accordance with the Dharma.

Fourth, regarding the similarity of size: according to this Vinaya, the large bowl has a capacity of three *dou*, the small one is one and a half *dou*, and the medium vessel may be inferred accordingly.
The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "If it is less than one and a half *dōng* (斗) or exceeds three *dōng*, the meaning of 'receiving and maintaining' [the precepts] is not fulfilled. It further says:

"The measures of *shēng* (升) and *dōng* used in various regions are each inconsistent and cannot be fixed as a standard; taking ancient measures and comparing them to the present, the upper bowl receives one *dōng*, while the lower is five *shēng*;
the middle can be inferred accordingly. However, when the Buddha first appeared in the world, the human form was exceptionally large."
Because food was also abundant, [the Buddha] limited it to five *sheng* as a fixed standard. Now, in this degenerate age, human stature has gradually diminished;

if one strictly adheres to this rule, I fear it will not be practical. Thus, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "In accordance with the various regions and lands, even if it is my own teaching, there is no fault in not practicing it if it is not considered pure in that place;
conversely, even if it is not my own teaching, one must not fail to practice it if it is considered pure in other regions."
One must not use an alms bowl; it is called a "proper vessel" because it must correspond to the size of one's body, as it is intended for a standard portion of food.

The *Vinaya* (Lower Code) states: "Eat according to the capacity of the belly and wear clothing according to the measure of the body; these should be sufficient and nothing more. Seeing this judgment, one must not keep small or inferior bowls.
If a bowl is less than four *sheng* (measures), one certainly may not receive it; nor may one receive a monastic bowl that is less than five [measures].

Once [the amount] exceeds four *śu*, it cannot be established as a "held quantity" (*dhāraṇa-saṃkhyā*) because nuns and others may receive and hold amounts less than four *śu*; therefore, it is separately designated and recorded.
Regarding the fifth [category], receiving and relinquishing, there is no textual passage in this Vinaya; according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it says: [text follows].
"Venerable Sister, attend with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [name], this pātra, a vessel of proper measure, now accept and maintain it.
(Recite three times. The formula for relinquishing it is as follows:
Sister, attend with one-pointed mind: I, the bhikṣuṇī [name], this pātra, a vessel of proper measure, which I previously maintained, now relinquish (recite once).
Regarding the sixth loss of the *dharmas* (the bowl), the *Pañcaśata-praśna-vastu* states: "If for one day one does not eat using the bowl at all, one commits a *pāyattika* offense;
however, this is permitted in cases of serious illness. The *Jianlun* (Dṛṣṭānta-śāstra) states:

"If one has previously received [the bowl] and it becomes perforated like a grain of millet, the formal holding (*parigraha*) is lost. If one seals the hole with iron filings, it must be formally received again. If...

If one buys another's bowl, completes the transaction, and the owner has already fumigated it and informed the bhikṣuṇī, but she does not go to retrieve it and more than a day passes, she commits an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*).
If another person knows that it has been fumigated and applies it toward the bhikṣuṇī...

If a nun hears that food has been prepared but does not go to fetch it, there is no offense even if the day passes. According to this Vinaya, if food enters a bowl through holes or cracks, provided one merely washes it and no remaining food remains inside, there is no offense.

(Based on this principle, even if a bowl is broken but does not leak, it still constitutes valid possession. Question: If one keeps only a single bowl and does not perform the formal rite of acceptance (*parigraha*), is there an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*) when the day passes?

Answer: There is no offense. Because this regulation concerns the practice of keeping [a bowl], it is similar to the three robes; however, one does incur an offense [if the formal rite is not performed].

One must not accept even minor offenses; if one possesses two alms bowls, one must be kept in constant use while the other must be formally purified (*pariśuddha*). Otherwise, one commits an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
This seventh protection of the Dharma is such that wherever this Vinaya is practiced, the robes and alms bowl shall follow together like the feathers and wings of a flying bird.
The *Shenmu lun* (Śarīra-mātṛ-śāstra) states that when it is time to beg for alms, each person should prepare their own bowl-cord or carry their own bowl.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that one must not use ash or soil to wash [the bowl] so as to remove its color; rather, one should use the juice of tree leaves to wash it.

The *Sānqián wēiyí* (Three Thousand Rules of Deportment) states that when washing the bowl, one should use either *zǎodòu* (soap powder) or *zǎojiè* (soapberry) as the two means of purification. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* further states that one must not approach a precipice [while carrying the bowl].
When washing at a water source, one should first wash the teacher’s bowl and afterwards wash one’s own bowl. One must not pour the residual water from one’s own bowl into the teacher’s bowl;
the same applies even when washing or dyeing robes. One should not soak the teacher’s robes together with one’s own. The *Mātṛkā* states: "One should not wash one's hands inside the bowl;
one should revere it as one would one's eyes. The *Pañcavargika Vinaya* states: "Guard the bowl as you would your own eyes."
When washing the bowl, one should hold it at a distance of one chi from the ground; for a ceramic bowl, it should be placed about five or six cun above the ground in a suitable location.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that breaking a bowl with an evil intent constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense. The *Wufen lü wubai wen shi* (Five-Part Vinaya Five Hundred Questions) states that one must not place it against a wall, but should instead wrap it in a cloth and hang it upon the wall.
Chapter Fourteen: On Pure Giving (Śuddha-dāna).
This chapter has five major sections: 1. The Donor; 2. The Method of Invitation; 3. Proclaiming Purity (Śuddhi-kathana); 4. Regarding the Living and the Deceased; 5. The Loss of the Dharma.
There are two types of primary donors: first, the indirect (pāramparyā), and second, the direct (tattvika). Because the direct donor is rare, it will not be discussed here;

for now, we shall clarify the indirect method. Within this, there are five distinctions regarding the objects given: first, robes; second, medicine; third, alms bowls; fourth, precious items; and fifth, grain.
Regarding the first three types of gifts, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and the *Sudarśana-vinaya*, one may receive them from any of the five classes of monastics.
After one has become a "successive donor" (*pāramparyadāyaka*), the latter two cases both require a layperson to serve as the "pure owner" (*śuddhika*). The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"Although it is permitted to receive and keep money, precious objects, and other such items, they must necessarily be given as a 'pure gift' (*śuddhadāna*) to a donor of sincere faith. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"First, seek out a layperson who knows the Dharma to serve as the pure owner. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "There are four types of persons for whom [the practice of] successive purification is not performed."
A donor: (1) one must not praise the person; (2) one must not bestow a good reputation upon them; (3) one should give pure gifts to the five groups of monastics;
(4) one must not give to laypeople. The *Vinaya* states that one should first examine whether the recipient is observant of the precepts, learned, and virtuous before acting as a donor.
Later, when obtaining the object, one should announce the donor's name in the presence of a bhikṣuṇī and declare it as a pure gift to the Saṃgha.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, and other texts, one must not speak [of the offense] in the presence of the donor, nor should one allow the person before them to know;
rather, one should go to a separate location and speak in the presence of a single person.

Regarding the second method of requesting [confession], the practitioner should fully maintain dignified deportment and approach a renowned person of great virtue from among a group of five or more monks.
Having clarified your pure intention, you should then request as follows:
"Sister, attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [name], now request the Sister to act as my successive pure donor for robes, medicine, and alms-bowls.
May the Sister, out of compassion, act for me as a successive pure donor for robes, medicine, and alms-bowls."
Therefore, [there are three ways of requesting].
When requesting the lower three assemblies, it is not necessary to say "Venerable Sir" or "Sister," etc.; one should simply say:
"I now request the *śikṣamāṇās* and others to act as successive pure donors (*pariśuddha-dāyaka*). I pray that you will do so. [One need only state this once.]

Regarding the meaning established by this text, if one relies on the five-membered syllogism (*pañcāvayava*) and so forth, it would seem that even without being requested, [the instruction] could still be accomplished.
Next, concerning the lay donor who provides money and jewels, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "First, seek out a layperson who knows the Dharma and speak to them;
if they do not understand, instruct them until they do. Then go to that layperson and say: 'According to the rules for bhikṣuṇīs, one must not possess [such items].'"

Regarding money, jewels, grain, and so forth, one now designates the donor as the pure master (*viśuddha-dānapati*). Later, when the money and jewels are exhausted, they are all given back to the donor;
the person previously mentioned replies, "Very well.

As for the third method of declaring purity (*śuddhi-uddeśa*), the *Samantapāsādikā* states: "If the items to be declared are numerous and scattered, they should be gathered together and bound into a bundle."
Having put it on, one should then speak thus: "This *vinaya* rule requires that you go before a *bhikṣuṇī*, take hold of the robe, and say:
'Venerable Sister, attend to me with one-pointed mind. This is [the robe] of so-and-so; it is an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*) for which the purification has not yet been performed.
For the sake of purification, I give it to you, Venerable Sister, so that it may be purified through transfer. (The one who accepts the request says:)..."
"Elder, attend with one-pointed mind. You have this long robe which has not yet been purified. For the sake of purification, give it to me;
I shall now accept it. (The recipient should then say: "To whom do you bestow it? (He replies: "I bestow it upon [Name]" (referring to the name of the donor).
"Elder, attend with one-pointed mind. You possess this extra robe (*cīvara*) which has not yet been purified. For the sake of purification, I give it to you;

I now accept it. You shall give it to [Name]. This robe is the personal property of [Name]; for the sake of [Name], you must guard and maintain it well, wearing and using it according to the occasion.

(The purification regarding medicinal bowls and alms bowls should be understood by analogy with this; however, while an extra robe may be kept for ten days, a nun must purify an extra bowl on the very day she acquires it, unlike the allowance for keeping an extra robe)."

The *Pōlùn* (Treatise on the Vinaya) states that money, precious objects, grain, rice, and so forth are all treated the same as "extra robes" (*dīrgha-cīvara*) regarding the ten-day purification (*daśāha-śuddhi*).
This *Vinaya* states that one should take them to a laywoman (*upāsikā*) or a monastery attendant (*ārāmika*), and inform them, saying:
"This is my property; it is not appropriate [for you]. You should know this. This is called "declaring purity" (*śuddhi-vyākaraṇa*).

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "One declares purity through mental reflection (*manasikāra*), directly saying, 'I thus relinquish [the old] so as to receive the new,' and changes it once every ten days.

The text is not clear; here the meaning has been extracted accordingly. In the event of difficulties, a nun living alone should maintain full dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) and hold the robe in her hands.

[The procedure is as follows: "I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], have this extra robe (atirekacīvara). I perform a formal act of purification (śuddhika-dāna) by giving it to [Name] (who may give it to anyone among the five groups of monastics as they wish;
from them, I shall take it back after ten days have passed, as previously described). I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], now receive it back from [Name] (after ten days have passed, as previously described)."
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], have this extra robe. I perform a formal act of pure giving (*śuddhaka-dāna*) by bestowing it upon [Name]. May they take and use it as they see fit.
(By relinquishing it in this manner, one may receive a new one every ten days.)
Regarding the fourth point, "the living and the deceased": the *Saṃghīti* states that the donor [must be known] within a radius of three *yojanas*;

the *Pañcavargika* states that the donor must know whether [the recipient] is on the road or not; the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya* states that if the donor goes to another country, they may seek another pure donor (*śuddha-dāyaka*).
(In this Vinaya, there is no such text; thus, both applications may be used according to circumstances.)

Regarding the fifth loss of the dharma, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If one dies and seeks another donor, with the exception of money, jewels, grain, and rice, all other surplus wealth must be purified (*pariśuddha*) before the five groups of monks.
By extension of this principle, regarding money, jewels, and so forth, whether a lay donor who acts as a purifier is alive or deceased is the same as previously stated.
According to this Vinaya, there are many difficulties, such as forgetting to perform the purification or being robbed by thieves, or having the perception that they have been lost.

If one does not transgress the limit of the day, and after losing [the robe] for five days, remembers it again, one may still perform the *śuddhi* (purification/declaration) after another five days have passed.
If one obtains a robe on the tenth day and forgets to declare it by the end of that tenth day, but remembers it later, one must declare it on that very day;

otherwise, one commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one forgets [the declaration] during the latter five days, upon obtaining the forgotten robe again..."
Regarding the *Daśāha-śuddhi* (Purity for Ten Days), the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā* states:

"If one has declared the purity of wealth, treasures, or clothing, and someone later lends them—if the treasure is returned as treasure and the money as money, or even if the clothing is returned as equivalent clothing, there is no need to declare purity again.
However, if they are not equivalent, it must be declared again (because their original nature is the same and greed is minimal). If the clothing is mended but does not reach the full measure..."

Regarding those that are one chi and six cun in length and eight cun in width, these also constitute an offense for exceeding the prescribed length; thus the *Pāṇḍulohitaka-vibhaṅga* (Pāṇḍulohitika-vastu) states:

"If one first possesses clothing that does not meet the required measurements, this clothing must be entirely relinquished, and one must perform a *duṣkṛta* confession. The *Mātṛkā-vibhaṅga* (Mātṛkā-vastu) states: "If a wicked bhikṣuṇī does not perform the *śuddhi-vidhāna* (declaration of purity), it constitutes an offense as soon as the item enters her hands;
it is not necessary to wait until the tenth day. The *Pāṇḍulohitaka-vibhaṅga* further states: "If one obtains new shoes, one should have a layperson wear them [to test their fit]."
Having walked five or seven steps, one purifies the five parts; having obtained new sandals, one has a *karmadāna* (pure person) put them on and walk seven steps.
Chapter Fifteen: On the Exposition of the Precepts (*Poṣadha*).
This chapter has six major sections: 1. Time and Season; 2. Conditions for Gathering; 3. Ritual Procedures; 4. Appointments and Delegations; 5. Guests.
The six old [categories] are explained briefly.
First, regarding the time, there are five [periods]: the first, fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth days; second, after the meal.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that the uposatha may also be performed before the meal, but one incurs an offense by performing the uposatha at dawn. This is compared to what follows.

Because the Bhikṣuṇīs had not heard it, the *Gāthā-śāstra* asks: "What is the Poṣadha? It refers to the relinquishing of all evil and unwholesome dharmas, the realization of the pure dharmas, and the ultimate holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Furthermore, observing for oneself every half-month whether one has committed an offense or not, such that body and speech are pure—this is called Poṣadha.
Third, the precepts may be recited either by day or by night. Fourth, regarding increase and decrease. Fifth, regarding the improper time; the following two [points] are below.
I shall not elaborate on this here as it is well known.
Regarding the second point, the *Pratimokṣa-sūtra* in five sections states that since gathering for the *poṣadha* at improper times hinders the practice of the Path,
the Buddha ordained that specific times be established so that the *karmadāna* (the officer in charge of affairs) would rise early in the morning and inform the Saṃgha.

"Venerable Sisters, please listen. Today is the [specific day] of the waxing moon (or the [specific day] of the waning moon). The community of monks is in harmony; at such-and-such a time and in such-and-such a place, we shall recite the precepts.

I inform the Sangha so that they may know. (One announcement suffices. Nowadays, monks and nuns treat these disciplinary laws lightly; because the recitation of the precepts is often held during the darkness of night, it causes future generations to lack proper decorum.)
Regarding the third ritual: in this present section, this Vinaya is insufficient; one must supplement it by drawing from other schools (*nikāyas*).

This Vinaya states: "When the day for the recitation of the *Poṣadha* arrives, the Elder (*sthavira*) should command the nuns, the male novices (*śrāmaṇera*), and the female novices (*śrāmaṇerī*) to sweep and sprinkle the Buddha-stūpas and the monastic courtyards, to have the high and low places leveled with mud, and to prepare various famous flowers in sets of five or three on platters."
Regarding the one or two bronze bowls for incense: nowadays, many people use these as food vessels or almsbowls to hold hot water;

The śrāmaṇerikās and others were all permitted to enter the hall and receive voting sticks (*śalākā*).
According to this Vinaya’s *Śīlaskandha-vibhaṅga*, śrāmaṇerikās are allowed to listen; however, according to other schools, they are not. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"When distributing voting sticks, if one asks the donor about the number of monks and does not know the total count, or if one distributes voting sticks and does not know the number of śrāmaṇeras, one should also have voting sticks distributed for them. If a person...

Regarding the distribution of *poṣadha* items, even a *śrāmaṇera* is entitled to receive his share. Although he does not go to the place where the *poṣadha* ritual is performed, because he receives a voting tally (*śalākā*), he also obtains a portion.

According to this Vinaya, since the distribution of tallies for receiving offerings applies universally to *śrāmaṇeras*, the same principle holds for the two groups of nuns (as indicated by "ni" below).
The tally must be at least as short as five fingers joined together, at most one cubit (*hasta*) in length, no thicker than the little finger, and no thinner than a chopstick.
Upon first entering the hall, one should first bare the right shoulder, remove one’s shoes and sandals, and join the palms to pay homage.
If one fears that the crowd will be too noisy and that it will be impossible to perform each individual prostration, one may simply bow the body and enter from the side, taking one's seat in order.

Recently, I have frequently observed monks and nuns at laypeople’s vegetarian feasts who, while seated upon their mats, perform prostrations to the Buddha and search through all the sūtras and vinayas.

I ask the virtuous masters of the Western lands: how can this lack of ritual propriety be anything other than sheer indolence? To prioritize physical ease while failing to maintain respect only invites self-reproach;
how can such conduct lead to the seeking of merit? When a subject bows to a sovereign, how could one remain upon a couch? Even a "King of Men" does not permit it;
how much less could a "Dharma King" allow such a practice to be casually adopted? Thus, the *Sāhasrika-vaipulya-vinaya-sūtra* states: "A bhikṣu must not sit upon a seat [while receiving offerings]."

Having performed prostrations, when first entering the hall, one should recite this verse: "Maintaining the precepts with purity like the full moon, Body and speech are bright and stainless, free from blemish;
The great assembly is in harmony, without conflict or dispute— Only then can the *poṣadha* be observed together.

Having spoken this verse, each person sits according to their rank. A junior nun arises to prepare the incense-water and pure water; when the assembly is large, three or five nuns are assigned to this task.
When the *bhikṣuṇīs* assist in performing the ritual, each must bare the right shoulder, remove their sandals and shoes, and fully maintain dignified decorum.
The *karmadāna* first takes fragrant water to wash his hands and bathes the counting sticks (*śalākā*). He may also bathe himself at the place where the silence is struck;

The Arhats and noble monks assembled, and together with the assembly of ordinary beings, they prepared fragrant bathing water for purification and arranged the voting sticks (*śalākā*) for the *poṣadha* ceremony to deliver sentient beings.
Having spoken this verse, he commanded a young nun to distribute the fragrant bathing water and pure water.

First, she distributed the pure water while also using a clean cloth to wipe their hands until dry. While receiving the water, he again spoke a verse, saying: "The water of eight virtues purifies all..."

Washing the hands and rinsing the mouth to remove impurities, the mind remains free from defilement and attachment; one upholds the prohibitive precepts without any transgression, and all sentient beings likewise act in this way.

The assembly descends from their seats. Each person shall, in turn, receive a tally according to the Dharma (reciting this three times; for śikṣamāṇās and śrāmaṇerīs, there is no need to call out [their names], but they must wait until the *karmavācanā* has been heard before calling them out).
When the recitation is finished, the *karmadāna* comes before the *sthavira*, kneels on his right knee, and hands the voting tally (*śalākā*) to the *sthavira*.
Then, all the monks follow the *sthavira* in a single file, kneeling with palms joined. As they are about to take the tally, one should recite this verse:
"The indestructible, unimpeded tally of liberation is difficult to obtain and difficult to encounter; now that I have attained it, I joyfully receive it upon my head."
The reception of all sentient beings was likewise. When it was time to return the voting sticks (*śalākā*), he again spoke a verse, saying:
"Possessing complete purity, receive this stick; possessing complete purity, return this stick. With firm joy and equanimity, without transgression—may all sentient beings be likewise.
Having spoken thus, he immediately gave them to others, who returned to their original seats. In this manner, they passed the sticks on in succession until they reached the Great [Assembly].
The *karmadāna* comes to the place of silence and stands there; he hands the counting sticks (*śalākā*) to the *sthavira*, and may either count them himself or have the *karmadāna* count them.
Having finished counting, he strikes for silence and proclaims:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, please listen. Next, the voting sticks for the śikṣamāṇās and śrāmaṇerīs shall be distributed.

After this has been said three times, one goes to where the śikṣamāṇās and others are, distributes the sticks, and once the distribution is finished, collects them and hands them to the presiding elder (upādhyāya).
Once the counting is complete, the karmadāna takes them all back, returns to a place of silence, stands there, and announces:

Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen. At this single residence, for the purpose of a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa, there are [number] bhikṣuṇīs, [number] śikṣamāṇās, and [number] śrāmaṇerikās, totaling [number] persons. Each is pure and has gone forth from the household life.
In unison, we shall recite the precepts. Above, this accords with the Buddha’s teachings; in the middle, it repays the four debts of gratitude; and below, it is for the sake of all sentient beings.
Each of you should recite from within the sutras these pure and wondrous verses (once).
The assembly of monks simultaneously joined their palms and recited this verse:
"Pure as the full moon, pure is the attainment of the poṣadha; when the actions of body and speech are pure, only then should one perform the poṣadha.
(This is from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.)
Having cast the tally, that karmadāna approaches the senior monk (sthavira), performs three prostrations, and addresses the senior monk, saying:
"The community of monks is in harmony; we request the Venerable Sister to recite the Vinaya for the assembly."
If the Elder speaks for himself, he says: "This precept-law is correctly recited by [Name]; [Name] shall recite it himself.
The Karmadāna, following the Elder’s instruction, must then chant it. If he is unable to do so, he should say: "The recitation of the precepts is entrusted to [Name];
however, because I am old and weak and my speech is muddled and foul, I fear it would delay the proceedings and disturb the Sangha."
Having requested a person among the assembly who is capable of reciting [the text], the *karmadāna* (Vina) should prostrate once more and then rise to go before the second *sthavira*.

There, he should inquire as before, no differently. (The preceding dialogue should be conducted in a voice loud enough for the assembly to hear; one must not speak in a whisper or produce signs of ill-will.
If the second *sthavira* is unable, one should simply request a person capable of reciting, without the need for further circumlocution down the line. Therefore, the Sangha...
Ji said: "Whether it be the senior elder (upādhyāya) or the next elder, they should recite; if one is unable, then one who is able to recite should be appointed to speak.
Once appointed, he shall strike the signal of silence and announce:
'May the Sisters of the Saṃgha listen! The Saṃgha appoints the Vinaya Master [Name] to recite the precepts for the Saṃgha. The Vinaya Master [Name], with a pure voice.'"
Ascending the high seat (one version says).
Once the monks have selected [the candidate], the Vinaya Master should rise, assume the full observance of dignified demeanor, proceed to the midst of the assembly, spread out his sitting mat,
perform prostrations toward the four directions, and then, kneeling with long knees, address the assembly as follows:
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], prostrate myself and pay homage, respectfully addressing the Saṃgha: I have been appointed by the Saṃgha to recite the Vinaya, yet I fear there may be errors.
I pray that those who recite together with me will generously grant their guidance and instruction.
Having finished the announcement, he performs another prostration and then ascends the seat.

The *vina* sprinkles the remaining scented water to the left and right, leaving a vacant space in the center for people to pass through; the same applies to the incense and flowers, which are to be scattered gradually.
When scattering the flowers, each person recites a verse as follows:
Scattering flowers to adorn the pure radiance, they form canopies of adorned jewel-flowers;
scattering various precious blossoms throughout the ten directions, they make offerings to all Tathāgatas (as cited from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra).
Having finished speaking, the *karmadāna* strikes for silence; those who are junior provide offerings while those with good voices perform the *brahman* chants.

When performing the *brahman* chants, one should recite the two-line verse beginning with "I prostrate and pay homage to all Buddhas. When it comes time to offer incense and recite verses, the Sangha simultaneously joins their palms and says:

The fragrance of precepts, the fragrance of meditative concentration, and the fragrance of liberation—clouds of radiant light pervading the entire Dharma-realm—make offerings to the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions;
those who see or hear them are universally perfumed and realize quiescent extinction. (This is from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.)

Although the offerings have concluded, the *karmadāna* must remain standing. When the preceptor recites until those who have not yet received full ordination have departed, the preceptor should pause his recitation to allow the *śikṣamāṇās* and *śrāmaṇerīs* to exit.

The *śikṣamāṇās* and others should then assume their proper dignified demeanor (*īryāpatha*), approach the Saṃgha, perform three prostrations, and remain kneeling for a long time to receive the instructions from the presiding elder.

The Elder shall inform the śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇerīs, and others: "Since your years are not yet sufficient and your practice is not yet complete, you are unfit to enter the number of the Saṃgha for formal acts (karmavācanā).

You must listen to the recitation of the precepts together with us; wait until your years are sufficient and your practice is complete, and after you have received full ordination (upasampadā), you shall then be permitted to participate in the recitation of the precepts.
Each of you should return to your respective places and engage in quiet reflection, chanting, and recitation."
Once the assembly has dispersed, one should then employ skillful means to perform one additional prostration and exit in order of seniority.

If the *śikṣamāṇās* and others have separate places for reciting the precepts, this [additional prostration] is not required. When the Precept Master calls out, "Let those who have not come speak their consent (*chanda*)," the Karmadāna replies, "The consent has already been spoken.
If there are no persons present to speak their consent, he should reply, "There is no one here to speak their consent. (If one wishes to appoint a teacher of nuns...)
The messenger and the preceptor should wait until the Sangha has appointed a messenger, and then inquire as described above.

Regarding the fourth point concerning the appointment of a messenger, the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Observation) states: "Initially, because women possess dull faculties, it was permitted for Bhikṣuṇīs to go to the Bhikṣu-saṃgha’s monastery to receive instruction.
Later, because people criticized this, the Bhikṣus went to the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha’s monastery to instruct the Bhikṣuṇīs. This should be done accordingly.
On the day of the *poṣadha*, when the Saṃgha has assembled, one asks for the consent (*chanda*) and inquires of the Saṃgha, saying:
"The Saṃgha is now in harmony; what shall we perform? They reply: "We shall perform the *karmavācanā* for appointing a person to provide instruction."
Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen. If the time for the Sangha has come, may the Sangha grant its consent.
We now appoint the bhikṣuṇī [Name] to go, on behalf of the bhikṣuṇī Saṅgha, once every half-month to the community of bhikṣus to request instruction for the bhikṣuṇīs. This is the formal motion.

Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen. The Sangha now appoints the bhikṣuṇī [Name] to go, for the sake of the bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, once every half-month to the assembly of bhikṣus to request instruction for the bhikṣuṇīs.

Which venerable sisters approve of the Sangha’s appointment of the bhikṣuṇī [Name] to go, for the sake of the bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, once every half-month to the assembly of bhikṣus to request instruction for the bhikṣuṇīs?
Those who consent remain silent; those who do not consent speak. The Saṃgha has consented.
A bhikṣuṇī named [Name] has been appointed for the sake of the bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha to go every half-month to the assembly of bhikṣus to seek instruction.
The motion having been completed, and because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
According to this Vinaya *karmavācanā*, once one person has been appointed, two others should be appointed from outside to accompany him as his associates when he goes before the Saṃgha.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If a nun gives instructions, she should instruct the master of the house.

If the monks are not ill and possess wisdom and clarity regarding the Vinaya, on the day of the *poṣadha*, the Bhikṣu-saṃgha should appoint one person in advance to receive the instructions from the nuns at the door of their quarters."
If a nun comes while he is sitting alone on his bed, she should stand before the Buddha hall; when other monks see her, they should point out the location where the nun is to be entrusted.
When this nun arrives before the room, the bhikṣu should go to his bed and sit down, taking one bhikṣu as a companion.
After the nun has performed three prostrations, she should bend her body and join her palms, saying:

"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. The community of nuns of [Name] Monastery is in harmony. For half a month, we prostrate at the feet of the bhikṣu-saṃgha and request a person to provide instruction for the nuns. (Recite this three times.)

After the bhikṣu has received the entrustment from the bhikṣuṇī, he says: "Tonight, at the time for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), I shall inquire of the Saṃgha whether [the assembly] is present or not.
He then asks the bhikṣuṇīs whether they wish to invite [the Saṃgha] individually or to invite according to the sequence of the monks;

he acts in accordance with their reply. Furthermore, he informs them: "Come early tomorrow morning," and asks whether it is acceptable, making the bhikṣuṇīs respond accordingly. He then performs another prostration.
She then returned to the *saṃghāṭī* (monastery) and said: "When a nun enters a monastery of monks, she should first stand beneath the gatehouse and announce her presence to the bhikṣus.

The bhikṣus should then assess whether her conduct is appropriate; if the nun is virtuous and well-behaved, she may enter without incident. If she is properly attired and equipped with her requisites, she is permitted to enter; otherwise, she is not permitted.
When the nun returns the following day, she should follow the same protocol as before and announce: 'Last night, the Saṃgha was assembled.'"
At that time, having fully conveyed the request, there was no bhikṣuṇī who could provide instruction, nor was there anyone skilled in preaching the Dharma.
Nevertheless, the Elder issued a command to the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, saying: "You must be diligent and energetic, practicing the Path according to the Dharma; be prudent and do not be negligent.

The bhikṣuṇīs joined their palms and said, "We shall receive and uphold this with reverence," and after bowing, they withdrew. Upon arriving at their own monastery, they were required to immediately strike the bell.
The bell is struck to assemble the community; those who do not come must announce their *chanda*. The nuns all gather within the hall and stand in order according to seniority.
The appointed nun stands before the head of the assembly, strikes for silence, and speaks as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, please listen. The Saṃgha has appointed me, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], to go among the bhikṣu-saṃgha to request a person to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.

Yet, there is no one in the Saṃgha who has already been authorized to instruct, nor is there anyone skilled in preaching the Dharma. Nevertheless, by the command of the Elder, I shall speak to the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs:
'You should be diligent and energetic, practicing the Path according to the Dharma; be careful and do not be negligent.'"

The assembly of bhikṣuṇīs all joined their palms at once and said: "We shall uphold [this] with reverence. We have extracted from the *Pañcavargika*, the *Daśabhāṇavāra*, and the *Mahāsāṃghika* Vinayas.
At present, these abbreviated methods are widely practiced because the extensive versions are difficult to employ; therefore, they have not been set forth here. Regarding this Vinaya:

if the entire community of bhikṣus is ill, one should send a messenger to perform prostrations and offer greetings; even if a separate group is incomplete in number, one should likewise dispatch a messenger to inquire after them.
Regarding the inquiry and salutation when the assembly of nuns is incomplete:

the meaning is that if there are five or more individuals among both the monks and nuns, and if among the monks there is one who has twenty years of seniority (*vassa*), these two methods—the extensive and the abbreviated—may be performed.
If the assembly is insufficient, one should simply perform the salutation and inquiry and then conclude. Next, the Preceptor of the Precepts asks the assembly:

"The Saṃgha is now in harmony; what shall we do? The Karmadāna replied, "We shall perform the *jñapti-karman* for the recitation of the precepts" (*śīla-vinaya*). (In the present day, many reply, "The *poṣadha* recitation of the precepts";
however, this response does not apply to a formal *karman*, as it would likely be contrary to the Dharma.)
The Preceptor should wait until the *karmadāna* has taken his seat before making the formal announcement (*jñapti*);

for if it were done while he is not yet seated, there would be discrepancies between those sitting and those standing, which would surely constitute the fault of a separate assembly (*pṛthag-saṃgha*). When the recitation of the precepts is finished, the *karmadāna* strikes the bell three times to inform outsiders that the recitation of the precepts is complete.
Then the *brahmacārin* recites the verses following the introduction to the Vinaya, chanting as follows:
The divine immortals and those with the five supernatural powers devised incantations and spells; for the sake of those who possess a sense of shame, they restrained those who lack it.
The Tathāgata established the prohibitions and precepts, reciting them every half-month. Having explained the benefits of the precepts, I prostrate in homage to all Buddhas.

The *Vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "One must not perform only half of a *bhāṣya*; to do so constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one does not understand the previous portion of the *bhāṣya*, it is permissible to recite the 'Worldly Bhāṣya' (*lokabhāṣya*) instead;
there is no need to labor over the 'Tathāgata Brahma-bhāṣya'. Once the Preceptor has descended from his seat and entered among the assembly, he bows in thanks, saying:
"I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], prostrate myself in salutation (*namas*). I respectfully thank the Sangha for appointing me to recite the Vinaya through the three karmas."
It was not done with diligence; there are many errors. I pray that the assembly will be compassionate and grant me their joyful approval.
Having finished speaking, the members of the Sangha should each recite a verse of self-congratulation, saying:

The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is the foremost joy; hearing the Dharma and practicing it with diligence brings the joy of peace and security; the harmony of the great assembly brings the joy of tranquility;
and sentient beings’ liberation from suffering brings the joy of deliverance.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states in verse:
"The appearance of the Buddhas is bliss; the teaching of the True Dharma is also bliss. The harmony of the great assembly is bliss; the gathering of those who have gone forth is bliss."

Thereafter, the three refuges are chanted and the assembly disperses (there are also those great virtuous ones who say that once the recitation of the precepts is finished, the Elder should perform the *poṣadha* blessing according to what is appropriate to the occasion, though there is no formal scriptural authority for this).
The fifth question: May a visiting nun (*āgantukī bhikṣuṇī*) who wishes to hear the precepts enter from outside the boundary? Answer: This Vinaya permits it for both residents and visitors.
When a visiting nun enters, she must not arrive at the place where the recitation of the precepts is to take place before the others, lest she disrupt their recitation.
She should wait until they have finished reciting the introduction (*nidāna*) and have asked, "Is this assembly pure? Then the visiting nun may join according to her seniority.

Having entered and paid homage, one should sit according to seniority and listen to the recitation of the precepts. If the Preceptor for Recitation sees a visiting nun arrive, he must immediately cease the recitation;

if he does not cease it, the visiting nun must reprimand him and stop it while waiting for the guest nun to be seated. Once the guest nun is seated, the recitation should proceed in order from that point.
