When the introduction has been finished and the recitation of the precepts is completed, one should enter among the assembly, pay homage to the Sangha by bowing in the four directions, and then remain kneeling while one person makes an announcement.
"Pure Clouds," [the preceptor] says: "Sisters of the Great Assembly, listen! The bhikṣuṇīs such-and-so, numbering so many, are all pure. (This is stated once.

Having made this announcement, they sit according to their order. The Preceptor for the Precepts follows the prescribed formula. If there are those who are not pure, each one is to be informed individually, saying:
Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, please listen. The bhikṣuṇī [Name] has committed a certain offense. Because she was pressured, she did not confess it during the recitation of the precepts;
she shall later perform the confession according to the Dharma.

Having finished speaking, one continues the discourse according to the preceding text. If many or an equal number of visiting nuns arrive, even if the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* has already concluded, one must have the host recite it again from the beginning;
if she does not recite it, she shall be dealt with according to the law. The Vinaya states: "If there are many, one should recite it again. Question:
When the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* has reached its midpoint, if one wishes to leave because of some necessity, may one do so? Answer: If there is a necessary reason, one must indeed leave.

It is said that if one wishes to go [to another monastery] but there is no one among the assembly capable of reciting the precepts, then on the day of the *poṣadha*, following the previous ritual procedure, one should simply appoint one person to preach the Dharma, recite the sūtras, and deliver the various exhortations, after which they may disperse. The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states:
"If one is of dull faculties and ignorant, and cannot go to another monastery to preach, one should at least recite a single verse."
Commit no evil; practice all that is good; purify your own mind—this is the teaching of all Buddhas. I pay homage to the Noble Assembly.

Having performed this, one may then disperse; it is improper not to recite [the precepts]. If, while on the seat for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), one recalls having committed an offense, one must immediately confess it through mental recollection, saying:
"I, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], have committed such-and-such an offense. I shall perform the confession according to the Dharma once the recitation of the precepts is concluded.
Having done so, I may then listen to the precepts. If one has doubts regarding an offense, one should reflect as follows:
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], have a doubt regarding a certain matter. I shall resolve it and perform the confession after the recitation of the precepts.
If one remembers having committed an offense before the recitation of the precepts, one should confess it; only after the confession has been made may one hear the Dharma of the precepts.
Regarding the sixth point, the brief exposition: if this *vinaya* encounters any of the eight difficulties—such as kings, thieves, water, fire, the sick, non-humans, or evil insects;

or if the assembly is large while seats are few; or if many are ill; or if it rains; or if there is strife; or if the night has grown long—due to such circumstances, the recitation of the precepts is permitted to be abbreviated.
The preceptor shall weigh the nature of these difficulties, whether they are imminent or distant, and observe whether the time is early or late.

If the assembly is large and distant, after explaining the three introductory sections, the remainder may be omitted. If the assembly is nearby, or due to circumstances such as illness or fever, one should explain the introduction and then omit the rest.
How is it omitted? After reciting the introduction to the *Prātimokṣa* and asking whether the members are pure, one should say:

Venerable sisters, these eight *pārājika* rules have been regularly heard by the Saṃgha. ... [omitted] ... Venerable sisters, these seven methods for settling disputes have been regularly heard by the Saṃgha.

From this point forward, it must be explained in detail. However, if a crisis should suddenly arise, one may recite only the introduction and then say, "The rest has been heard by the Sangha as usual.

If even the introduction cannot be recited, one should say: "On such-and-such a day, at the time of the *poṣadha* for the recitation of the precepts, let each member of the Sangha rectify their body, speech, and mind;
be diligent and do not be negligent. (Having said this, they may disperse. If the leader of the assembly is skilled at governing the community, whenever the assembly is at its height...

In summer or winter, when the weather is extreme and there are monks who are elderly, weak, or afflicted by cold and heat, the *karmadāna* (Venerable of Affairs) should briefly recite the *Prātimokṣa*.
When the assembly gathers at dawn, the *karmadāna* announces: "On this day for the recitation of the precepts, the weather is intensely hot or extremely cold; I fear the Sangha may become exhausted.
The great assembly should gather early so that I may perform a brief recitation. Do not fabricate excuses or give rise to weariness and indolence. If one conducts the ceremony in such a manner...
The assembly is also called "skillfully governing the great multitude," for their minds are free from sorrow or regret.

If the fivefold requirements for performing a *karmavācanā* are met but the Saṃgha cannot reach harmony, one should perform it prior to the *poṣadha*; since the *poṣadha* is a formal regulation of the Saṃgha, the assembly dares not disperse.

Next, to clarify the procedure for individuals: if there are two or more persons at the place of residence, they should sweep and sprinkle the area by the time of the recitation of the precepts (poṣadha), prepare the requisites for the uposatha exactly according to the previous ritual, and wait for visiting nuns to arrive.
If there are four or more people, a full recitation must be performed; if there are two or three people, they should each recite to one another, saying: [as follows].
"Venerable Sister, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. Today is the fifteenth day for the Sangha’s recitation of the precepts.
I, the Bhikṣuṇī [Name], am pure. (Recite this three times.
If addressing two nuns, one should say: "Venerable Sisters, please attend to me with one-pointed minds... The remaining words are the same as above. If there is only one person, one should...
"I now declare that on the fifteenth day, I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], am pure. (Recite three times.
*The Bhikṣuṇī-śrāmaṇeraka of the Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Fascicle Upper, Part Two;
*The Bhikṣuṇī-śrāmaṇeraka of the Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Fascicle Middle, Part One.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan of Zhongnan Mountain.
Chapter Sixteen: On the Summer Retreat (*Varṣā*).
This chapter has eight major sections: 1. The Intent of the Regulation; 2. The Time of the Settlement; 3. Summer Intercalary Months; 4. Facing the Head [of the Sangha]; 5. The Mind.

"Mindfulness of the six [rules], forgetting which constitutes the seventh; and the eighth concerns the boundary and the shifting of the summer retreat. Regarding the first point concerning the regulation of the mind:
this Vinaya universally regulates all three seasons, yet its intent lies in compassion for sentient beings. Furthermore, it specifically focuses on the summer months due to three types of faults:

first, wandering about without purpose hinders the cultivation of the path and one's practice; second, it causes injury to living beings, which violates the spirit of loving-kindness (*maitrī*); and third, [it leads to] the accumulation of various transgressions.
In reality, the three reasons for this are as follows: since it would otherwise incur worldly censure and reproach, the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) was established to prevent these three faults.

Regarding the second point, the time of the formal commencement (*bandhana*): although this Vinaya mentions three periods—early, middle, and late—according to the actual text of the procedure, there are strictly two.
That is to say, commencing on the sixteenth day of the fourth month is the "early" period, while from the seventeenth day onwards until the fifteenth day of the fifth month constitutes the other.
Regarding the period from the sixteenth day onwards, all agree that the subsequent single day is designated as the "prior" (pūrva) and the twenty-ninth day as the "subsequent" (paścima).

In this Vinaya, for the Mahāsaṃghika Bhikṣus, failing to enter the prior retreat constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense; for the Bhikṣuṇīs, failing to enter the prior retreat likewise constitutes a *duṣkṛta*, while failing to enter the subsequent retreat constitutes a *pāyattika*.

Furthermore, failing to observe the retreat according to the Mahāsaṃghika rules also constitutes a *pāyattika*. The Abhidharmakośabhāṣya states: "One may enter the retreat in a place free from five faults: first, [the fault of] being too large..."

1. It is difficult to obtain the necessities one requires when seeking them from afar in a village settlement. 2. If it is too close to a city, it will hinder the practice of the path and its cultivation.

3. If there are many ants and mosquitoes, it causes harm to both oneself and others. 4. There must be someone upon whom one can rely; such a person must possess five virtues: i. To seek what has not been heard and cause it to be heard; ii.

To cause what has already been heard to become pure and refined; iii. To be able to resolve the net of doubts; iv. To master both the Way and secular affairs without obstruction; v. [To possess the remaining virtue of being capable of providing guidance.]
There are five obstacles for which one may not enter the rains retreat (*varṣā*): harboring wrong views; having attained right view; being without a donor to provide medicine and food;
and these other three [obstacles]. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a relative invites a bhikṣuṇī, she should first instruct them to invite a bhikṣu;

if they are unwilling, she must not accept the invitation. The *Samantapāsādikā* states: "A bhikṣuṇī may observe the rains retreat within half a yojana of a bhikṣu’s residence; if she exceeds this distance, it is not permitted."

If, during the preceding summer retreat, a donor has invited a bhikṣu for the sake of a bhikṣuṇī, but the bhikṣuṇī has already completed her retreat, or if the bhikṣu has not come due to some circumstance at the beginning of the subsequent summer retreat, he should invite another bhikṣu to come.
If another cannot be obtained, and there are difficulties on the road, he may remain in retreat. If, having completed the initial retreat, the bhikṣu has a matter of business...
After the *bhikṣuṇī* has departed, one should realize that those who have already entered the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) may not move away; they may remain there without fault.

When the summer retreat concludes, one must not perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation ceremony) in a place where no *bhikṣu* is present; one should seek out a location where the ritual can be performed.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, even if one is in the *varṣā* alone with a single *bhikṣu*, one should inquire about the *poṣadha* at the half-month interval; if no such person is available, one should go three *yojanas*.

Because the internal community collectively establishes the boundary for inclusion, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "There was a bhikṣu who did not himself uphold the Vinaya nor rely on one who upheld the Vinaya;

while observing the summer retreat (*varṣā*), he experienced doubts and had no place to inquire. Thereupon the Buddha said: 'One should observe the summer retreat relying on a place where there is one who upholds the Vinaya.
If the dwelling is cramped, it is permitted to go to the vicinity of the Vinaya-holder once every seven days for a round trip, remaining at a distance within that area.'"

Regarding the *Prātimokṣa-vinaya*, it states that based on the rainy season retreat (*vassa*), one may go to ask questions; this does not apply to those who do not rely on the extensive recitation of the two divisions of the Vinaya masters, for whom such an act would incur a *thullaccaya* offense.
The meaning is that even great monks (*bhikṣu*) and men are required to dwell in the presence of a Vinaya master, and whenever they have doubts, they must go to consult him.
It is like an infant who cannot be separated from its nurse for even a moment, lest it incur sin and be drowned in the deep current; so too is it now with the community of nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*).
In their dealings with affairs, they lack discernment and constantly deviate from the prescribed rules; their dispositions are dull and stagnant, and they take pleasure in worldly customs.
Wandering alone at will, they do not uphold the precepts; sometimes they reside in remote monasteries on the frontiers, or stand isolated in bustling cities where no other monks dwell.
Consequently, their movements lack benevolence and their gait violates propriety; the Eight Respectful Precepts are rarely heard of among them, nor are their three karmas purified.

To merely add the sting of a bee or a scorpion, to treat the laity with the reverence due to a *śrāmaṇera* while conversely showing arrogance toward one's own *ācārya*, and to act as a teacher to one's own disciple—when I reflect quietly upon these matters, I truly feel deep indignation.

Regarding the intercalary month during the third summer retreat: if the intercalary month falls in the fifth or sixth month, the ninety-day *varṣā* (rainy season) retreat will certainly last one hundred and twenty days. If the intercalary...
Regarding the fourth month: from the sixteenth day of the fourth month until the first day of the intercalary month, those who have completed their retreat all remain for the fourth month.
If they complete it from the second day of the intercalary month onwards, the duration gradually decreases because they have exceeded the intercalary month.

If they complete it from the first day of the fifth month up to the sixteenth day, they all remain for three months. If there is an intercalary seventh month, [the calculation] begins from the fourth...
Those who enter the retreat on the sixteenth day of the month or on the first day of the fifth month shall remain for three full months, as the intercalary month has not yet arrived.
Those who enter the retreat from the second day of the fifth month onward shall remain for four months, because the ninety-day period is not yet complete when including the intercalary month.
Fourth, having properly cultivated the deportment in the presence of a single nun, one says:
"Sister, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], am observing the three-month summer retreat at a certain monastery.
This is for the purpose of repairing dilapidated rooms" (recite this three times).
In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the person before him replies, "Do not be negligent. He answers, "I shall uphold it.
Furthermore, when asked, "Upon whom do you rely to uphold the Vinaya? he replies, "The Master So-and-so. [The teacher] tells him, "If you have doubts, you should go and ask him.

If he intends to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*) in a village, in the mountains, or under a tree, he must then change his previous [intention of staying at] a monastery and relinquish his quarters.
Regarding the words for "breaking" and "preparing," it is stated directly:
"Sister, attend with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], now rely upon a certain household in a certain village for the three-month summer retreat (recite this three times)."
Some may say they observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*) based on the Emperor’s domain, or that they observe it based on the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);

none of these are valid, and one instead incurs the offense of ignorance and lack of training. Why, then, is it required to repair and maintain the dwellings within a monastery? The answer is: the maintenance of monastic quarters serves to benefit three periods of time;
what was prepared by those of the past is utilized by those of the present, and [what is maintained] by those of the present [will be used by those of the future].

One should repair [the dwelling] in preparation for the future; if it is not maintained, the continuity of the three periods will be severed. For one who enters the later summer retreat, one should say:
"Sister, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], shall observe the summer retreat for the next three months at this certain monastery (*saṃghārāma*).
This is for the purpose of repairing the dilapidated rooms" (recite this three times).
Regarding the fifth mental reflection: it was considered improper for a bhikṣuṇī to perform this mental reflection;

however, according to the *Daśādhyāya-vinaya*, during times of famine, it was permitted for a bhikṣuṇī to rely on a relative and dwell alone, which is why this specific passage is set forth. Having fully observed the proper deportment, she approached the Buddha and said:
If a bhikṣuṇī named [Name] now relies upon a certain village and a certain household for the three-month summer retreat (recited three times).

Regarding the sixth point concerning "forgetting" and "accomplishing": according to this Vinaya, "forgetting" refers to not having the mental intention; if one has come specifically for the sake of the retreat, it constitutes the formal establishment of the retreat.
As for the statement "having come," there is concern that those who have long resided [there] may not be permitted [to count as newly arriving]. If they are long-resident persons...

One must observe this period during the summer retreat; if one forgets and fails to announce it, one must still measure the distance traveled. Furthermore, if a visiting nun does not perform beneficial services, this [period] is not established.
Regarding the seventh point, the boundary (*sīmā*): this Vinaya states that (1) one foot enters the boundary, (2) both feet enter the boundary, and (3) one...
If one places both feet within the monastery, or if the light of dawn appears in the east while one is entering, it is not said that those who come from outside fail to fulfill [the requirement].

Regarding the eighth point, the "shifting of the summer retreat" (*varṣā-cāra*), this Vinaya recognizes two kinds of obstacles: namely, the obstacle of life (*jīvita-vighna*) and the obstacle of the holy life (*brahmacarya-vighna*). First is the obstacle of life.

This refers to spirits, ghosts, thieves, and the like, as well as predatory beasts and venomous insects, who—unable to obtain food, drink, medicine, or servants at their will—if one were to dwell peacefully here, would take one’s life.
Therefore, the Vinaya states: "If I remain here, it will surely create obstacles for my life.

Thus, the Buddha permitted those in these two kinds of *brahmacarya*-obstacles (the first being the aforementioned) to depart. Regarding the second *brahmacarya*-obstacle: this refers to being seduced by a man.

If one fears violating a grave precept, the Buddha also permits departure. Once arrived at that place, if the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) is to be established, one must diligently seek a place to reside from the very day of departure.
Until such a residence is obtained, even if one stays overnight, the *varṣā* is not broken, as this is not due to a deliberate intention of negligence or contempt.
Conversely, if the opposite occurs, it is not established; once a residence is secured, the rules of the summer retreat follow accordingly.
If one eats there, one cannot leave the boundary without cause, fearing that it would violate the rules of the summer retreat (*varṣā*).

If there is no difficulty at the original location, one likewise may not return, because the boundary has already been established. According to this Vinaya, if two difficulties arise while observing the summer retreat at a lay residence, one should inform the donor (*dānapati*) and seek to move elsewhere.
Whether the donor consents or not, one should simply depart on one’s own. According to other schools, it is not stated that one loses the status of having completed the summer retreat (*varṣā*).
Now, according to the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, one obtains the summer retreat; thus the treatise states that "shifting the summer [location] does not break the *anvaya*. Question:

If one encounters circumstances and leaves the boundary, spending the night there and forgetting to receive the formal authorization (*jñapti*) for the seven-day period, does one obtain the summer retreat? Answer: None of the various schools have a textual ruling on this matter.

Only the *Pañcaśata-praśna-vastu* states: "If during the summer one forgets to receive the seven-day authorization and goes outside the boundary, but remembers and immediately repents upon returning, one obtains the merit of a single sitting (*ekāsana*)."

Question: If one exceeds three days of absence without formal leave (*kṣānti*), does the *varṣa* (rainy-season retreat) not become valid? Furthermore, if one encounters circumstances and goes outside the boundary, only to find the way blocked by water or land, or otherwise interrupted by various obstacles such that one cannot return to the original boundary, is the *varṣa* lost?

Answer: There is no textual ruling on this point in the various schools (*nikāya*). However, the Great Virtuous Ones of antiquity, having weighed the meaning of the Tripiṭaka, established that the *varṣa* may still be obtained under certain conditions:
if it was for the benefit of the Triple Gem, or for matters concerning friends or major affairs, and one did not exceed [the permitted time], then the *varṣa* is not lost.
Regarding the "Elements" (dhātu): by opening up [the discussion of] other mundane and useless matters, one will not doubt the breaking of the summer retreat.
Chapter Seventeen: On Receiving the Extra Days (ādiśa).
This chapter has six major sections: 1. Conditions for Receiving; 2. Mutual Use; 3. The Method of Receiving; 4. Obtaining a Double Allowance; 5. Encountering...
Six difficult points regarding the five benefits.

First, concerning the conditions for receiving [a day’s leave]: this Vinaya states that the conditions for receiving a day’s leave must involve matters of great benefit to the Triple Gem, or being invited by a *dānapati* to perform good deeds or eliminate evil;
one may then depart. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "For whose sake does one receive a day’s leave? For seven [purposes]."

When receiving [offerings] from the assembly, one should go to receive them for the purpose of generating merit and eliminating evil; whether one sends a messenger or does not send a messenger, it is equally permissible to receive them.
However, if one hears on the way that [the donor] has died, has reverted to lay life, has joined a non-Buddhist sect, or if there are the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), one must not go.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if one seeks robes, bowls, medicinal herbs, and so forth for one's own private benefit, all such acts constitute "receiving" [on behalf of others]. The *Riyi* (義) states that those who are poor should [act in this manner].

Those who have opened [the summer retreat] for the sake of wealth should be prohibited from leaving; however, if one is seriously ill and cannot endure the daily provisions, it is not a violation of the summer retreat to depart.
Thus, the Vinaya states that those such as attendants or caregivers may leave at will without offense.

Yet, if one seeks profit for a livelihood by falsely associating with the noble and eminent to beg for grain or wheat, or if one accepts employment to supervise scriptures, images, or the construction of Buddhist altars, or if one is indolent...

If one’s thoughts are distracted and not continuous, such that one day is spent receiving [offerings] for only a single object, or if one passes through many matters, or if the objects themselves are unreal and one falsely constructs external conditions—such useless matters as these do not qualify as receiving the summer retreat (varṣā).

Since it does not qualify as receiving the retreat, yet one reckons it as such out of false pride and self-importance, and thus presumptuously accepts the faithful offerings (śraddhā-deya), if the calculation reaches its full term, one commits a grave offense (pārājika). As the *Śāstra* says:

If one commits a grave offense by accepting offerings during the summer retreat, as addressed in the *Five Hundred Questions*, even if one uses the wealth obtained from breaking the precepts to construct a Buddha image,
one will still not escape hell, let alone attain merit.
Second, regarding mutual application: the question is whether mutual application is permitted. The answer is that the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"If one has received the seven-day [passage] to a village and the seven days have not yet expired, and the task to be performed is not yet finished, one may return to the original location. The Buddha said: 'As long as there are remaining nights, one should inform [the community] before departing.

The meaning is that this refers to being permitted to inform [the community] regarding the original matter and then use it for other purposes; it does not mean using it for matters entirely different from the original one.
If one receives the *jñapti* (formal authorization) for the sake of matters pertaining collectively to the Three Jewels, it is permissible to use the funds interchangeably;
for example, if one intends to perform Buddha-related activities, one may use funds designated for the Dharma or the Sangha, because there exists a common basis for receiving the *jñapti*.

If there is a great benefit, such as privately commissioning scriptures or images, or when responding to or declining an invitation during one's turn in the monastic assembly, these constitute grounds for receiving the *jñapti*. However, in the case of declining an invitation, one must ask the original host for permission.
It is accomplished.
Regarding the third procedure for receiving the *saptāha-vidhi* (the seven-day rule):
"Sister, attend closely with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], now receive the seven-day rule to go outside the boundary."
Due to a certain matter, I am returning to this place to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*). I inform you, Noble Sister, [saying this] three times.
In this legal procedure (*vinaya*) for face-to-face communication, there is only the name "receiving" (*pratigraha*), but no formal text for the act of receiving;

according to the traditional interpretation, one may stay outside for only six nights, and on the seventh day, one must necessarily return. If one observes the retreat within a defined boundary (*sīmā*), the precepts are not obtained.

On the site, the *jñapti* (formal motion) for extending the period [of the rains retreat] is not required because the mind is fundamentally directed toward that location; furthermore, the two boundaries (*sīmā*) are distinct and may not be used interchangeably.
If one observes the rains retreat based on a boundary site (*śīma-kaṭhina*), the same applies: even staying overnight within them, they may not be interchanged. Question:

May a nun receive the formal motion (*karmavācanā*) for extending the period? Answer: Since there is no textual authorization in any of the teachings, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that during the rains retreat for nuns, there is no formal motion to seek permission.
Because they travel for the sake of performing the Buddha’s work and the Sangha’s work through polishing [images and vessels], it is known that nuns do not do so.

The meaning is that because nuns are women and weak, solitary travel is not permitted; if they were to remain abroad for many days, there would be fear of being beset by difficulties and imminent peril, which is truly most terrifying.

Therefore, the Sage’s intention, knowing the proper time, established prohibitions and defenses that do not allow for such limits on departure. Yet today, there are those of virtue who still follow human sentiment.
Regarding the interpretation that this constitutes a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act), I respectfully consider that this principle is likely not so.

Even if there were many matters to be accomplished, if one is summoned by a king or a minister while abroad, it may not be possible to conclude them within seven days; how then could one repeatedly receive the seven-day leave?
If the task cannot be completed within seven days, one may go directly even if it constitutes a violation of the rules regarding difficulties.

Question: Regarding the fourth case, where one receives a heavy [period of probation], may one receive it again? Answer: Examining the meaning of the text, it is for the purpose of generating wholesome merit and benefiting others;

thus, receiving it again is not doubted. The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Lüelun) also permits receiving it again for seven days. As for the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Shisong lü) which does not permit it, this is due to differences between the various schools (*nikāya*).
The Tripitaka Master Wuxing (Bopa) of the Great Tang also permitted receiving it again, as did the Venerable Masters of the Western Regions.

Those who arrive [at the time of the *pravāraṇā*] do not hear the method for receiving [the rains residence] alone (the detailed explanation of obstacles and difficulties is fully contained in the *Sengchao*).

Fifth, regarding encountering difficulties: according to the Vinaya, one may receive the seven-day permit (*saptāha-sīmā*) and go outside the boundary for the sake of parents, brothers, sisters, or others;

because these private relationships give rise to wholesome conditions and extinguish unwholesome ones, one may intend to remain until that purpose is fulfilled. If the days pass and the difficulty subsides, one then attains the summer retreat (*varṣā*). If the difficulty ceases, [one returns].
One must return with urgency and may not remain stationary, lest one incur the suspicion of breaking the summer retreat (*varṣā*). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"During the summer, if one goes to harmonize with the Saṃgha, one must proceed directly on the road without turning back; once the harmony has been achieved, one shall return immediately. Thus, it is clear that remaining stationary would certainly constitute a breach of the summer retreat.

The sixth [point], the five benefits: after the summer retreat ends on the sixteenth day of the seventh month and continues until the fifteenth day of the eighth month, this period is called the *kārttika* month;

translated here as the "Month of Merit" (*guǒdé yuè*), it is so named because the summer sitting involves great toil, and these five benefits are opened for the sake of providing profit and benefit to the bhikṣuṇīs.
What are these five benefits? First, one may accept invitations for meals from multiple sources; second, one may eat separately from the assembly.

Third, one may go to another’s house before or after a meal without needing to announce one's departure; fourth, one may keep extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*) without declaring them as pure (*aviśuddha*);

fifth, one may stay overnight separated from one’s three robes (for nuns, five robes are permitted; the first three [allowances] apply to the period before a meal, while the latter two apply to both periods regarding robes). The *Jianlun* states:

"Those who perform the formal boundary-binding (*sīmā-bandhana*) on the sixteenth day of the fourth month obtain these five benefits; those who do so from the seventeenth day onward do not, for this is termed 'rewarding the prior and penalizing the subsequent.'"

In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are five types of persons who are not permitted to receive the *anagga-cīvara* (the robe for the rainy season retreat): first, one whose bowl has been suspended; second, one who has broken the summer retreat;
third, one who has abandoned the path; fourth, one who is deceased; and fifth, one who has failed to entrust their belongings. There are ten kinds of faults for breaking the summer retreat:
first, being censured by all Buddhas; second, being censured by devas and worldly people; third, the breaking of the summer retreat itself; fourth, the incurring of transgression; fifth, [not]...
1. One may receive the *guṇa-cīvara* (merit robe). 2. One may not receive five types of benefits. 3. One may not accept alms-offerings. 4. One may not receive robes for the *varṣā* retreat.
5. An evil reputation may spread. 6. One may later regret it and fall into hell.
Section Eighteen: The Chapter on *Pravāraṇā*. This chapter consists of eleven major sections:
1. The underlying intent; 2. The two periods of time; 3. The assembly of the Saṃgha; 4. The appointment of officials;
5. The selection of persons; 6. The performance of the ritual; 7. The five virtues; 8. The *pravāraṇā* ceremony; 9. The abbreviated procedure; 10. Miscellaneous rules.

First, regarding the regulation of the mind: when one cultivates the Way for ninety days, refining both body and mind, many people become deluded about themselves and fail to recognize their own transgressions;

it is therefore appropriate to rely upon the pure assembly to bestow compassionate instruction. By freely proclaiming one’s own offenses and allowing the Sangha to examine and raise them, one manifests internally that there is no private concealment and externally that one appears pure; hence, it is called *Pravāraṇā* (Self-Indulgence).
Regarding the second period: according to this Vinaya, one may perform the *pravāraṇā* on either the fourteenth or the fifteenth day of the seventh month;
furthermore, within the precept concerning the "garment offered in haste," one may also perform the *pravāraṇā* on the sixteenth day—thus there are three periods.

Moreover, if it is unknown when the *pravāraṇā* should be held, the Buddha permitted that during the morning meal or the afternoon meal, the *sthavira* (senior monk) should make a formal announcement.

Venerable Sisters, please listen. Today is the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight; the community of monks has assembled at [place name] for the *pravāraṇā* (the invitation to point out faults). [The *karmadāna* may also perform the formal announcement.
Regarding the third assembly of the monks, the meaning is that one must have at least five persons before one may formally announce the appointment for the *pravāraṇā*.

Even those who have broken their summer retreat or failed to observe the *varṣā* (rainy-season residence) are not excluded from this; although they do not possess the status of having completed the summer, because the principle of censuring offenses is the same, they must necessarily rely on the assembly to invite the Sangha.

Regarding the formal procedure of censure (*codanā*) according to this Vinaya: if those who have entered the later retreat (*paścimikā varṣā*) wish to perform the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) together with those who entered the earlier retreat (*pūrvikā varṣā*), they must still wait until the days are complete before returning;
even for śrāmaṇerīs and others, they must all assemble because the purpose of the censure is the same—they may only depart once the Saṃgha has announced their departure.

Regarding the fourth messenger: according to this Vinaya, when the Bhikṣuṇīs have completed their summer retreat (*varṣā*) and the Bhikṣu Saṃgha has completed its summer retreat, it is permitted to appoint one Bhikṣuṇī to go among the great Saṃgha (the Bhikṣus) for the sake of the Saṃgha to announce the *pravāraṇā*. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"Two diligent and knowledgeable Bhikṣuṇīs who understand the Dharma should be appointed to go before the Saṃgha and perform the formal motion (*jñapti*) to harmonize the Saṃgha."

"The Saṃgha is now in harmony. What should be done? [The questioner] replied: "Appoint a certain bhikṣuṇī to go before the Saṃgha and perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of inviting [criticism] regarding the three matters."

"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen. If the time is right for the Sangha and the Sangha grants its consent, let the Sangha appoint the bhikṣuṇī [Name] to go before the Great Sangha of bhikṣus on behalf of the bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha to announce the three matters of self-examination regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected. This is the formal motion."

Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen. Now, the Bhikṣuṇī [Name] is appointed for the sake of the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha to go before the Mahāsaṃgha and announce the three matters of self-examination regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.

Which of you venerable sisters approves of the Saṃgha appointing the Bhikṣuṇī [Name] for the sake of the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha to go before the Mahāsaṃgha and announce the three matters of self-examination regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected?
[The assembly] remains silent. Whoever does not consent, let them speak. The Sangha has consented.

A bhikṣuṇī named [Name] has been appointed for the sake of the bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha to go before the Mahāsaṃgha and announce the three matters of self-examination regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected. This being concluded, the Sangha consents by remaining silent.
One should uphold this matter in this way.

Furthermore, two or three nuns should be orally appointed as companions and go among the great assembly of monks; having prostrated at the feet of the Sangha, they should bend their bodies, join their palms, and say:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha has completed the summer retreat; the Bhikṣu-saṃgha has completed the summer retreat.
The Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha requests the *pravāraṇā* regarding the three matters—what has been seen, heard, or suspected. May the Venerable Saṃgha, out of compassion, speak to me.
If I perceive any transgression, I shall confess it according to the Dharma. (Recite this three times.)
After the bhikṣuṇīs have finished speaking, the Saṃgha of bhikṣus remains silent for a long while. The Elder should then address the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:

"The assembly, from the highest to the lowest, is all silent; none speak of having seen a transgression. This is truly because within the bhikṣuṇī community, the three types of action are restrained internally, and externally there are no three [unwholesome] matters.
Being pure both internally and externally, there are no deficiencies or offenses. Each of you should accordingly practice the Path with diligent effort and be cautious; do not be negligent."
A bhikṣuṇī who has performed the *pravāraṇā* according to the Dharma shall transmit this instruction to inform the assembly so that they may know it.

The bhikṣuṇīs should respond, saying: "We receive and uphold this with our heads bowed. Having further performed three prostrations, she shall then return. On the following day, at the time for the *pravāraṇā* of the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, the wooden gong shall be struck to assemble the bhikṣuṇīs.
Those who do not come shall announce their consent (*chanda*). Once the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha has assembled, each shall stand according to her seniority, and the appointed bhikṣuṇī [shall proceed].
Standing before the elder, she proclaimed the instruction for the great assembly of monks, saying:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen! The Sangha has appointed me, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], to go before the great assembly of monks to report matters seen, heard, or suspected.
The entire assembly, from the highest to the lowest, remains silent; no one speaks of having seen their transgression. This is surely because the community maintains internal restraint."
Regarding the three types of karma, there are no external factors; both internally and externally they are pure, with no transgressions whatsoever.
Each person should accordingly practice the Path with diligent effort and careful heedfulness, never being negligent, and perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony in accordance with the Dharma.

Having proclaimed this, all the nuns simultaneously join their palms above their heads and each says, "I shall receive and uphold [this] upon my head. Subsequently, the nuns perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for correction) in a composed and orderly manner.
The Vinaya states: "After the Great Assembly (the monks) has performed the *pravāraṇā* on the fourteenth day, the Sangha performs the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day.

Because these two assemblies depend upon one another, the dates and times are fixed. However, if the Great Assembly is ill, or if they form a separate group, or if the assembly is not harmonious, or if the number of members is incomplete—[in such cases, the procedure may differ].

A *śikṣamāṇā* should send a messenger to inquire after the health of the Great Saṃgha. Even if a nun is ill, or even if she has not yet completed her training period, she must also inquire after the Great Saṃgha.
If one asks why a nun who does not know [the situation] must inquire after the Great Saṃgha, the answer is:
if she knows they are not in harmony, she can act as a mediator to reconcile them for their sake.
Fifth, regarding the examination of persons: according to this Vinaya, one must possess two sets of five virtues (*pañca-guṇa*) to be fit for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
The first set of five virtues is: (1) not being biased by affection; (2) not being biased by anger; (3) not being biased by fear; (4) not being biased by delusion;

and (5) knowing what constitutes *pravāraṇā* and what does not (these five are the five virtues for the *pravāraṇā*). The second set of five virtues is: (1) knowing the proper time and not performing it at an improper time; (2) being truthful and not... [text fragment]

[One should] not speak falsely; [one should] benefit [the person] rather than seeking to destroy them; [one should be] gentle rather than harsh; [one should have] a compassionate heart rather than harboring anger.
(These five are the five virtues for one who points out faults. If one does not possess these two sets of five virtues, one will not know the proper time to point out faults;

fearing that one might disturb the Sangha, it will instead result in self-reproach. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "One must appoint two or more people, even up to many, [to act on behalf of] the community..."
Regarding the mutual confession (*pārivāsika-pratideśanā*): the *Three Thousand Dignified Manners* states that one must appoint two persons to perform the *pravāraṇā* for the Saṃgha;

those possessing the five virtues (*pañca-guṇa*) shall mutually confess their offenses and must not seek others. This is because once the *pravāraṇā* is concluded, other persons have not been appointed by the Saṃgha.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* state that those of virtue should be appointed to perform this. (In the present day, there are many who are young and act improperly during the ritual.)

Sixth, regarding the one who presides over the Dharma: before appointing the five virtuous ones (pañcavarga), one must first offer incense and pure water for washing, distribute counting sticks, and chant the number according to the previously explained method for the *Poṣadha*.
One should inquire about and modify the wording of the *Poṣadha* by adding the formula for the *Pravāraṇā*.

Thereafter, the five virtuous ones are appointed, and the Elder presides over the Dharma. When presiding over the Dharma, there is no need to call the nuns of the five virtuous ones to stand [in attendance], lest it constitute a schism in the assembly (*nānāsaṃvāsika*).
Question: Is the Saṃgha assembled and in harmony? Answer: The Saṃgha is assembled and in harmony. Question again: Have those who have not received full ordination departed? Answer:

Those who have not received full ordination have already departed. (If Śikṣamāṇās or others depart at this time, the procedure is the same as previously explained during the Poṣadha; there is no difference. Question again: Have the Bhikṣuṇīs who did not come conveyed their consent (*chanda*)?
If there are those conveying consent, they should say: [as follows].
Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], have received the consent (*chanda*) from her for the *pravāraṇā*.
She has granted me that consent for the *pravāraṇā* regarding the legal matters of the Saṃgha. (One recitation suffices.)
In the present time, there are many who, relying on the method for reciting the *Prātimokṣa*, transmit their consent (*chanda*) or receive it;

if a nun receives the transmission of another's consent within her own room, she cannot correct it before the Saṃgha, and must instead be sent back to her original room to inquire of that nun regarding her *pravāraṇā*.
Furthermore, if a nun conveying consent speaks erroneously before the Saṃgha, she may correct herself while seated; this applies even to those in border regions who have not studied the Vinaya.
It is a profound delusion to claim that when there is an occasion for illness during the *pravāraṇā*, it is not permitted for others to transmit their consent (*chanda*).

Furthermore, it was asked: "The Saṃgha is now in harmony; what shall we do? The answer was: "We shall perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) by appointing a person for the *pravāraṇā*. It was further asked:
"Who among the assembly is capable of acting as the one endowed with the five virtues (*pañcaguṇa*) to conduct the *pravāraṇā* for the Saṃgha? The reply was: "So-and-so is capable."

Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen. If the time is right for the Sangha and the Sangha is willing to grant its consent, let the Sangha appoint the bhikṣuṇīs [Name] and [Name] to act as the recipients of the *pravāraṇā* for the Sangha. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen. The Bhikṣuṇīs [Name] and [Name] are appointed by the Sangha to act as the recipients of the *pravāraṇā* for the Sangha.
Those Venerable Sisters who consent to the appointment of the Bhikṣuṇīs [Name] and [Name] as the recipients of the *pravāraṇā* for the Sangha should remain silent;
those who do not consent should speak. The Sangha has consented to appoint the Bhikṣuṇīs [Name] and [Name] as...
The Sangha has completed the appointment of the person to receive the *pravāraṇā*. Since the Sangha remains silent, it consents; this matter is thus upheld.

Regarding the seventh set of five qualities (*pañcavarga-dharma*): once the Sangha has appointed [the monk], he should immediately rise from his seat and go before the *sthavira*, prostrate at his feet, and remain kneeling.
If it is in the open air, he should stand within arm’s reach and make the formal announcement (*jñapti*) to harmonize the Sangha, saying:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen. Today the Sangha performs the *pravāraṇā*. If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha grant its consent and listen:
we shall perform the *pravāraṇā* in harmony. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).

Next, regarding the method for spreading grass mats, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "On well-prepared ground, one should spread grass mats and then perform the *pravāraṇā*; all [participants] must do so together."
Baring the right shoulder, kneeling with both knees on the ground, and joining the palms together, one should request as much as desired.

Then, seeking out soft and clean grass, one should cut a portion for each person according to the number of monks present and place it before the *upādhyāya*. The *guṇavara* (virtuous monk) takes the grass and distributes it;

starting from the *upādhyāya* down to the lowest-ranking monk, once a portion has been delivered to each, the *guṇavara* must also take a portion for himself. Holding it in his own hand, he proceeds to his original seat.
Having taken up their positions, they then spread the mats. If the assembly is large, they should have three or five junior nuns assist in laying them out.

Once this is finished, one endowed with the five virtues approaches the senior-most monk (*upādhyāya*), says: "The entire Saṃgha shall sit upon the grass; let each person baring the right shoulder, kneel with palms joined, and perform the *pravāraṇā* according to the Dharma.

Having made this announcement, the Saṃgha all exerts themselves in self-examination (*ātman-vidhūta*) according to the ritual procedure for recitation as taught in the *Ekottarika Āgama* by the Tathāgata.
The procedure is the same as when the Saṃgha sits upon grass mats; he addresses the bhikṣus, saying, "Each of you take your respective seat of grass;
I wish to perform the *pravāraṇā*," and so forth, as explained at length there.
Regarding the eighth method for *pravāraṇā*: first, one who possesses the five virtues comes before the senior monk (*sthavira*) and spreads out a large sitting mat.
The second *pañcavāstuka* (the monk of five virtues) kneels and stands before the next seat;
on both sides within the rows of the assembly of monks, long, wide mats must be spread so as not to soil the feet of the *pañcavāstuka*.

When the Elder sees the *pañcavāstuka* approaching, he immediately adjusts his robes, kneels with his right shoulder bared, and joins his palms; all the monks do likewise. Thereupon, he speaks as follows:
Sister, attend with one-pointed mind. Today the Saṃgha holds the Pravāraṇā ceremony. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], also perform the Pravāraṇā.
If you perceive, hear, or suspect any offense, O Elder Sister, out of compassion please speak to me.
If I perceive an offense, I shall confess it according to the Dharma. (Recite three times.)
After the Elder had finished speaking, she returned to her original seat. This first group of five virtuous nuns (pañca-vargīyā) then moved to stand before the third Elder;
the second group of five virtuous nuns received the confession as before. In this manner, they proceeded in succession until reaching the lowest-ranking nun.

The Vinaya permits sick nuns to remain wherever they find it comfortable. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, each of the two groups of five virtuous nuns returns to their respective seats and sits down.

Regarding the procedure for departing from one's own position after the confession of offenses has been concluded: according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, once the community of monks has finished their recitation, the five virtuous ones go before the senior monk (*sthavira*) and announce, "The community of monks has unanimously completed the invitation to confess (*pravāraṇā*). Only then do they pay their respects and withdraw.

Regarding the ninth, the abbreviated recitation: if there are eight difficulties or other circumstances as previously described during the *Poṣadha*, the *Pravāraṇā* is permitted to be performed in an abbreviated manner.
Five virtuous monks shall then make the formal announcement on one's behalf.

Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen. If the time for the Sangha has come, may the Sangha grant its consent to hear this: because of present difficulties, each member of the Sangha shall now perform the *pravāraṇā* by means of three utterances.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
After the formal announcement (*jñapti*) has been made, the assembly of monks faces one another, each reciting three times, and then disperses.
Nowadays, some groups of nuns hold their *pravāraṇā* (self-criticism) in low voices, or five virtuous nuns receive the *pravāraṇā* from others all at once; both of these are contrary to the Dharma.
Therefore, the Vinaya states: "One must not hold a *pravāraṇā* in whispers or in a noisy, chaotic manner; it must proceed one by one in order, starting from the senior."

While seated for the *pravāraṇā*, one should speak with clear and distinct voices so that the entire Saṃgha may hear. The above explains the procedure for six or more persons; if limited to five, the ritual differs slightly.
If there are five monks among the men and five nuns, it is not permissible to announce the *chanda* (consent).

First, inquire after their health and assemble them in one place. Then, perform a *jñapti-karman* to appoint one person of fivefold virtue (*pañcavarga-guṇa*), and finally appoint another person; these two must not be appointed simultaneously.
Regarding the two individuals, because these two do not count toward the quorum of the Saṃgha, even if there are six or more people performing the ritual, there should be no difficulty;
nevertheless, one may not simultaneously perform the *karmavācanā* for both at once.

At the time of the *pravāraṇā*, one virtuous person (*pañcavarga*) sits together with the Saṃgha, while another virtuous person successively receives the *pravāraṇā* from them. When the matter is fully concluded, [the procedure for] the two is finished.

If five *bhikṣuṇīs* of good virtue speak to one another regarding other matters as previously described, and if there are only four or fewer *bhikṣuṇīs* within the boundary, they may perform the *pravāraṇā* by means of face-to-face confession (*pratyakṣa-pravāraṇā*), but this does not conform to the formal communal rite (*saṃgha-karma*).
Regarding the face-to-face confession, it is said: [as follows].
"Venerable Sisters, please attend with one mind. Today is the day of the Saṃgha’s *pravāraṇā*.
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], am pure. (Recite this three times.

As for the remaining three persons, they should address one another as previously described. If two persons are facing each other, one should say: "Venerable Sister, please attend with one mind. Is it not so?

It must be said: "Sisters, if one relies on the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* during a time of famine and stays alone, the nun should perform a mental confession (*manasikāra*) regarding her relatives, saying:
'Today the Saṃgha performs the *pravāraṇā*. I, the bhikṣuṇī [name], am pure. (Recite this three times)."

Regarding the tenth miscellaneous rule: as for the question of why one says "I see my offense" when facing the Sangha, but says "I am pure" when facing an individual, the answer is that when facing the Sangha, it is sufficient to state that one sees the offense because the purpose of formal disciplinary action (*karma*) is fulfilled;
when facing an individual, one says "pure" because the individual's jurisdiction over the discipline does not encompass everything.
If the mind is directed toward the Sangha, yet after the Sangha and the individual have already performed the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults), more guests arrive who are few in number—

Regarding the announcement of purity (*pārisuddhi*) and so forth, it is further explained: if, after two persons have performed the ritual, three more persons arrive, one should perform the *pravāraṇā* according to the monastic rule (*saṃghakarma*).

If two nuns arrive, it is likewise the same as the *pratimukha* (face-to-face) method. If four or fewer persons are present, even for offenses ranging from a *thullaccaya* down to a *dukkaṭa*, one must first confess them and then perform the *pravāraṇā*.
If one has committed an offense of the first or second category (*pārājika* or *saṃghādisesa*), one should confess it in private before a single nun.

Regarding the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism), the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that one may not perform the *pravāraṇā* in another location while observing the rains retreat (*varṣā*) within this specific boundary.

According to this *vinaya*, those who have completed the prior rains retreat (*pūrvavarṣā*) may distribute the summer robes after the *pravāraṇā*; however, those who observe the subsequent rains retreat (*paścimavarṣā*) may only receive these items once the full period has expired.
If one fails to return to the rains retreat after it has concluded, they commit an offense.
Chapter Nineteen: On Teacher and Disciple.
This chapter contains thirteen major sections: 1. Names of Teacher and Disciple; 2. The Purpose of Dependence; 3. Exemption from Dependence; 4. Combined Dependence; 5.
Rules for General Practice; 6. Rules for Formal Announcement; 7. Rules for Requesting Scriptures; 8. Rules for Repaying Kindness.
9. The Dharma of Having No Teacher; 10. The Dharma of Examining the Teacher’s Virtue; 11. The Dharma of Requesting a Teacher; 12. The Dharma of the Teacher’s Guidance;
13. The Dharma of Rebuke and Confession.

Regarding the first [section], the titles of teacher and disciple: if one asks what is meant by the terms *ācārya* and *upādhyāya*, the answer is found in the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing), which states:
To reprove one for seeing what is not an offense as an offense is called my teacher (*ācārya*). Within the shared wholesome Dharma, he instructs and causes me to know;
this is the meaning of *ācārya*. *Upādhyāya* means "one who knows"; knowing what is an offense and what is not an offense is called an *upādhyāya*.

Thus, this Vinaya says: "Whether I have committed an offense or not, the teacher does not know. Furthermore, another interpretation states that an *upādhyāya* is so called because he provides the power for [the student's] birth [into the spiritual life].

The *ācārya* is one who provides correct practice; the disciple is one who learns following behind me, thus being a younger brother; and the "son" is so called because his understanding is born from me.
Second, regarding the intention of reliance: in the *Śikhālaka-ṣaḍdigvidhi-sūtra*, it is taught that a disciple serving a teacher should be complete in these respects.

There are five intentions [the teacher should maintain]: first, one should respect and revere them; second, one should be mindful of their kindness; third, one should follow whatever instructions they give; fourth, one should never tire of repaying their kindness;
fifth, one should praise the teacher’s teachings from time to time. Furthermore, there are five intentions with which the disciple serves the teacher:

first, one should cause them to understand quickly; second, one should cause them to surpass the disciples of others; third, one should cause them to know and not forget; fourth, regarding all doubts and difficulties, [one should resolve them for them].
To explain and resolve [the attachment to] the five desires so that disciples' wisdom may surpass that of their teachers, the *Saddharma-smṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:

"If one fears the teacher, this is called 'inferior observance of the precepts. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya*, a teacher who ordains a disciple for the sake of providing for themselves commits an offense.
One should cause that person, by virtue of being ordained by me, to cultivate all wholesome dharmas and attain [liberation]."
Regarding the attainment of the fruit of enlightenment, the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* states: "For five summer retreats (*varṣa*) or less, one should receive instruction in the Vinaya-piṭaka from others;

after five summer retreats, having fully mastered it, one should study [the higher teachings]. What is meant by 'studying the Vinaya'? It refers to reading, reciting, and explaining its meaning. This Vinaya further states:
"A preceptor (*upādhyāya*) should regard his disciple as a son, and the disciple should view the preceptor [as a father]."

Regarding the meaning of "viewing [others] as one's father": those who wish to view others as children must possess four intentions: first, providing instruction and admonition; second, compassionate mindfulness; third, sympathetic affection;
and fourth, receiving and supporting them with food and clothing. Those who view others as their own father likewise possess four mental states:
first, intimate love; second, respectful compliance; third, fear of causing distress; and fourth, honoring and reverently supporting them—just as a minister or a son serves a sovereign or a parent.
Therefore, the Vinaya states: "In this way, by treating one another with mutual respect, honor, and consideration, the True Dharma shall endure for a long time and flourish.
Third, regarding those who obtain exemption from formal dependence (*niśraya*), there are eight types of persons in total; six are found in this Vinaya and two in other schools. This Vinaya...
1. Delighting in solitude; 2. Guarding one’s dwelling place; 3. Illness; 4. Attending to the sick; 5. Completing [the required years]; 6. Having six or more years of seniority; 7.
Possessing wisdom and conduct such that there is no one superior to oneself in the dwelling place; 8. A time of famine where there is no food; 9. As stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra*:
"If one fears death from hunger, one should dwell in a place where one sees the Upādhyāya every day"; 10. Fearing that this may not be possible, if [one stays] for ten days...
Whether it be every five days, once a month, or every half-yojana, one should come to see the *upādhyāya* at the time of the *pravāraṇā*.
One should practice the Eightfold Path with a mind that finds satisfaction in this. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The various *bhikṣus* should each diligently practice the Path;

since there is no one to serve as their *niśraya*, they should give rise within their minds toward the senior *bhadanta* in the assembly, regarding him as their *niśraya* and dwelling with reverence as toward a teacher."

Fourth, regarding the combined cases of dependence, there are ten persons in total. This Vinaya states: (1) the preceptor has passed away; (2) one knows that the path of renunciation has been abandoned;
(3) the preceptor has resolved to go beyond the boundary; (4) the preceptor has relinquished the right to maintain disciples; (5) the disciple’s circumstances have led him to another region;
(6) the disciple, being dissatisfied with his dwelling place, seeks superior conditions elsewhere; (7) he has not yet completed six years of residence; (8) he is unacquainted with [the rules].
Because of the net of the teachings, the Vinaya states: "If one is foolish and lacks wisdom, one must rely upon another for as long as one lives. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"Even if one has received the precepts for many years, if one does not know the five dharmas, one must rely upon another for as long as one lives. These five are: first, not knowing what constitutes an offense; second, not knowing what does not constitute an offense;

third, not knowing what is light; fourth, not knowing what is heavy; and fifth, not having extensively recited the Prātimokṣa so as to master it thoroughly. The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* (Mātṛkā) also explains this.
It is said that one who has attained a hundred years of seniority (*śatavarṣa*) but does not know the Dharma should rely upon one who has ten years of seniority and knows the Dharma.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are four types of those who do not properly know the Dharma and do not properly know the Vinaya: they cannot establish themselves, nor can they establish others, and must rely [on another] for as long as they live.

These nine categories—whether foolish or wise—the "foolish" refers to those who are by nature perverse, deluded, arrogant, and frequently commit various offenses; the "wise" refers to those who, having committed an offense, [seek guidance].

One should immediately know that if, while performing repentance and purification according to the Dharma, one’s resolve is not upright and sincere, or if one relies upon another, these constitute violations.

The *Vinaya-mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "Regarding those who do not recite the precepts: if a person intentionally does not recite them, or if they previously recited them but later forgot them, or if they have dull faculties and are unable to master the recitation—these three types of persons may not be exempt from the requirement of relying [upon a teacher].
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "There are four faults in not reciting the precepts."
First, one must not keep a disciple; second, one must not be separated from one’s *niśraya*; third, one must not act as an *upādhyāya*; fourth, one must not act as an *ācārya*.
Regarding the fifth, the rules for common practice (*sāmānya-caryā-dharma*): this *vinaya*-master and his disciples have seven rules for common practice. First, the community...
1. When the Saṃgha inflicts disciplinary punishment upon the preceptor, the disciple shall attend to him and cause the Upādhyāya to be compliant with the Saṃgha;
he shall act so that [the preceptor] follows the Dharma without opposition, seeking the removal of his offense so that the Saṃgha may swiftly grant him absolution from the offense. 2.

If the Upādhyāya commits a Saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, the disciple shall exhort and instruct him according to the Dharma to cause him to confess it; for this purpose, he shall assemble the Saṃgha to perform the *parivāsa* (probation).
3. Regarding offenses such as leaving the monastery at night: (The procedure for a bhikṣuṇī undergoing *mānatva* for fifteen nights). 4. If the preceptors fall ill, the disciples must attend to them;

they should have others look after them until they recover or until their lives end. 5. If the preceptors do not wish to remain in their dwelling place, the disciples should move themselves elsewhere. 6.
If the preceptors have doubts, the disciples should instruct them according to the Dharma and the Vinaya to eliminate them. 7. If the preceptors... [text ends]

If a disciple holds wrong views, the teacher should instruct them to abandon those wrong views and abide in right view. Regarding these seven types of disciples, they should be protected by means of two things:
namely, the Dharma and material requisites (such as food and clothing). [As mentioned above, this rule applies equally to the *upādhyāya* and the disciple. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If the *upādhyāya* or *ācārya* commits an unrighteous act, the disciple must not address them with harsh words; rather, in accordance with the rules for admonishing, one should offer gentle counsel to the teacher. It says: "One should..."
If [the teacher] acts thus, one should not act thus; if the preceptor does not accept these words, the disciple should leave and go far away.
If it is the *niśraya-ācārya* (teacher of dependence), he should take his robes and bowl, go beyond the boundary for one night, and then return. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"If the teacher commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and seeks the Saṃgha to request a formal act (*karmavācanā*), the disciple should sweep and sprinkle the area, arrange the seats, assemble the Saṃgha, and request the formal act."

Venerable teachers, as for the sixth method of formal announcement (*jñapti*): this Vinaya states that whenever one is about to perform any action, one must announce it to the teacher so that they may be informed.

At the time of the announcement, one should assume the proper dignified posture, kneel with the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and say: "Venerable sir, please take heed. I, [Name], for the sake of such-and-such a cause..."

Therefore, when intending to go to a certain place, one must inform the Venerable Master of the companion’s name so that the Master may weigh the propriety of the matter—considering the destination, the business to be undertaken, and the appropriate time—and grant permission to depart. If even a single point is contrary to these requirements, it is not permissible to let them go.
Furthermore, the companion must clearly understand the Vinaya teachings, be manifest in their observance of the precepts, and be capable through a combination of both senior and junior members.
Regarding the initial allowance for departing, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one intends to travel, one should inform the teacher two or three days in advance so that he may know;

this applies except when using a tooth-stick for defecation or urination, which does not require notification. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "In all matters one undertakes, one must inform the teacher;

however, these three—paying homage to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, defecating or urinating, and chewing a tooth-stick—do not require notification. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One does not need to notify [the teacher]."
The teacher may accept half a thread or half a morsel of food [from a disciple]. If one takes a full thread without informing the teacher, one incurs an offense.
If one is unable to inform the teacher for each individual item, it is permissible to inform him collectively; this is also permitted according to the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing).

Regarding a disciple following the teacher, they must not distance themselves more than seven paces from the teacher. The *Śrāmaṇera-Ācāra* states: "When a disciple follows the teacher, he must not [step over] his feet."

Following in the footsteps of the teacher involves five further matters: first, one must not pass through people's homes; second, one must not stop on the road to converse with others; third, one must not look left or right;
fourth, one should keep the head lowered while following behind the teacher; fifth, upon arriving at the house of a donor (*dānapati*), one should stand to one side;
when the teacher instructs one to sit, one should then sit.
Seventh, regarding the request for the scriptures and Dharma: this Vinaya states that at dawn, one enters the preceptor’s room to receive the scriptures and inquire about their meaning.
The *Śrāmaṇera-sūtra* says: "If entering the teacher’s room, one should snap the fingers three times. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says:
"When a disciple visits the teacher, he should avoid six places: first, not directly in front; second, not directly behind; third, not too far away; fourth..."

1. One must not stand too close [to the preceptor]. 2. One must not occupy a high position. 3. One must not stand upwind. 4. [One must not stand] facing the wind. 5. One must not stand on elevated ground. 6. One must not stand upwind.
Regarding the eighth point, "Repaying Kindness," this Vinaya states that at dawn one enters the *upādhyāya*’s room, removes the vessels for excrement and urine, and announces, "The time has arrived.
Furthermore, three times a day—at dawn, midday, and dusk—one pays respects to the *upādhyāya*. Additionally, one performs two types of service.

One must not decline or make excuses for laborious tasks; rather, one should fully carry out all matters as instructed by the teacher according to the Dharma. These include: first, the repair of rooms and dwellings; second, the mending and washing of robes.
If sent to another region, one must not remain there on account of internal personal reasons.

As stated in the *Sengqiji* (Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya): "The disciple should rise early and enter the preceptor’s room with the right foot first. Having done so, he should prostrate himself at the preceptor’s feet and inquire:"
Whether one sleeps peacefully or not, even a bhikṣu of a hundred years who lacks wisdom should rely upon a bhikṣu of ten *varṣas* (years of seniority), no different from a disciple serving a teacher.
(The same applies to bhikṣuṇīs. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Except for prostrating at his feet, everything else should follow the teacher's instructions.
A sutra says: "One should visit the teacher or preceptor three times a day; if the teacher is not seen when visiting, one should carry soil [to offer]."
Using lumps of earth, wood, or grass as markers for the seasons— such as fanning one's teacher three times a day during the heat of the sun—
if there is a bhikṣu who lacks respect and faith toward that teacher or his preceptor (upādhyāya) and speaks ill of them,
he will, in a future life, fall into a specific minor hell called *Tāḍanapothana* (The Beating and Thumping). Having fallen into that place, [he shall suffer].
In that hellish realm, one’s single body with four heads is scorched; furthermore, there are various insects called "copper-beaks" (*tāmramukha*) that constantly devour the roots of the tongue.

Even if one hears a single four-line verse from another and carries the preceptors (*upādhyāya*) and teachers (*ācārya*) upon one's shoulders for a thousand kalpas, or at times bears them on one's back or wears them as a crown, one would still be unable to repay their kindness. — *Niraya-sūtra* (Hell Sutra)
If one speaks of the faults of one's preceptors or teachers as a disciple, even if those faults are real, upon the teacher’s death they will enter hell and have their tongue consumed.
If, having obtained fine food or delicious fruits, one does not first give them to one's parents, teachers, or monks but eats them oneself, one will be reborn among the hungry ghosts;
if later reborn as a human, one will be poor. If a person harbors malice toward their elders or teachers, they will enter the Iron Axe Hell.

After [suffering in] hell, one is reborn among venomous snakes; if, with a malicious mind, one mimics the words of one's parents, teachers, or elders, one enters the Melted Copper Hell and is subsequently reborn as a human who stammers.

The *Saṃghīti* states: "If someone asks you, 'What is the name of your Upādhyāya or Ācārya?', you must not state the name of the Upādhyāya or Ācārya directly. You should reply: 'The name is due to causes and conditions.'"
"O so-and-so, if a disciple perceives four kinds of unrighteousness in their preceptor, they should offer an apology and depart, saying to the preceptor:
'First, I act according to the Dharma, yet the preceptor does not know it; second, I do not act according to the Dharma, yet the preceptor likewise does not know it;
third, I have committed an offense, yet the preceptor neglects to instruct or reprimand me; fourth, even when I repent for an offense, the preceptor does not know it.'"
Regarding the duration of the ninth stage, the Dwelling Without a Teacher (*aśaikṣa-vihāra*): this Vinaya permits one to first wash the feet and drink water, and only thereafter rely upon a teacher.
The *Kṣudraka-vinaya* states that when first arriving at another place where one is not yet well-acquainted, one should select a teacher for two or three days.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that if there is no qualified teacher, one is permitted [to stay] for five or six nights; if there is a qualified teacher, one must rely upon them even for as little as one night. If one does not so rely, it constitutes a transgression.
[Otherwise] one incurs an offense.
Tenth, regarding the qualifications of the preceptor (*ācārya*): according to this Vinaya, there are five types of *ācāryas*:

first, the *pravrajyā-ācārya*, meaning one who, relying on the teachings, receives the ten precepts; second, the *upasaṃpad-ācārya*, meaning one who, for the purpose of receiving full ordination (*upasampad*), presides over [the ceremony].
The *karmācārya* (preceptor of ritual acts) refers to the teacher who instructs one in the *vinaya* (ritual decorum).

The *sūtrācārya* (preceptor of the sūtras) refers to the one from whom one receives the sūtras. The *niśrayācārya* (preceptor of dependence) refers to the one from whom one receives formal dependence (*niśraya*).
The meaning is that while the former four are collectively termed *ācāryas*, the one explained here—according to the treatise—is specifically the *niśrayācārya*.
Because Li was to take over the position of the *upādhyāya*, he had to thoroughly investigate the Sūtras and Vinaya until his understanding was complete and clear before he could serve as a *saṃgha*.
It is said that one must not arbitrarily request someone as a teacher (*niśraya*); rather, one must be accomplished in five qualities: first, receiving and mindfulness;

second, respect; third, shame (*hrī*); fourth, remorse (*apatrāpya*); and fifth, delighting in dwelling [in the Dharma]. The *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* states: "Whenever one wishes to rely upon another person, one should carefully evaluate them."
One should be able to promote wholesome dharmas; furthermore, one must inquire of others: "What is this bhikṣuṇī’s virtue in the precepts like?
Is she capable of providing instruction? What is her retinue like? Are there no disputes? Only if [the candidate] possesses none of these faults should one rely upon this Vinaya.
Regarding the qualifications of the two masters, there are three points: first, exclude those who are young and select those who are old, having at least twelve years of seniority (*varṣa*).
One who has served as an *upādhyāya* for six *varṣas* (summer retreats) or more becomes an *ācārya*. Although the number of years may be complete, one must possess wisdom.
Third, although one possesses the two aforementioned virtues, one must diligently instruct and admonish disciples.
There are likewise seven kinds of common practices for an *ācārya*, as previously explained in the section on the *upādhyāya*.

Eleventh, the method for requesting a teacher: Because this Vinaya was corrupted by many instances of improper conduct due to the death of preceptors (*upādhyāya*) and the resulting lack of anyone to provide instruction, the Buddha permitted that one have a reliance teacher (*ācārya*).
One should rely upon and receive instruction from them according to the same rules as for a preceptor, so that through mutual reliance the Buddha-dharma may increase and spread even further.
When making the request, one should fully observe the proper decorum and go before that teacher.
It is said:
"Sister, attend with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], now request the Sister to be my preceptor for dependence (*niśrayācārya*).
May the Sister act as my preceptor for dependence; by depending upon the Sister, I shall attain accordance with the Dharma."
[The candidate] stands [and recites this] three times.
The preceptor says: "So be it; I grant you dependence (*niśraya*); do not be negligent" (this applies to each matter according to the path). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If the preceptor does not respond with his consent, the rite of dependence is not established."
Regarding the twelfth method of gathering [disciples], the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that one should teach the Dharma of the Tripiṭaka three times each day.

If one cannot teach it extensively, one should at least have them briefly understand the meaning of the gravity of the precepts and the principles of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*).

Whether during the time of receiving the scriptures, reciting together, or practicing meditation, this is called "instruction" (*śāstrīya-upadeśa*). If it is not so, then even explaining as little as "do not be negligent" constitutes its meaning.

It is said that if one requests a teacher, one must possess four intentions: first, the intention to request that the teacher take one under their care, thinking, "I shall rely upon them with their compassionate mindfulness and pity";
second, the intention to request the Dharma for the path to nourish the spirit, so that through their instruction, practice may be perfected and wisdom attained;

third, the intention to express one's own state of mind, thinking, "I am able to rely upon them, regarding them with love, respect, and the thought of them as my parents"; and fourth, the intention to manifest one's own capability.
"Practicing by relying [on others]" refers to the two mental states of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*). Only when one possesses these four dharmas is one free from fault;
