otherwise, one will merely drift aimlessly and never achieve success. Once the fivefold reception of the precepts is complete, the preceptor should personally guide [the disciple] for six years.
If he instructs another to do so, and that other person acts contrary to this, he commits a *pāyattika* offense. The disciple, in turn, should rely upon and serve the *upādhyāya* for six years.
Once one has received the precepts according to the Vinaya, one must not be separated from one’s *upādhyāya*. The *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing) states: "The *upādhyāya* often has many disciples;

he should retain one person to provide for him, while the others may read and recite as they please. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a disciple faces danger from a king, the teacher must manage the situation;
if there is plundering by bandits and so forth, he must seek money to ransom them. To fail to do so constitutes an offense. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The *upādhyāya*..."
There are four kinds of disciples regarding whom one should judge the propriety of their stay: 1. One who receives the Dharma but not food—such a person should remain. 2.
One who receives food but not the Dharma—such a person should not remain. 3. One who receives both the Dharma and food—such a person should remain. 4.

If one receives neither the Dharma nor food, there is no need to consult the teacher; whether by day or by night, one should depart. The same applies to an *ācārya*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "It is suffering..."
Regarding the four phrases on dwelling in the blissful dwelling, they are the same as those in the *Five Hundred Questions*. It says:
"If one's teacher has no unlawful conduct yet lures away another śrāmaṇera, he commits a grave offense.
Thirteenth, the method for reprimanding and repenting: Whenever a disciple commits a transgression, the preceptor must necessarily reprimand them according to principle. As for this reprimanding...
In performing such a Dharma rite, one must point out the transgressions so that the offender submits their head and repents according to the offense. This Vinaya states:
"If a teacher reprimands a disciple without first pointing out the transgression, and the disciple asks, 'What fault have I committed that you reprimand me? the *Saṃghāṭi* [monastic code] says:

if the disciple does not accept the teacher's reprimand, one should inform the administrative officer (*karmadāna*) to impose a fast; if the former was particularly violent, the teacher should depart from afar."

Even if one stays for only a single night, returning again is permissible and free from fault. The *Sūtra on Good Precepts* states: "A teacher who does not expel or reprimand a disciple is worse than a butcher or a *caṇḍāla*.
A butcher does not destroy the True Dharma and will not necessarily fall into the three evil realms;
however, if one keeps wicked disciples, one will certainly be reborn in the evil realms. Furthermore, to keep a retinue of followers for the sake of fame and profit is a deviation."
In the *Five Hundred Questions on Seeing People as Disciples of Māra*, it is said:

"If a teacher does not instruct his disciples and the disciples consequently break the precepts, they fall among the nāgas; later, upon meeting again, they return to harm their teacher. The underlying meaning is this:

if one reprimands a disciple, one should first weigh one's own joy and anger, and next weigh the gravity of the disciple's prior transgression; outwardly manifesting stern authority while inwardly harboring compassion.

They speak bitter words and urge [the disciple] with severity to cease, yet they commit further offenses; furthermore, there is no teaching in the sutras regarding the method of striking disciples with a staff.

We frequently see monks and nuns repeatedly inflicting blows and beatings that pierce through to the very marrow of those before them. Consequently, they cite the parable of the three sons from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, but this fails to grasp the intended meaning of the teaching.
For those [sons] were all abiding in the stage of being an only son, where their compassionate mind is without distinction.

If one practices such punitive methods as currently using canes and whips to torment sentient beings, they will all become enraged and fiercely incensed, venting their hearts' malice and inflicting pain upon others;

how could this be comparable to the thought of a great compassionate father regarding his only son? The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* states that for upper-grade offenses there is expulsion, for middle-grade offenses there is subjugation, and for lower-grade offenses there is reprimand;
it likewise contains no method of corporal punishment with canes or sticks. This Vinaya, however, prescribes lifelong censure for a younger brother.
If a disciple commits an offense at the beginning of the summer retreat and the teacher’s anger does not cease by the end of the retreat; or if the teacher rebukes her in her absence;
or if the teacher rebukes her yet continues to accept her offerings—these are all contrary to the Dharma and constitute an offense. This Vinaya states:
"When a teacher rebukes a disciple, she should request other bhikṣuṇīs to lead her to the presence of her *upādhyāya* or *ācārya* for discipline, so that she may quickly repent."

Observing [the disciple's] submissiveness and gentleness, and knowing the proper time, the preceptor should receive the confession. The disciple should go before the two masters, perform the full ritual of deportment, join their palms, and say:
"Sister, I now confess; I shall not do it again. If she does not grant permission, the disciple should confess at the three times of the day.
If the Preceptor-Teacher (Upādhyāyī) still does not permit it, the disciple should immediately humble herself, comply with her will, and seek release from the offense she has committed. If...
To investigate and determine the transgression, the *upādhyāya* and *ācārya* shall decide whether to accept or reject [the matter], and it shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
○ Chapter Twenty: Paying Homage. This chapter has eleven main sections:
1. Paying homage to temples; 2. Paying homage to the Buddha; 3. Paying homage to the Dharma; 4. Paying homage to the Saṃgha; 5. [Meditative] concentration...
I respectfully offer my salutations in six matters: first, honoring the temple; second, revering the scriptures; third, respecting the precepts; fourth, venerating the Three Jewels;

fifth, showing filial piety to parents; sixth, repaying the kindness of patrons; seventh, providing medical care; eighth, performing funeral rites; ninth, [the matter of] medicine; and tenth, [the matter of] funerals. Regarding the first, honoring the temple:

I constantly reflect that as the Buddha-Dharma declines, the monastic resolve of the ordained monks and nuns becomes lax, and their various practices fail in every undertaking. Consequently, the halls and shrines fall into ruin, the dwellings collapse, and the gates and walls decay.

Filth and refuse overflowed the steps, and the tracks of human footprints were severed; the monastic community lived as transient sojourners, neither repairing nor wiping [the premises], which fell into daily decay.

They committed sins and transgressions without ever ceasing for a moment. Consequently, pungent vegetables, wine, and meat were vied for as offerings in the monks' quarters, while incense, flowers, banners, and canopies were rarely provided to the Buddha halls.
Prostrations performed during the six periods of the day were devoid of sincerity from the outset, and the three karmas were merely empty talk.
Furthermore, they may harbor bees or stinging insects, or share lodgings with others, partake in drinking and feasting, and openly assemble for the performance of stringed and wind instruments.
This allows evil persons to incite slander and destruction; what was intended to flourish is first struck down like a whirlwind, and what has just begun to burn is finally extinguished by smoke.

Thus, it causes the spirits of the underworld to manifest their power and the benevolent deities to abandon their protection. That monasteries suffer such calamities without apparent cause is solely because the nuns have violated their precepts, thereby inviting worldly reproach.

Censure and reproach also arise from the lack of discipline within the community. The "Monastic Testaments" (Sīgǔ sìgào) of the ancient masters consist of ten chapters; I have briefly summarized three or five of them rather than recording them in their entirety.

Some are called *dōngchǎng* (place of practice), some *sì* (monastery), some *wúshēng* (non-arising), some *tíngdú* (cessation of poison), some *xì'è* (stopping evil), some *jìmò* (quiescence), and some *jìngzhù* (pure abode). These seven names follow their respective meanings and each has its own symbolic significance. Now...
At that time, how could those who dwell there be called by name? The *Sūtra on the Extinction of Minor Dharmas* states:
"When the kalpa-fire arises, that which was once a monastery shall not be burned by the kalpa-fire, even until the Diamond Realm becomes a mound of earth. In the *Five Hundred Questions*, it is said:
"Formerly, a Brahmin examined a bhikṣu and found him possessed of the marks of a devaputra. At that time, the bhikṣu entered the temple and took [the image]..."

Leaning a *khakkhara* (monk’s staff) against the wall of a Buddhist monastery (*buddha-stūpa*) after having paid homage to the Buddha and then departing resulted in the loss of one's noble status and other benefits. (In the present day, monks and nuns are quite knowledgeable regarding respectful etiquette, yet they openly commit transgressions;

how could this not be comparable to the sin of leaning a staff against a *vihāra*? The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that it is better to rebuild a dilapidated Buddhist temple than to do otherwise. The *Nigaṇṭha-sūtra* says:
"If one dislikes a stupa, a temple, or various images, and removes or destroys them, sending them elsewhere—such [actions] are evil."
Humans are included within the category of those who oppose sentient beings; this is countered by the superior grade [of practice]. The *Daśacakrakṣitigarbhasūtra* states:

"If one destroys a monastery or kills a bhikṣu, at the time of death, all their limbs will ache, they will remain mute for many days, and upon dying, they will fall into the Avīci Hell to undergo all manner of sufferings.
The *Dharmasaṃgraha-śāstra* states: "A caitya is called a stūpa. The *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states that there is...
A *śarīra* is called a *stūpa*; that which lacks [relics] is called a *caitya*, or a *tāpa*, or a *thūpa* (which is translated here as "tumulus" and also termed a "square mound").
A *caitya* is translated here as "temple" (*miao*; *miao* meaning "appearance" or "likeness"). The *Yashajie zhuan* states:

*Devabhāṣāra* (the Sui dynasty translates this as "Heavenly Travel")—*deva* refers to the king and *bhāṣā* (travel) refers to the monastic site; because the king established it at that location, it is named "Heavenly Travel. Traditionally...
The term "sì" (寺) is a secular Chinese administrative office; it signifies a "jurisdiction" (*si*) or a "succession" (*si*).

As for *zhàdòutíshē* (柘鬪提奢)—the Sui dynasty glosses this as "any place where monks reside"—the older term *zhāotí* (招提) is a corruption and abbreviation. In the past, people removed the character *dòu* (鬪) and the *shē* (奢), and furthermore, they erroneously replaced *zhà* (柘) with *yǐ* (以).
Because the two characters *zhāo* (招) and *zhà* (柘) are visually similar, this error has persisted for a long time. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "To construct... [text ends].
Regarding the donation of a dwelling to the *saṃgha* known as the *Cātuddisa*, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"If there is a donor who donates a dwelling for the community of monks (*bhikṣu-saṃgha*) and then transfers it to the community of nuns (*bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha*), this is called an illegal gift, an illegal acceptance, and an illegal use. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If there is a donor who donates a dwelling or other facilities to the community of nuns, they should yield them to the community of monks; if they accept them without yielding, [it is improper]."
The Buddha said, "This violates the laws of reverence.
Second, as for those who pay homage to the Buddha: nowadays, both monastics and laypeople are deficient in sincerity while arrogance and indolence grow ever stronger.

They treat the sacred countenance with contempt and disdain, regarding themselves as superior. Consequently, although old images abound, filling the halls and rooms, their pedestals and halos have fallen away and their hands [are broken]."
The feet were left exposed amidst mud, wood, filth, and scattered soil; thus, the seats of blue lotuses frequently tilted and the marks of the white tuft repeatedly faced peril.

The precious stupa collapsed of its own accord while the majestic countenance stood towering. Even if one were to fashion and cast an image with the mind, the features and the sublime form would often be incomplete or riddled with flaws;
or else, in vying for high or low prices, one might increase or decrease the sacred characteristics.

In pursuing the base and seeking to save effort, one acts according to personal whim; this causes one’s physical appearance and deportment to change so drastically that they no longer resemble those of the Western Refinement (Xīhuá).
Acting according to one's passions is as worthless as excrement and soil. Consequently, it leads the ruler to harbor thoughts of destruction and the subjects to maintain an attitude of disrespect.
When good and evil lack evidence, the multitude of evils compete to arise; even the Most Holy One does not bestow grace, but instead incurs self-dishonor. Reflect on this quietly.
Is it not the case that one’s own faults are likewise so? The *Āgama* Sūtras state: "Those who lack a heart of reverence toward the Buddha-dharma shall fall among the dragons and snakes.
Because they have come from such a state in the past and still lack respect now, they are prone to excessive sleep.

Furthermore, when the Buddha ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, King Udayana requested Maudgalyāyana to act as a master craftsman for us to observe the form of the World-Honored One upon his descent.

When one comes to create [an image], after three ascents, three examinations, and three descents, one finally attains the true form. When the World-Honored One descended, this image went out to welcome the Buddha;

the Buddha patted its head and prophesied that it would bring benefit in the future. Regarding the merit of my own veneration, the *Jingxiangzhu mo lun dao* (Sutra on the Image-Maker Not Being Called a Servant) states:

"The patron of the sutra and image must not be called a 'servant of the Way,' nor should the artisan who crafts the sutra and image be called a 'hired laborer. Both the one who creates the Buddha image and the one who makes the offering obtain merit."

If one were to attempt to measure and describe the merit [of such a person], it would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon. Such a person who accepts my instructions is a true son of the Buddha;

with such sincerity, even a small amount of merit created becomes vast. Question: Among lay practitioners, is it permissible for those who create scriptures or images to take payment? Answer: One must not take payment.
To take wealth as if selling one's own parents is a transgression exceeding the three thousand [offenses]; it is truly heaven [to refrain].
Māra, those who have departed from my Buddha-dharma are not my followers: those who drink alcohol, eat meat, or consume the five pungent roots;
though they may fashion scriptures and images as numerous as motes of dust, their merit is extremely slight and hardly worth mentioning.

At the time of the kalpa-ending conflagration, these things do not enter the treasury of the Sea Dragon King; such toil yields little fruit. For the sin of disrespect, one shall die and fall into hell under its jurisdiction.

If the artisan’s work is of no benefit and the devas do not grant their protection, it is better not to create [the image] at all. By worshipping with a straightforward mind, one obtains immeasurable merit.

Regarding the various types of images listed above, those that possess many merits but few [flawed] characteristics will result in the artisan having incomplete sense faculties for five hundred lifetimes.
First, one who exerts their utmost sincerity attains the supreme and wondrous fruit and ascends [to higher realms] first.

Third, regarding the veneration of the Dharma: in this present age of the Semblance Dharma (Sāṃprata-yuga), the teaching has degenerated in accordance with the people, such that the monastic and the lay have become confused and transmit errors, turning their backs on the truth.
They pray to heterodox paths and follow heterodox masters; they receive the Dharma from evil friends rather than associating with virtuous ones.

They do not cultivate the internal scriptures but devote themselves exclusively to secular books; some read the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi* lewdly, while others are addicted to the Confucian Classics, interpreting them as incantations for spirits and ghosts or as spells for cursing.

They may regard auspicious or inauspicious matters, such as playing the lute, chess, singing, or games, as their primary occupation; they may treat the lecturing on Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras as secondary or non-essential;

or, when requested to read without payment, their tongues may curl up and their faces darken with sorrow; yet when hired for wealth to recite, they fear they cannot produce a clear and resonant voice.
They may transcribe sacred texts with many errors and omissions, neither collating them nor maintaining ritual purity, and even share these works with others.
Their lodgings were beneath eaves where wind and rain leaked through, and insects devoured and rotted their texts;

or they were altered and expanded with secular language, titles, and chapter headings that muddied the sacred scriptures. This led to the "disorder of the West River" and the suspicion that Confucius offered a rat as a sacrifice.
Thus, the *Yupuo* (Jade Rough) Sūtra lacked the power of spiritual efficacy, and its recitation failed to provide relief from suffering, inviting the world’s ridicule and slander.

It is said that the Buddha’s blessings cannot redeem one who lacks evidence of merit, for their transgressions increase until they fill the heavens; thus, the *Jingfujing* (Sutra on Reverencing Merit) states:

"Good son, regarding the law of transmigrating through births, if even a single word is inverted, misplaced, or defiled by a dot or mark, one shall fall into the path of delusion for five hundred lifetimes and not hear the True Dharma.
This Vinaya further states: "If a bhikṣu reveres the Buddha, the Saṃgha, and the precepts, this is the True Dharma."
If one does not revere [the teachings], the True Dharma will swiftly perish. The *Mahāpadma Sūtra* states:
"Those who receive the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts but do not protect them for the future each say, 'I am [a follower] of the Mahāyāna Dharma. It is like the dark of night;

each says of themselves, 'I have attained the Buddha-dharma,' yet they undergo the sufferings of the Iron Spikes Hell, which are difficult to describe. Upon emerging from that hell, they become mute and deaf."
The *Māyā-sūtra* states: "If a young bhikṣu personally reviles the Vinaya in the midst of the assembly, you should know that the Dharma will not long remain before it perishes."

Fourth, regarding the veneration of the Sangha: in these degenerate times, the knowledge and mastery of both monks and nuns have become meager while their accumulated transgressions grow ever greater.

Their clothing and ornaments deviate from the inner scriptures, and their conduct conforms to that of worldly laypeople. Their understanding is like peering through a tube or looking up at the sky from a small opening; yet they presume to critique and correct the great masters.
Inciting one another, they collectively commit faults and seek out each other’s shortcomings, making it difficult for contentious emotions to subside. There are even some who...

They indulge recklessly in the six sense-faculties and gallop toward the three poisons; they align themselves with the bright faction yet harbor delusion and evil, feeling aversion toward the pure assembly.

Relying on their official status and influence, they unjustly oppress the virtuous and confine them in prisons and dungeons, forcing them to return to lay life. Yet, while acting as good men themselves, they alone stand out as leaders among the masses.

Or, within a single monastery, they establish two separate boundaries (*sīmā*); the great courtyard and the meditation hall are distinct, and they perform the *poṣadha* ceremony and wear the dharma-robes separately.
If one greedily covets fame and profit, the Buddha’s prohibitions and the hearing of the precepts will instead lead to the acknowledgment of one's own faults.
There may be cases where bells are struck at two locations and the assemblies gather separately; by contending over their respective numbers, they give rise to strife and resentment.

Consequently, this causes the monastics and the laity to harbor feelings of partiality and alienation, the monasteries (*gārāma*) to exhibit signs of discord, the *Buddhapiṭaka* to bear the analogy of birds and mice, and the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* to speak of monkeys.
This is like the ancient tale of the man from Ye-dan who, having failed to learn how to walk, returned crawling on his hands and knees.

When a rooster intends to crow at dawn, what could have caused it to instead become a cawing crow? Alas! Alas! This pain and injury are difficult to endure. Contemplating this principle deeply, one must surely be cautious. Thus, the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:
"There are two kinds of fetters for those who have left the household life: first, the fetter of views; second, the fetter of gain and offerings. Furthermore—
There are two kinds of abscesses: first, seeking out the faults of others; second, concealing one's own transgressions. The *Sūtra on Resolving Doubts during the Semblance Dharma* states:
"Various bhikṣus claim of themselves, 'I am a Dharma Master,' 'I am a Vinaya Master,' or 'I am a Meditation Master.
These three types of practitioners claim they can extinguish my Dharma, yet they do nothing more than mutually revile one another. The *Sūtra of Mindfulness of the Correct Dharma* states: "For..."

To preach the Dharma for the sake of seeking wealth and profit is called the inferior gift; to preach the Dharma for the sake of fame and to speak more excellently than others is called the middling gift;
to preach the Dharma for the purpose of increasing the wisdom of sentient beings is called the superior gift.

Alternatively, there may be a bhikṣu who takes no pleasure in meditation or recitation, but instead sells his musical instruments to seek wealth from others; by failing to provide appropriate medical treatment to the sick, he is reborn in the Black Rope Hell.
The *Wǔbǎi wèn shì* (Five Hundred Questions on Matters) states: A bhikṣu was devoted to clothing and was obsessed with it day and night.

He died from illness and was reborn as a snake. It returned to coil around his robes. After the Sangha had finished the funeral rites for the deceased bhikṣu, they took his robes and bowl and performed the ritual procedures.
The snake extended its neck and spat venom; those among the monks who had attained the Path exhorted the snake to depart, whereupon it entered the grass.
When one is poisoned, a fierce fire breaks out and burns the body until life ends and death leads to entry into hell. The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states:
"In the past, when the Buddha saw all people, there were none who did not incline their bodies, humble themselves, and pay respectful homage.

The *Śāstra* states that one may sit upon a mat on the ground together with those who have not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Regarding the sixth point, "prostrating with *vaṃdana*": this is translated as "deliver me. The *Vinayamātṛkā* states that *vaṃdana* means "reverence.

The *Śabda-śāstra* states that *praṇāma* is translated here as "obeisance. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that there are three factors to an obeisance: first, [the body]; second, [the speech]; and third, [the mind].
Prostrating with the mouth [the lips], the two knees bent, and the head touching the ground constitutes the highest form of salutation. Furthermore, there are three grades of salutation:

the lowest is the bowing of the hands (yī), the middle is kneeling, and the highest is the prostration with the head to the ground (jīshǒu). There are also three categories of a Bodhisattva’s salutation to a Buddha:

first, the category of repentance; second, the category of sympathetic joy; and third, the category of requesting the Buddha [to teach]. The *Dìchí lùn* states that one should perform the salutation by bringing the five wheels (the two knees, two elbows, and forehead) to the ground.
The *Āgama-sūtra* states that the two elbows, the two knees, and the crown of the head are called the "five wheels" (also known as prostrating with the five limbs). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"If there are many people, one may pay separate homage to the teacher and perform a general salutation to the others before departing. The *Sāhasra-vidhi-sūtra* states that there are five points for circumambulating a stūpa:
first, bowing the head while looking at the ground; second, not treading upon insects; third, not looking left or right; fourth, [not...]
Spitting on the ground, not speaking with others, and furthermore, one should contemplate the kindness of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states:
"The dharma for those who have left the household life is that they do not prostrate to kings, nor should they prostrate to their parents. The *Five Hundred Questions* states:

"A disciple may prostrate at the tomb of a teacher to repay his kindness" (based on this, it is permissible to prostrate even while the remains have not yet been buried). This is slightly less restrictive than the Vinaya.

The *Niṣadyika*, the *Śikṣamāṇā*, the *Bhikṣuṇī*, and the *Bhikṣu* [may perform the prostration] toward the Tathāgata and his stūpa in this manner, proceeding successively from the lowest to the highest, until even a *Mahābhikṣu* may prostrate to the Tathāgata and his stūpa. According to the *Five Hundred Questions on Matters*:

"When circumambulating a stūpa, it is not an offense for women to follow provided there is a *Upāsaka* present. (By analogy, when a *Bhikṣuṇī* circumambulates a stūpa, it is not an offense for a man to follow. This is what is seen [in the texts].
The *Śāstra* says: "One should circumambulate the Buddha three times, perform prostrations in the four directions, and depart.

Joining the ten fingers and palms together with hands raised to the crown of the head, one should walk backward until the Tathāgata is no longer visible; then, performing prostrations once more, one should turn back and proceed forward.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Before a stūpa, one must not pay homage to others. The *Daśabhāṇavāra Vinaya* states: "Before a Buddha-stūpa or a Śrāvaka-stūpa, [one should act] oneself..."
The *Wǔbǎi wèn shì* states that one must not pay homage [to those engaged in the following]:

before a Buddha-stūpa, when a bhikṣu has committed an offense (*pācittiya*), while defecating or urinating, while naked, while shaving one's hair, while preaching the Dharma, while chewing a tooth-stick, while rinsing the mouth, or while eating rice or fruit;

in all such cases, one should not pay homage. The *Wǔbǎi wèn shì* further states that clean and polished boots and shoes may also be worn when paying homage to the Saṃgha, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
One must not be like a dumb sheep that does not speak; one should inquire after others: "Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you at ease?

Are you not weary or suffering on the road? The *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* states that a precept-breaking bhikṣu who receives the respectful prostrations of a precept-keeping person incurs eight forms of contempt:
first, becoming foolish; second, being mute; third, having an ugly countenance; fourth, his...

First, their faces are distorted so that those who see them mock them with derision; second, they undergo five rebirths as female slaves in poverty; third, their bodies are emaciated and their lifespans are cut short;
fourth, they are not respected by others and constantly bear an evil reputation; fifth, they do not encounter the era of a Buddha;
and sixth, these transgressors of the precepts will find that there is not even a place on the great earth where they can spit.

Seventh, regarding the Eight Respectful Precepts (*gurudharma*): The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī addressed the Buddha, saying, "I pray that you will permit women to leave the household life and receive the precepts.
The Buddha said, "Stop, stop! Do not speak such words. Why is this?

All Buddhas of the past did not permit women to leave the household life. All people rely upon the Buddha; they may remain at home, shave their heads, don the *kāṣāya*, and apply themselves diligently."
"By practicing diligence, one attains the fruit of realization; future Buddhas shall also be like this.
I now permit you to take this as your dharma. Thus she requested three times, yet the Buddha would not grant her leave.

Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī then wept bitterly, shaved her own hair, and so forth, until the Buddha taught her the Eight Weighty Rules (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*), after which he permitted her ordination. The *Mātṛkā* states that Ānanda acted on behalf of the women.
When people sought to leave the household life, Kāśyapa reprimanded Ānanda for ten matters:

First, had women not left the household life, various donors (from this point downward, "head" refers to the beginning of each item) would have constantly set out food in individual vessels by the side of the road, kneeling alternately to offer it to the śramaṇas;
second, they would have constantly provided robes and bedding on the roads for the śramaṇas to seek and use.
Third, one should always mount elephants, horses, or carriages by the side of the road and prostrate with the five limbs upon the ground, requesting the śramaṇas to step over them as they pass.
Fourth, one should always spread one’s hair upon the middle of the road, requesting the śramaṇas to step upon it as they pass.
Fifth, one should always, with a respectful mind, invite the śramaṇas to one’s home to provide for their needs. Sixth, one should always...
1. One should give rise to a mind of reverence, sweep the ground clean, remove one’s own garments, spread them upon the ground, and invite the śramaṇas to sit.

2. One should even remove all the upper garments from one’s body, sweep the dust from the feet of the bhikṣus. 3. One should even constantly let down one’s hair to brush away the dust from the feet of the bhikṣus.
4. The majestic power of the śramaṇas surpasses that of the sun and moon; how much more so [the power] of others!
How could non-Buddhists ever look directly upon a śramaṇa? Tenth: if women had not gone forth [into homelessness], the Buddha’s True Dharma would have remained for a thousand years;
now it is reduced by five hundred. For one hundred years, those who attain liberation will be firm;

for one hundred years, those who attain meditative concentration will be firm; for one hundred years, those who maintain the precepts will be firm; and for one hundred years, those who uphold the teachings will be firm.
Indeed, through a hundred years of extensive learning, one attains firmness in giving. The *Jianlun* (Treatise on Firmness) states:
"The reason women are not permitted to leave the household life is out of respect for the Dharma. If women were ordained, the True Dharma would not endure for five hundred years.

Because the World-Honored One established the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) for the bhikṣuṇīs, the True Dharma is restored to last for a thousand years. This is according to the *Māyā-sūtra*.
It is said that after one thousand one hundred years, the bhikṣus will act like worldly people, engaging in marriage and acting as matchmakers.

In the midst of the great assembly, they will slander the meaning of the Vinaya, saying: "Nowadays, the community of nuns follow the teachings by acting as matchmakers and accepting commissions from the laity.
They run about through the streets and thoroughfares, treating the Great Saṅgha with levity; they disregard dignified decorum, insulting those above and below, or even traveling alone."
Traveling alone or wandering through villages, coming and going like those of lowly station, is the very source of the extinction of the Dharma; it is specifically due to this.
Although the rules of the Dharma are numerous and cannot be fully recounted here, we shall now follow only the essentials, which do not exceed the Eight Points of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*).
Herein are listed the eight names; I pray that you will practice them accordingly, so that the True Dharma may endure for a thousand years and not fall into ruin. This Vinaya states: First—
1. A bhikṣuṇī who is one hundred years old, upon seeing a bhikṣu who has newly received the precepts, must go out to meet him, prostrate, inquire after his well-being, and invite him to sit.
2. A bhikṣuṇī must not revile or slander a bhikṣu. 3. She must not report the faults of a bhikṣu to another bhikṣu;
however, a bhikṣu may report the faults of a bhikṣuṇī. 4. Once a śikṣamāṇā... [has completed her training].
1. One who studies the precepts should seek to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*) from the Saṃgha; 2.

A nun who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense should undergo *mānatva* for half a month within both divisions of the Saṃgha; 3. A nun should seek a teacher (*anuśāsaka*) from the Saṃgha every half-month;
4. One should not reside in a place where there are no monks; 5. Upon the conclusion of the summer retreat (*varṣā*), one should...
One should go before the Saṃgha and request those who will grant the *prātimokṣa* examination (*pravāraṇā*). These eight rules should all be respected, honored, and praised;
for as long as one lives, they must not be violated. The *Madhyama Āgama* states: "If a bhikṣu permits a bhikṣuṇī to inquire about the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, only then may she question him;
if he does not permit it, he commits the fifth offense against the venerable teachers. The *Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya* states: "When a bhikṣuṇī enters the assembly of great bhikṣus..."
Within the monastery, one should prostrate with the head at the feet of every single bhikṣu. If one is old or ill and unable to do so, one may prostrate collectively according to one's capacity;
fearing that it might not be exhaustive, one should say: "I, the nun [Name], prostrate with my head at the feet of the entire Saṅgha.
If a bhikṣu enters a bhikṣuṇī monastery, he must be greeted with prostrations; it is not permitted to revile him, saying, "This man has violated the precepts," for such an act constitutes an offense.
The physician is a mahallaka who knows nothing; even regarding actual offenses, he may not speak of them. A bhikṣu, however, may speak of a bhikṣuṇī’s actual offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī, out of pride, does not respectfully welcome him or prostrate at his feet, she commits an offense of transgressing the rules of respect (*vairūpya-dharma*).
The Mahāprajāpatī Bhikṣuṇī Sūtra states: "If a bhikṣu points out the faults of a bhikṣuṇī, the bhikṣuṇī must reflect upon herself and must not [retaliate]."
Speaking in loud voices: furthermore, a bhikṣuṇī should revere the saṃgha of bhikṣus as she would the Buddha.
This Vinaya states that if bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇerīs, and others offend the bhikṣus, the Buddha said they should be summoned and punished;
if they do not repent and reform, the *saṃgha* should perform the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu..."
If a *śrāmaṇerī* commits an offense against her relatives, she should be spoken to with gentle words; she must not be rebuked.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that if a nun sees the Great Assembly of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*) and does not rise, it is a *pāyattika*. According to this *vinaya*, if one monk calls for one nun, or even for many nuns, they should go;
if they do not go, they are to be dealt with according to the law. Question: For what reason was it established that nuns depend upon the monks? Answer: [It was established by] Mahāprajāpatī.
The Bhikṣuṇī Sūtra states: "Women desire only to delude others with their beauty and prolong their own lives;
they keep disciples yet do not wish to pursue learning, knowing only the affairs of a moment. Therefore, they rely upon the monks."
Eighth, regarding repaying kindness: Piṅgala’s parents were impoverished; he supported them with food and clothing.

The Buddha said: "If a person for a hundred years carried their father on the right shoulder and their mother on the left shoulder, even while discharging excrement and urine upon them, and provided them with the most rare and precious garments of the world, they still could not repay even a moment’s kindness.
From this day forward, I permit [the practice of supporting one's parents]."
If a bhikṣu does not provide for his parents with all his heart, he incurs a grave offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If one's parents do not have faith in the Triple Gem, one should manage their affairs sparingly; if they have faith, one may provide for them freely so that they lack nothing.

If one's parents are poor and lowly, one should bring them to the monastery and give food to them with one's own hands; all such actions are permissible. The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "If one's parents are poor..."

One must first bestow the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, and the Ten Wholesome Actions, and only then grant the gift. If one is not poor, although they have received the precepts, it is not appropriate to give [the gift].

The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "The merit and karmic fruit of filial obedience and making offerings to one's parents is equal to the merit of a Bodhisattva in his last birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
It further states: "If one teaches two people to perform wholesome deeds, one cannot receive their gratitude."
That is to say, one's parents. Therefore, a bhikṣu should always be filial and support his parents without missing the proper seasons;
he should train himself in this way.
Ninth, regarding medicine: according to this Vinaya, for elderly or sick bhikṣus who are unable to walk, the use of a walking-drawn carriage is permitted.
Regarding carriages or vehicles, one should exclude cows, grass horses, and the like; this rule for *niṣadyā* (nuns) should follow the previous discussion in the *Vinayavibhaṅga*.
It states that if one acts as a physician, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. However, if one prepares medicine for the five groups of renunciants (*pañca-varga*), it is permissible.

Furthermore, if a preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or parents who are ill are in the monastery, a disciple may likewise prepare medicine for them. This also applies if one's parents, though poor or low-born, are residing within the monastery and receiving support.

Pure attendants (kappiyakāraka)—whether brothers, sisters, uncles, aunts, or maternal relatives—may all be employed for the compounding of medicines. If no such person is available, one may borrow from one's own kin;
if they do not return it, one must not demand it back. This applies even up to the seventh generation. Regarding the "Five Hundred Questions," it says:

"If a practitioner of the Way acts as a physician out of a compassionate heart, he must not take the goods for his own personal use. Even if others insist on giving them to him, he should not accept them."
Whether one is ill or not, one must not practice the inhalation of vital breath (*vāyu*) or spit at swellings, as these practices are identical to those of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that for the purpose of knowing the sequence of medical treatments and so forth, one may study writing; however, one must not neglect one's duties out of a desire for excellence. Divination, physiognomy, and inquiring about the fortune or misfortune of others are not permitted.
According to this Vinaya, one must not sell divinations, recite mantras, or prescribe medicines to treat illnesses, because such matters may involve falsehoods leading to slander.
To disparage a virtuous person; to teach others to recite scriptures or study worldly treatises for the purpose of subduing non-Buddhists;

for a newly ordained bhikṣu to teach mathematics; for a bhikṣuṇī to study incantations, medicine, and the like—these incur a *pāyattika*. To use hair that has been burned to ash, mixed with water and strained, as a remedy for vomiting;
to use sandalwood for a feverish ailment; to use aloeswood (*agaru*) for a poison-related ailment; or to use decomposed medicinal herbs for a field [remedy].
Regarding *madhyama-nīti*, it must also be taken with water; the *Pañcavargika* states that *agaru* (sandalwood) worn on one's clothes wards off insects.
When reciting mantras, one must not eat salt nor sleep on a bed. This is the Buddha’s permission regarding the methods for divine mantras.

The *Mahāsāṃghika* states that for small boils or abscesses, one should grind wheat and apply it as an ointment. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that impure fats and salt may be consumed; this Vinaya considers them impure.
Use *sū* (ghee) to irrigate the nose.
Tenth, regarding the conclusion of the funeral rites: this Vinaya states that if laypeople come to the monastery, one should employ skillful means to dismiss them;

however, if they praise the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, one may comply with their wishes as far as possible. If they die, the Sangha shall carry them away and discard them for the sake of maintaining the purity of the *ārāma*.
Ji said: "A bhikṣu must not call his father, mother, brothers, or even his maternal aunts by their names;

he may only address them as *upāsaka* or *upāsikā*. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: The Buddha told Ānanda, 'From this day forward, whenever bhikṣus address a high official, they shall call him 'Your Excellency';
when addressing one of lower rank, they shall call him 'Worthy One. They should regard one another as elder brothers."
From now on, a younger brother must not use the names given by his parents;

furthermore, a junior bhikṣu must address a senior bhikṣu as "Venerable" (āyuṣmat), and a senior bhikṣu must address a junior bhikṣu as "Junior" (kumāra-bhikṣu). This rule applies equally to bhikṣuṇīs.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that one must not address one another with secular terms such as "Mother," "Father," "Elder Brother," or "Younger Brother"; rather, one should address fellow monks as "Teacher" (ācārya) or "Preceptor" (upādhyāya).

Regarding the terms *upādhyāya* and *ācārya* (in the present day, monks and nuns address their *upādhyāya* and *ācārya* as "Āśi" [Master] and address their fellow students as "Mr. So-and-so"; this is a profound lack of understanding). The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"When members of the four castes enter into the Buddha-dharma, they are all equally called 'seeds of the Śākya' and must not rely on their secular surnames.
The *Jianlun* states: "One may call a maidservant 'Elder Sister,' but one must not call her a 'maiden.'"
Chapter 21: Section on Following the Precepts (Śīlānuvartana-varga).
Part One: A Concise Explanation of the Five *Pārājika* Offenses (Applicable only to the first four for fully ordained monks; for nuns, there are a total of three hundred and forty-eight rules:
eight in the first section, seventeen in the second, two hundred and eight in the third, and [four] in the fourth).
The work consists of eight fascicles; the fifth fascicle contains one hundred and seven rules for the settlement of disputes, totaling three hundred and forty-eight precepts.
It is a false worldly tradition to claim there are five hundred precepts. Furthermore, there are also five hundred precepts in the *Sūtras*, the *Vinaya*, and the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*;
these represent only a total count and do not have specific individual names.
The precept against sexual misconduct is violated when four conditions are met: first, the primary path—the rectum, the vagina, or the mouth; second, the presence of a defiled mind;
third, the application of effort; and fourth, contact with the object. Even if the primary path enters only as much as a hair’s breadth into any of these three places, one violates this rule.
Furthermore, if one inserts a child’s organ into one’s own mouth and manipulates it, even if there was originally no lustful intent, the act constitutes an offense at the moment of entry.
If one experiences pleasure, one commits an offense under the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. Regarding the requirement that it pass the teeth, according to this Vinaya:

if, due to circumstances such as enemies or bandits, one's male organ is forcibly held and made to enter the three orifices, provided one has no lustful mind oneself—such that from the initial entry until its withdrawal there is not even a single thought of experiencing pleasure—one does not commit an offense.
However, if at any point one experiences pleasure, [an offense is committed].
If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī mutually instructs another person to commit [an offense], it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if the other person does not act upon the instruction, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

Regarding the three lower assemblies (*śrāmaṇera*, *śrāmaṇerī*, and *śikṣamāṇā*), whether they instruct one another to act or not to act, it is always a *duṣkṛta*. If they nevertheless proceed to act, they shall be expelled (*pravāsanīya*). There is no offense in the following cases:

if one is asleep and lacks conscious awareness (this refers to the exemption when one is coerced by an enemy); or if one does not experience pleasure (this refers to the exemption when an enemy acts against another). All [cases] are thus.
There is no intention of sexual misconduct (meaning that one does not transgress due to the absence of a defiled mind).

The precept against stealing is complete with six conditions: first, the object belongs to another; second, the perception that it belongs to another; third, the intention to steal; fourth, the object is of significant value;

fifth, the employment of means; and sixth, the removal from its original place. Transgressing this constitutes an offense. Within this context, the classification of theft based on the object is expanded into thirteen categories of gravity.
1. One Buddha; 2. Two Dharmas; 3. Three Sanghas; 4. Mutual application of the Three Jewels; 5. Mutual application within the essential substance; 6. Mutual application between images and the Jewels;
7. Mutual application of things themselves; 8. Lending; 9. Guests; 10. Human property; 11. Non-human property; 12. Property of animals; 13.
Miscellaneous clarification of the karma of theft.

First, regarding the theft of property belonging to the Buddha: the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that if one steals items belonging to a Buddhist monastery (*buddhārāma*) or articles used for offerings within a vihāra, and there is a guardian who values them, it constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*).

The *Vinayavibhaṅga* states that for stealing property of the Buddha and the like, the gravity of the offense is determined in relation to the original owner, because such an act cuts off their merit;
(since the Buddha has no sense of "mine," stealing from him results in a *sthūlātyaya*). The *Śarīrapūjā-śāstra* of the *Daśabhāṇavāra* discusses the theft [of relics].
The Buddha taught that when making offerings with a pure mind, one should reflect: "He is my disciple, and I am also his disciple.
In such a case, there is no offense. The *Śāstra* states: "If one steals less than five *karṣas* of the Buddha’s relics, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if five or more, it is a grave offense (*pārājika*), because by selling them for a livelihood, one commits a grave offense."

Second, regarding the theft of Dharma objects: this Vinaya states that at one time there was a case of someone stealing another’s sutra scrolls, whereupon the Buddha declared, "The words of the Buddha are priceless;

to calculate their value based on paper and ink constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that if one borrows another’s sutra and refuses to return it, causing the owner to harbor suspicion, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* (a secondary offense).

This is because the intention has not yet been finalized; had it been finalized, it would constitute a grave offense. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states that stealing another’s secret formulas constitutes a grave offense. The *Pañcaśata-praśna* likewise [states this].
Regarding the matter of treasures buried underground: if they are for the purpose of providing offerings and assemblies for the Triple Gem at a vegetarian hall, one may take them without fault.
One must not blow dust from atop the scriptures with one’s mouth, nor burn them; to do so constitutes a grave offense, as if burning one’s own parents.

As for those who do not know this constitutes a transgression, it is not a violation. The principle is as stated before: taking śarīra relics does not constitute a violation because it is done with the intention of the donor.
If the passage is open, and it is not open in other places, one should also incur the grave offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*); the same applies to whether the passage is passable or impassable.
Third, regarding the theft of property belonging to the Saṃgha: if there is a guardian who expects protection from that guardian, one incurs a grave offense;

if the custodian steals it himself, according to the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (or *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*), stealing property belonging to the Saṃgha constitutes a grave offense (referring to property held in perpetuity for the Saṃgha). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one takes what is surplus..."
If one eats after returning to the quarters, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense. The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* states: "One who eats without striking the bell commits the offense of theft;

furthermore, if one sees food in an empty monastery and steals and eats it, one incurs an offense according to the quantity, whether much or little" (according to the treatise, this constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*). The *Susheng jing* (*Upāsakaśīla-sūtra*) states: "Regarding the theft of the property of a deceased bhikṣu:

if the *karman* has not yet been performed, the offense incurred from the Saṃgha of the ten directions is light (meaning that if there are fewer than five people, one merely commits a *sthūlātyaya*); if the *karman* has already been performed..."

If one intends to obtain [an object] from the *saṃgha* present before them, it constitutes a grave offense (meaning that if five persons are present, it is a grave offense). If, at the time of death, one steals an item entrusted by the deceased according to the deceased’s instructions, the offense is determined according to the person to whom the item was intended to be given.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one steals with a thieving mind an excellent object belonging to the *saṃgha* worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a grave offense;
if it is worth one *kārsāpaṇa* or more, it is a *sthūlātyaya*."

Regarding the fourth point, the mutual use of the Three Jewels: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that if the temple administrator (*māmādhi*) mutually uses the property of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, it is said not to constitute an offense.

The Buddha said that while such acts would constitute a *pārājika* offense [if done improperly], in the present time, when monks and nuns manage the property of the Three Jewels—taking up the Sangha’s provisions, riding the Sangha’s donkeys and horses, or employing the Sangha’s family members to perform services for the sake of the Buddha and Dharma—it is all permitted according to the rule.

The Vinaya states that there are five offenses for violating the rules regarding precious objects. The *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* says that the property of the Buddha and the property of the Dharma may not be used interchangeably;

this is because there is no one who acts as a steward for the property of the Buddha and the Dharma, nor is there anyone with whom one may consult or report matters, unlike the property of the Saṃgha.

Regarding the permanent endowments (*sthavira*) and the temporary lodgings (*caitya*), when there is a mutual need, a monk in charge of affairs may seek the consent (*chanda*) of the Saṃgha by distributing voting tallies (*śalākā*). If they are in harmony, he may use the property of the Saṃgha.

In repairing a Buddhist stūpa according to the Dharma, one may employ those who have attained harmony with the Saṃgha; if there is no such harmony, one should encourage laypeople to perform the repairs.

If there is even a single coin belonging to a stūpa, because the donor gave it with a sincere heart, both devas and humans should conceive the notion of "Buddha" and the notion of "stūpa" regarding that object;
even if it is worn away by wind or rotted by rain, it must never be traded for precious goods.
Regarding offerings made with items belonging to a *tathāgata-caitya*, the *Five Hundred Questions* states that if there is no one to set a price, it is permissible.

Furthermore, if a shrine hall originally did not exist and an image is placed within it, monks may stay overnight together in accordance with the Dharma provided they erect a partition; this does not constitute an offense. This is because when the Buddha was in the world, he also stayed in the same room as his disciples.
According to the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, on land belonging to the Saṃgha from the four directions, those who are not in harmony may not perform such acts.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that flowers from trees within the monastic garden may be taken to offer to the Buddha’s stūpa.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that firewood from trees within the courtyard should be taken in small or large quantities for use in the heated hall (*jantāghara*), the kitchen, or separate rooms;

one must not take more than necessary. If there is no fixed limit, one may take as much or as little as required, provided it is dry and withered. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* further states: [as above].
Regarding the meaning of using tree bark, leaves, and so forth according to the needs of a bhikṣu: although there is this allowance, one must still exercise self-restraint in their use.

The karmic retribution for damaging the property of the Sangha is extremely grave; even stealing as little as a single hair’s breadth incurs an offense that binds one before all the ordinary and holy beings of the ten directions.
Thus, in the *Vaipulya Sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Puṇyasaṃbhava says: "Even the five heinous crimes and the four grave offenses I can save from, but theft I cannot."

Regarding the property of the Sangha, I do not save those who misappropriate it. The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states that the sin of stealing the property of the Sangha is equal to the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*).
The *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi Sūtra* states that using the property of the *saṃghika* (belonging to the community) carries a transgression greater than the sin of killing eighty-four thousand parents;
such calamities are incurred because one violates the precepts. Therefore, practitioners should urgently and deeply investigate this matter.

Fifth, regarding the mutual use of objects based on their substance: for example, using paint originally intended for Śākyamuni Buddha to depict Maitreya; using it for the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* to depict the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*;
or using it for a monk’s cell to provide food for the Sangha—all such acts violate the original intent of the offering and constitute the offense of "mutual use.

The *Five Hundred Questions* states: "Using the colors belonging to the Buddha to create the forms of birds or beasts constitutes an offense, except when [the image] is located within the Buddha [shrine]."
Previously, for the sake of making offerings, one does not commit an offense. The *Jianlun* (Treatise on Views) states:

"If a donor presents a garden or fruit as an offering intended for robes, medicine, and other requisites, yet with a thieving mind one diverts them to be shared as food, one incurs a grave offense (*pārājika*) based on their value. If they were intended for the construction of a monastic dwelling but are diverted to be made into monastic food, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Furthermore, if a residence is lacking in provisions and the residents wish to disperse so that no one remains to guard it [and the property is thus lost], [the same applies]."

If one obtains the permission of the Saṃgha to reduce the use of heavy items such as those from its gardens or orchards for the purpose of making food, and guards them, then in times of rebellion or chaos, it is permitted to take them away;

once the rebellion ceases, they must be returned to their original place. If one wishes to make offerings to this image, one may instead offer to that image, though this incurs a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*).

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If a monastery building is ruined, one may sell the bedding and other belongings belonging to the Saṃgha to repair the dwelling. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: "One may take [the items]..."

If one steals property belonging to the Sangha of the four quarters with the intent to transfer it to another monastery, one incurs a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*), because the property must be returned for the use of the Sangha;

thus, it cannot be considered a case of "restitution. It is said that if one acts on behalf of the Sangha, where there is no place to beg for alms along the way, it is permitted to harmonize with the Sangha by carrying food while traveling;

the manner of obtaining such food follows the previous rule. According to the *Samantapāsādikā* (Shanjian lü piposha), regarding the text on guarding a monastery: when managing the monastic estates, fields, oil-mills, or watermills, one acts as the administrator (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*).

If one strikes a bell to obtain food, or if an administrator, on behalf of the Saṃgha, inspects and leads the Saṃgha’s *kappiya-kāraka* (steward) and livestock to another monastery, estate, or field to consume the Saṃgha’s grain, fodder, or beans, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrongdoing) according to the aforementioned *Vinaya-vibhāṣā*.

However, if one acts privately for the sake of oneself or an acquaintance—even if the person involved is a Saṃgha steward—and the value of the livestock reaches the required threshold, it constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*). This is the rule regarding the land.

If a monastery has fallen into ruin and no one is present to take its property to another monastery, and later, when the land returns to tranquility, someone brings this property back to the original monastery, it shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.

If there is no one [to claim it], [the property] shall remain as it is. If there is someone, they shall rightfully restore it to the original monastery. If they do not, they shall be punished according to the law.
Sixth, regarding the mutual exchange between images and treasures: it is a transgression to treat the Three Jewels of the established community (saṃgha) and buried treasures as interchangeable.

Seventh, regarding the mutual exchange of Buddha-property: the *Wubai wenda* (Five Hundred Questions) states that one may purchase Buddha-property to provide offerings for ritual implements, but one must not sell it;
furthermore, silk offered upon the Buddha’s body may be used to make robes for the Buddha, and when a pillar in the Buddha hall is damaged, it may be replaced.

Regarding the offering of pillars to the Saṃgha, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that the Saṃgha may not use them. The Buddha said that lending out property belonging to a Buddhist stūpa is permitted.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that if flowers offered to the Buddha are in great abundance, one is permitted to sell them and purchase incense, lamps, and other offerings;

if they are still in excess, they should be sold and placed within the "Inexhaustible Treasury" (*akṣaya-nīvi*). The *Pañcaśata-praśna* states that if a banner was previously offered to the Buddha, it may be taken to make other things.
Regarding the use of items for Buddhist affairs: if the donor does not permit it, one must not use them.

Eighth, concerning lending: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that when lending between the two types of property—those belonging to the stūpa and those belonging to the Saṃgha—one must clearly record the transaction with a formal document, noting the time it was lent and the time it is to be returned.
When officials hand over their duties, they must read the records before the assembly and clearly announce and entrust them.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that if one borrows property belonging to a stūpa or the Saṃgha for personal use and then dies, the value must be repaid.

The *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* further states that one may borrow wealth to build a private residence. The *Sujāta-sūtra* states that if a sick person borrows property from the Triple Gem, they must repay tenfold;
it is feared that this leniency does not extend to those who are not ill.

Regarding the ninth point, "guests and others," this Vinaya states: "If one knows those who are learned in the Dharma and Vinaya, wherever they go, one should welcome them and provide them with food and drink.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) states that because such persons take the place of oneself, they must be provided for. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If there are evil bandits, fools, craftsmen, kings, or ministers who possess the power to cause harm or benefit, one should give them a drink."
Regarding the rule on giving food in five portions: if a layperson enters the monastery and is not given food, they may develop a sense of resentment.

The Buddha said that one should give it to them, even using an inferior vessel; yet if they still resent it, the Buddha said one should give it using a fine vessel. (This means that if one sees faults in the Sangha, one should give; however, for those of high intelligence and virtue, one should explain that "faith-food" is difficult to digest, rather than attributing it to stinginess or the like.

To dismiss such cases with this statement would not be incorrect. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: if a sick person requests expensive medicine from the Sangha, one should provide medicine worth two and a half coins.

The *Jian lun* (Treatise on Views) states: "If a lay attendant (*kappiya-kāraka*) is assigned to work in shifts, the one on the upper shift shall be provided with food and clothing, while the one on the lower shift shall not;
however, those who perform long-term service shall be supplied with food and clothing. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"If a hired laborer has been employed for a single day but encounters adverse conditions such as wind or rain and is unable to work, the Buddha commanded that they be given wages commensurate with their labor."
Regarding the tenth [offense], stealing another's property: the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing) states that if a bhikṣu, for the sake of another individual or even the Three Jewels,
guards and protects wealth with diligence— locking it securely and storing it away in a room— and yet a thief steals it through a hole or from within the house by force,
such that the guardian is unable to prevent it, the offense is still incurred against the original owner based solely on the intent.
It is not appropriate to demand compensation if the person in charge was negligent or lax and failed to diligently record the items, resulting in their theft by a thief;

however, the monk who was guarding the goods must compensate for them. Regarding the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if one receives another’s entrusted property while traveling and it is damaged or destroyed on the road:
if it was thrown away or broken out of good intentions, one need not compensate; if it was thrown away or broken out of malicious intent, one must compensate. Borrowed items are treated similarly.

Regarding other objects, regardless of whether they were given with good intentions, if they are broken, one must compensate for the full value. The meaning is this: nowadays, many people with good intentions wash and repair others' bowls;

if such a well-intentioned person damages or breaks them, according to this principle, it is not permissible to demand compensation from the owner, yet if one does so, calculating the monetary value, one commits a grave offense (*pārājika*).

Furthermore, if someone steals an object while the owner is absent—even if the thief originally had no intention of relinquishing it—and later sees that the owner has not actually abandoned their claim, the thief may not take it back by force; to do so constitutes a grave offense.
Therefore, according to this *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, at one time there was a bhikṣu who seized the property of a robber; the Buddha declared this a *pārājika* offense.

However, if one steals from someone present before them while the thief’s mind is wavering and the original owner has not yet relinquished their protective intent, it is permissible to take it because the principle of the owner's intent is stronger.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that there is no offense if one obtains [the goods] by chasing a thief and using conciliation, or if one obtains them through intimidation, or if they are given because the person was pursued by others out of fear.
One may take [the robe] because it serves to establish one as its owner; however, one must not beg for it from a thief.
If another person gives it voluntarily, one may take it, provided that it has been dyed with a discolored (ruined) color. If there is an original owner who recognizes it, it should be returned.

If a thief or a bhikṣuṇī claims the robe, and the original owner sees it, one must not simply seize it by force; rather, it should be returned to the original value (since the object belongs to this [claiming] nun). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: "If..."
If a person has been arrested by authorities and entrusts their unlisted property to a bhikṣu, it may be taken; however, if the items have already been listed, they may not be taken.
If the items are offered to a Buddhist stūpa or the Saṃgha, they may be taken and should be carried out openly rather than being concealed.

If asked what these items are, one should reply that they are the property of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha. If they are not permitted, they must be returned. Thus says the *Pāpā-vinaya* (or *Bā-lùn*).

If one carries out contraband goods across a boundary, it is an offense; if the person carrying them dies, the offense is grave. Furthermore, it violates the royal decree and constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (transgression).

If the king’s subjects are liable to death for such an act, stealing and carrying them out constitutes a grave offense. Apart from these cases, if one does not intend to steal, there is no offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If a bhikṣu uses skillful means to avoid paying official taxes on his belongings, he does not commit a grave offense, provided that: first, he did not enter into an agreement [to evade them]; and second, it was not done through improper means."
Because I am subject to taxation, this Vinaya states that a bhikṣu is exempt from the duty of paying taxes, unlike laypeople who must pay duties on goods required by officials.

If a bhikṣu conceals or falsely claims ownership for another, he incurs a grave offense (*pārājika*). The commentary explains: "In the present age, many monks and nuns act as proxies for laypeople, falsely claiming ownership of carts, oxen, and other items to evade taxes;
if the value is calculated, they commit a grave offense. The *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* states: "If a madman carries goods himself..."

If a bhikṣu takes what has been offered by someone who does not recognize their parents or relatives, he may accept it; however, if the parents can be identified and they do not give it with their own hands, he must not accept it.

Regarding the eleventh case, stealing non-human property, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Stealing from another's covered grave, or from within a shrine containing banners, canopies, or spirit temples."

Regarding the theft of objects protected by others, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that stealing the property of non-Buddhist stūpas or items used for divine sacrifices constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*).

This is also determined as a grave offense with respect to the protecting owner. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that stealing garments, flower garlands, and other such items belonging to celestial deities constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.

This is determined as a *sthūlātyaya* with respect to the object. The *Karmavibhaṅga-śāstra* states that taking five *kārsāpaṇa* or more of another person’s property is a grave offense, while four *kārsāpaṇa* or less is a *sthūlātyaya*.

The *Xia qing lan jian lun* (Treatise on the Lighter and Heavier Aspects of the Vinaya) states: "Taking the property of ghosts and spirits, or objects tied to trees that have no guardian, constitutes no offense" (this refers to cases where non-humans do not guard them).

Twelfth, regarding the theft of animal property: according to the *Shisong lü* (Ten Recitation Vinaya), taking the remains of a tiger’s prey is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), because the expectation [of ownership] has not been severed.

Regarding "remnants of a lion," there is no offense because the expectation [of ownership] has been severed; the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* states: "It is auspicious for one who takes what has been left over as food by all birds and beasts.
Thirteenth: Miscellaneous Clarifications on the Act of Stealing. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "Noble and base, locations, and so forth" refers to the value [of the object] in this land.

If one reduces five [units] in that land while directly exceeding five in this land, or directly exceeds five in this land while reducing five in that land, it is all severed according to the original location.
If, with a thieving mind, one proclaims of the ground, "This land is certainly mine," and the owner of the land conceives doubt, the offense is *duṣkṛta* (light transgression).
If the owner loses their mind, the offense is grave. If one comes to question the Saṃgha and the monks give an answer in agreement, all are grave. If there is a dispute over a garden or field...

To violate reason by making a judgment, or even to engage in various forms of verbal misconduct such as falsely claiming to have completed the summer retreat (*varṣā*) or proclaiming oneself a great master, if the value of the object obtained reaches five *māṣaka* coins or more, it constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*).

Even citing a single instance establishes the time of the offense; even a single hair or a single grain of barley is considered grave because the ground [upon which it rests] is of immeasurable value.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that whether one plays with dice by moving the pips or moves pieces on a chessboard, it is grave (meaning it is grave when wagering material goods, and minor when not).

Regarding those who do not commit an offense: according to the Vinaya, taking with the perception that it belongs to oneself, taking with the perception that it is one's own property, taking what is discarded (pāṃsukūla), taking with the perception of temporary use, or taking with the thought of a friend—none of these constitute an offense.
A "friend" must possess seven qualities: first, being able to perform what is difficult to do;

second, being able to give what is difficult to give; third, being able to endure what is difficult to endure; fourth, confiding secret matters to one another; fifth, mutually concealing each other’s faults; sixth... [text ends]... [the seventh quality].

Not abandoning others when they encounter suffering, and not treating them with contempt because they are poor or lowly—those who can practice these seven dharmas are virtuous friends to whom one should attach oneself.
Regarding killing and lying, they are briefly explained as in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
The offense of touching is established through six conditions: first, it is a human male; second, there is the perception that he is a male; third, both parties possess a defiled mind;
fourth, the area below the armpits, above the knees, and behind the elbows; fifth, there is physical contact; sixth, upon experiencing pleasure, the offense is incurred.
If a nun touches a male’s light part with her own heavy part, or a male touches a nun’s light part with his own heavy part, this [is likewise an offense].
In both cases, the gravity of the offense depends on whether the contact is essential or non-essential. Regarding the gravity of the situation where two parties touch one another, this Vinaya states:
if one has clothing and the other is naked, their touching constitutes a *thullaccaya*; if both have clothing, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if one holds hands with a man, or grasps his vessel, rope, staff, wooden stick, or the like, it is not proper conduct (*anācāra*) and constitutes an offense of *pārājika* for each individual man involved, provided there is movement of lustful intent.
Regarding the offense of *sthūlātyaya* for stealing: if the path through a city gate is narrow and crowded, one may wait until it is less busy to pass through;
if there is a wound or abscess in a minor location, one may have a man treat it, provided he is first made aware by two women who seize him firmly so that the woman does not perceive the man.

If the wound is in a major location, one must have a female teacher (*bhikṣuṇī*) treat it. The *Jian lun* (Samantapāsādikā) states: "If a bhikṣu touches a bhikṣuṇī, and the bhikṣuṇī’s body does not move..."

Regarding the offense incurred by receiving pleasure in various situations, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that there is no transgression if one perceives [the person] as a parent or child, or if touched by adverse conditions such as water, fire, knives, or staves, provided there is no defiled mind; yet, it further maintains that a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*) still remains.

The commentary explains that nowadays, at places where assemblies for the fast are held, there are instances where nuns personally perform tasks such as distributing water and incense; this is ultimately not appropriate and should be entrusted to men.
A daughter-in-law should be most careful; when she acts on her own, she should suspend [the object] so as not to let it touch the hand of a man.
The same applies to various utensils and other items.
Eight matters constitute a grave offense (*guru-dharma*); five conditions complete it: first, it is a man; second, the perception that it is a man; third, there is defilement.
Regarding the four groups of seven matters of the mind that have not yet been confessed: if one performs eight actions, one commits this offense according to the Vinaya.

"Grasping the hand" refers to cases where it is light from the wrist downward and heavy thereafter. "Grasping the robe" means taking hold of the upper garment on the body. "Entering a secluded place" refers to leaving the vicinity where one's companions can see or hear;
standing together, speaking together, or walking together also constitutes leaving the vicinity of sight and hearing. "Physical contact" means the two bodies touching one another.
If one meets at a prearranged location to engage in sexual misconduct, and both the nun and the man harbor defiled intentions, the commission of the first seven offenses constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one does not repent and completes the eighth offense, it is a *pārājika*. According to this principle, committing all eight offenses by grasping the hand does not constitute a grave offense (*pārājika*), as the underlying act is one and the same;
likewise, if a single man commits all eight, or if one commits them all at once, the same applies.
If one commits the eight offenses with eight men, all eight commit grave offenses (*pārājika*), yet there is no sequential order; the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is likewise.

Regarding those who do not commit an offense, this Vinaya states: "If there is someone to whom one offers prostrations, confesses transgressions, and receives the Dharma, and one does not perform evil deeds in a secluded place, there is no offense.
This is because in both cases there is no defiled mind. As for the "dark room" mentioned in the text below, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense, intended to provide an opportunity for conversion.
The precept on concealing another’s grave offense is established as an offense through six conditions: first, being a fully ordained bhikṣuṇī; second, the other has committed a grave offense;

third, knowing that the other has committed a grave offense; fourth, forming the intention to conceal it; fifth, not confessing it; and sixth, the appearance of dawn, at which point the offense is incurred.

(If one lives alone with no one present, the concealment is not established. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣuṇī who has been subject to formal censure conceals it while her mind is deranged, she does not commit an offense; if she is insane..."
Regarding the concealment [of a fault]: according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if one knows that a nun has committed an offense, one should speak of it to others.

However, if the person who committed the offense is violent or possesses great power, and one fears there may be dangers to life or to the celibate life (*brahmacarya*), one should form this thought: "The retribution for their karmic actions and offenses is something they themselves shall know.

This is illustrated by the analogy of a fire breaking out and burning a house; one should only save oneself and not concern oneself with other matters. Thus, one attains the state of mental composure.
One should immediately cease the argument, saying: "If [the confession] were not accomplished because one intends to reveal it, then it would not be pure.
This is because there is a fault in both cases regarding a person previously known who refuses to reveal it, as each must confess.

Just as for one who has committed an offense, the repentance is not accomplished if they do not reveal it; if one intends to reveal it, one should name the person who committed the grave offense and state each of the names of the offenses individually."
In this manner, the confession is fully accomplished. If one does not obtain the name of the person [to whom one confesses], the offense is termed "unconcealed.
