If the person before whom one has already confessed receives that confession, it is unnecessary to speak of it again; to do so would result in the fault of infinite regress.
If that offender has already confessed of their own accord, and another person harbors a mind of concealment, no concealment is established, because the root [offense] has already been confessed.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "A bhikṣuṇī must not disclose a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) in the presence of a bhikṣu; she must instead confess it before another bhikṣuṇī.
If she does not recognize the characteristics of the offense, she may go to a bhikṣu to inquire generally for clarification, and then return to the bhikṣuṇī to confess.

According to this Vinaya, if she knows a bhikṣuṇī has committed a grave offense, she may speak of it at the time of the morning meal, the afternoon meal, or even during the first, middle, or last watches of the night."

Regarding the occasional non-offenses when the light of dawn appears simultaneously with the *laṅkā* [pre-dawn] period: there is no offense if one has no person toward whom to confess; or if one intends to confess but the light of dawn appears before doing so;
or if one does not confess due to obstacles such as the danger of life or the presence of a *brahman* (or other such impediments). In all these cases, there is no offense.
*The Concise Commentary on the Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya of the Four-Part Dharmaguptaka School*, Middle Volume, Part One;
*The Concise Commentary on the Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya of the Four-Part Dharmaguptaka School*, Middle Volume, Part Two.
Section Two: A Brief Explanation of the Seventeen Saṃghāvaśeṣa Offenses (Thirteen for Bhikṣus).
The offense of acting as a matchmaker requires six conditions for its completion: (1) a person; (2) two individuals, one male and one female; (3) the perception that they are a man and a woman;
(4) the intent to act as a matchmaker; (5) the completion of the formal communication; and (6) the receipt of the message and its transmission back and forth.

According to this Vinaya, if one facilitates a union for even a single thought-moment, or for a brief duration such as a momentary interval, one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. This applies from the time one receives the message from the man’s family...
At that time, Kila informed the woman’s family; if Tilaka promised to return her, it was a *sthūlātyaya*;

if he made a written contract stating she was not his wife, it was still a *sthūlātyaya* as long as they had not yet formally divorced. If Tilaka’s marital rites were already severed and he no longer cohabited with her, it was a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a master keeps many wives and concubines but does not treat them equally, leading to strife, and one wife becomes intimate with a bhikṣu..."
One who mediates for the sake of peace or reconciles a husband and wife who are discordant;
one who encourages a woman or girl living in a forest hermitage (*araṇya*) to return home when a bhikṣu arrives at their house (fearing that she might trouble her husband or cause discord);

one who acts as a long-term messenger by hiring a woman for a man or a man for a woman—according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, these constitute matchmaking; according to this Vinaya, such a person must inform the Saṃgha.
If a *karmadāna* (lay attendant) provides wedding requisites and asks the Saṃgha for their approval, all such remnants [of the property] are subject to the following:

if one uses items improperly, one commits a grave offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*). The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* states: "If one acts as a matchmaker by arranging marriages for unborn fetuses, or if one arranges one's own marriage, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"Even if one seeks out fine stallions for others and facilitates their mating, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense. Regarding other animals, the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

[Fragmentary. It is said that for a person’s precepts to be complete, four conditions must be met: first, speaking before a secular official; second, speaking with a lay householder (*avadātavasana gṛhapati*); third, setting forth the details of the matter;

and fourth, taking up the pen to draft a formal record—by doing so, one commits an offense according to the characteristics of this Vinaya. "Speaking" refers to going before an official to dispute matters of right and wrong.
If one has been brought before the authorities and the official’s subordinates have drafted a report, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense if one does not state the name of the person involved;

however, according to the *Vinayavibhāṣā*, if one speaks of the person before the official and causes the official to confiscate property, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense and must repay whatever amount of the confiscated goods was taken.

If one’s property has been seized, one may petition the authorities for protection, but must not state the names [of the accusers]; if the authorities investigate and identify them, they shall punish them, and the petitioner incurs no offense.
If a person enters a monastery and cuts down trees, one must not seize their axe or hatchet; rather, one should return the value of five *māṣakas*.
It is said that if one is insulted or oppressed by others, one may speak to one's parents, relatives, or those who possess power to provide protection.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if a *bhikṣuṇī* becomes angry and reviles someone before a judicial official, and the person she originally struck is present, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; however, if she reviles him in the presence of other people, it does not.

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that for a female bandit to receive the full precepts (*upasampadā*), five conditions must be met: first, she is a bandit whose crime merits death; second, one knows her to be a female bandit;

third, one does not consult the king or his ministers; fourth, one unilaterally confers the full precepts upon her; and fifth, the offense is committed once the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is concluded. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says:

There are two kinds of thieves: first, those who steal property and violate the king’s law, whom the king intends to kill; second, those who violate the person [of their husband], whom the husband intends to kill.

Regarding these, if the *upādhyāya* knows [the offense], it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if the *ācārya* knows, it is a *duṣkṛta*; if the *saṃgha* knows, it is a *duṣkṛta*; if no one knows, there is no offense.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if one forms the intention to ordain a female thief, and proceeds through the preparatory rites up to the assembly of the *saṃgha* for the three *karmavācanās*...

If the *marjana* (rubbing) is not yet finished, it is auspicious in all cases; if the three *karmas* are completed, the *upādhyāya* incurs a *śeṣa* offense, and the preceptor incurs a *pārājika*. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, giving [ordination] to one who has already left the household life is a *vyatikrama*;
giving [it] to one who has already studied the precepts is a *duṣkṛta*; and giving [it] to one who has already received full ordination is a *śeṣa*.
The four rules on crossing rivers alone: these four rules constitute a single precept. First, regarding the rule on crossing a river alone, it is established through four conditions:
first, there must be river water; according to this Vinaya, if one cannot cross the water alone, it does not matter whether it is deep or wide.

Now, following the *Dhūtaguṇa-vinaya*, as long as one crosses the water by lifting one's robes—differing from traveling on land—it constitutes a violation within the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), because the difficulty of the situation is the same.
Therefore, as in the case of a village within a district, it is an offense even if one enters alone; however, if there is a bridge, it is permitted as usual.

Second, regarding crossing alone: if, as before, a nun enters the water quickly and both feet step onto the bank, and a subsequent nun then enters the water alone and steps onto the bank, she may take the preceding nun as her companion;
this is not an offense. It is also not an offense if one travels by means of a carriage, boat, or the like.
This Vinaya states: That nun must seek out another nun to cross with her. When entering the water, they should adjust their robes according to the depth of the water.
Upon reaching the opposite shore, they should gradually lower their robes and then step onto the bank. If she does not wait for her companion, she commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

Third, there is no offense if there is no other cause, such as life-threatening or *brahmacarya*-threatening dangers, or if her companion has died. Fourth, crossing alone constitutes a *pāyantika* offense.

Upon reaching the shore, one commits an offense; this means that if there is no sense of mutual assistance among companions, entering a village alone constitutes an offense when four conditions are met:

first, it must be a human village, regardless of whether it is within a formal boundary (*sīmā*); entering such a village alone always constitutes an offense. According to this Vinaya, for a nun traveling alone to a village, the offense is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting of the community) for every village she reaches.
If she travels through a desolate wilderness where there are no paths, even if she covers the distance of a single drum-roll, it is likewise a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. "Village" [is defined as follows].

It is auspicious (kṣema) to travel alone within a single boundary (*dhātu*). (Accordingly, if one travels alone within a single precinct (*kṣetra*) or within a single household, one incurs only a *duṣkṛta* offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If one goes with a companion to the boundary of a city or town, they should remain within arm's reach of each other as they enter the boundary.

If they are beyond arm's reach and one passes through the boundary alone, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense. Second, traveling alone; third, being without a valid reason; fourth, crossing the boundary. Thus [the offenses].

Regarding the offense (the Old Commentary states: "If one wishes to enter a village, even if there is a cross-road, as soon as one crosses it, an offense is committed"; however, this lacks textual basis in the various schools and logically it should not be an offense).

Therefore, according to this Vinaya, if there is no boundary, one commits the offense only when traveling alone for the duration of a single drum-beat's interval and being out of sight or hearing of one's companion.

If one reaches the gate and does not wait for the companion, but both feet cross the threshold of the gate, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If there was already a nun within the village, there is no offense, because the prior nun serves as one's companion.
If one leaves the village, the offense of staying alone is incurred only upon crossing the threshold; thus, three conditions must be met for the full offense.
As for the offense of sleeping apart, it applies regardless of whether one is in a monastery or a village, and whether one is on a separate bed, a separate mat, or even side by side.

One should remain within arm’s reach of another and check upon one another to avoid the fault. If one was originally within arm’s reach but later becomes separated due to heavy sleep, [the fault is not incurred].

Regarding the offense of sleeping apart from a wooden structure: because one commits the offense by turning over even slightly while separated, the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that "sleeping together" means that if one turns over so that one's outstretched hands do not reach the other, each instance constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that they should remain within arm's reach;
during the night, one should search for the other with the hand three times. One should not search all three times at once, but rather at the beginning, middle, and end of the night.
During each of the three watches of the night, one should seek out [the other monks] to ensure they are within five *yojanas* of one another;
if they are not within reach, there is a *sthūlātyaya* offense for the first, middle, and last watches. At the appearance of the dawn light (*aruṇa*), there is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

Second, there is no offense if there is no cause or condition, such as life-threatening or *brahmacarya*-threatening difficulties, or if one seeks solitude. Third, a separate offense is incurred for each instance of lying down [alone]; this refers to the root precept regarding walking alone at the rear.

If one intentionally walks away from one's companions in a place where they can see or hear one, one commits an offense; likewise, if there are no extenuating circumstances, one commits an offense even if walking with a companion.

According to this Vinaya, if one is separated from both seeing and hearing [one's companions], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension); if one is separated from either seeing or hearing [them], it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). Next, regarding when crossing water does not constitute an offense:
if one crosses gradually with a companion without losing dignified decorum (*īryāpatha*), or if one crosses by boat, by bridge, or by stepping across a beam, or if one crosses together [with them].
Accompanying a corpse, abandoning the path, traveling long distances, and other such difficulties do not constitute an offense.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that there is no offense if the water is narrow and shallow and one is without fear, or if one enters a village. Regarding "no offense" in the case of sleeping alone:

according to this Vinaya, it refers to sleeping with two nuns in a place where they can reach each other by stretching out their hands; if one nun goes out for the sake of relieving herself (defecating or urinating), [the other remains].

If one goes out for the purpose of receiving or reciting the scriptures, or if one delights in quietude and stays alone to practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), or if it is for the sake of a sick nun—such as boiling soup, porridge, or preparing meals—even in other difficult circumstances, there is no offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a sick nun is surrounded by thieves in a besieged city, staying alone is not an offense;
traveling alone is not an offense provided one does not leave the range of sight or hearing; or if there is one nun who is large [and capable]."

Regarding urination during various difficulties and the like, in all such cases there is no offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One must not exit the boundary of a village, except when traveling on a road to relieve oneself;
if one happens to lose their companions and has not yet reached the next [village], there is no offense. It is the same in the case of illness. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If one flees due to fear and, because of old age or illness, cannot keep pace with their companions, there is no offense."

The offense of receiving clothing, food, or requisites from a man with a lustful mind involves five conditions: first, it must be a man; second, one must perceive him as a man; third, he must offer the clothing or food with a lustful mind;
fourth, one must know that he offers the clothing or food with a lustful mind; fifth, upon receiving and taking possession of them, the offense is incurred. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If a nun has no lustful mind, yet a man offers her clothing, food, medicinal decoctions, or leftovers; or if someone gives her clothing..."

Regarding the bowl and its requirements, although one does not speak with the mouth, if one manifests bodily signs—such as drawing figures on the ground or writing characters—it is known that there is a desire for [the gift].

To accept [in this manner] constitutes a *pāyantika* offense, because it is considered encouraging the recipient to accept. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Because of this, a nun provided food to the Saṃgha but gave it preferentially to nuns she favored;
both recipients committed a *pāyantika* offense."

The precept against encouraging a man with a lustful mind to accept food, clothing, or monastic requisites involves five conditions for an offense: first, the person must be a male; second, he must offer food with a lustful mind;
third, one must know that the other offers it with a lustful mind; fourth, one must speak words of urgent persuasion to encourage him to accept it;
and fifth, the completion of these words constitutes the offense. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, each instance of such persuasive speech constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

The offense of corrupting the family (*kuladūṣaka*) through expulsion and slander for violating an admonition requires six conditions: (1) performing an act that corrupts the family; (2) not having reformed one's mind;

(3) being formally expelled by means of a *jñapti* motion; (4) slandering the Saṃgha in defiance of reason; (5) the Saṃgha having issued a formal admonition according to the Dharma; and (6) committing the offense upon the completion of the third admonition.

According to this Vinaya, corrupting the family itself constitutes only a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing); it is only at the subsequent time of expulsion, slander, and violation of the admonition that the full offense is incurred.

Among the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, there are four types of defiling families (*kuladūṣaka*): 1. Defiling a family based on the household itself: This occurs when one gives the property of a single family exclusively to another family;

the owner of the original family becomes angry, while the recipient feels joy. Thus, the recipient gains fame and profit, incurs the ridicule and slander of the laity, and defiles the family. 2. Defiling a family based on material gain: This occurs when one receives gains according to the Dharma but bestows them unrighteously upon the laity. If the recipient repays the kindness, it is acceptable;

however, if they harbor resentment, it causes the donor’s virtuous intention to regress and violates the principle of impartial giving. 3. Defiling a family based on relatives and friends: This involves relying on the influence of kings, high ministers, or lay officials to act with partiality, thereby causing the laity to feel either anger or favoritism. 4. Defiling a family based on the Saṃgha: [This refers to using the authority of the monastic community to manipulate or harm a family.]

*Galaṃ-ujjhita-kula* (Polluting the Family): This refers to giving flowers, fruits, or other offerings from the Saṅgha to laypeople (*avadātavasana*), causing them to constantly long for monastic gifts and to mistake what is improper for what is right; therefore, it is called "polluting the family. The *Pāpabhikṣu-vinaya* states:
"To perform various evil deeds that destroy the virtuous mind of faith and respect is called 'polluting the family.

An evildoer who acts in this impure, defiled, and turbid manner will further obtain evil fruits. Thus, if one gives even a small thing as a gift to a layperson [with such intent], it constitutes this offense.

Even if one were to erect variously adorned stupas made of the seven treasures and establish monasteries like Jetavana, and provide the four requisites of support to all the holy ones throughout Jambudvīpa, it would not equal the merit of sitting in quietude and purely maintaining the precepts—thereby making offerings to the true Dharma-body.
Regarding "not transgressing," this Vinaya states: "If one provides [support] to one's parents, the sick, or those who are imprisoned..."
There is no offense for those confined in prison or for those working as laborers within a monastery.
This concludes the ninth brief commentary on the third section, the *Nissaggiya* (requisites) rules. (The Great Bhikṣus likewise possess thirty such precepts, twelve of which differ from these).

The precept regarding staying apart from one's robes (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*) consists of six conditions: first, the five robes belonging to oneself; second, having accepted the formal procedure (*dharmic-acceptance*);

third, the robes and the person being in different locations; fourth, not having relinquished them or been reunited with them; fifth, being without a valid cause or condition; and sixth, the appearance of dawn. Regarding the person and the robes being in different locations, there are four types of distinctions.

The first is "obstruction by defilement" (*rajas-āvaraṇa*), meaning that if there is a man within the same boundary, it is called an obstruction by defilement. Therefore, the Vinaya says: "In all cases..."
When a bhikṣu removes his robes and his body is exposed in a layperson's house, the Buddha said: "Except within the village or outside the boundaries of the village.

Thus, one knows that when a robe is not contained within the village, it is termed an "obstruction by defilement" (rañjanāvaraṇa). Second is the "obstruction by separation" (vyavadhānāvaraṇa): according to this Vinaya, if the path—whether by water or land—is cut off and so forth, one does not commit an offense regarding being separated from one's robes.

Third is the "obstruction by circumstance" (cittāvaraṇa): according to this Vinaya, this refers to cases such as the perception of loss or seizure, wild beasts, threats to life, or the perils of the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya), where the robes are lost.

Regarding the non-offense concerning robes, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "When a king enters a territory to stay overnight, even if his calls of nature are nearby, these do not constitute the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*), because they are separated by [the king's] intention.
Fourth is the obstruction of boundaries. According to this Vinaya, there are eleven kinds of natural robe-boundaries:

first, the monastery; second, the village boundary; third, the tree boundary; fourth, the threshing-floor boundary; fifth, the cart boundary; sixth, the boat boundary; seventh, the house boundary... [and so forth].
The eighth is the boundary of the hall; the ninth is the boundary of the storehouse; the tenth is the boundary of the granary; and the eleventh is the boundary of the araṇya.
Regarding the two boundaries—the monastery and the village—each is established by four marks. If these are present, they do not constitute multiple boundaries;

rather, because the principles of the "monastery" and "village" boundaries are predominant, the preceding nine boundaries are subsumed into a single boundary. However, if these four marks are not complete, all the boundaries remain distinct and arise separately.

There are eleven types of boundaries (*dharmapada*) because they arise [from different conditions]; thus the Vinaya states "various boundaries" (referring to the three internal obstructed boundaries). First, a perimeter wall; second, an enclosure fence that does not encircle the entire area;
third, a fence or wall that does not encircle the four sides; fourth, an enclosure with buildings on all four sides.

This Vinaya further states that each of these eleven boundaries has its own "sphere of influence" (*pradeśa*), which extends an additional thirteen paces. Thus the Vinaya says: "It is the distance reached by a stone thrown by an average person."
Regarding the location for this view, the *Śāstra* states: "A person of medium stature" refers to one who is neither robust nor frail;
taking such a person, one throws [an object] with all one's strength to where it falls, rather than where it rolls (the calculation of the various masters' opinions is thirteen paces).

If one places a robe within any of the eleven types of boundaries while one's own body is outside the boundary and one sleeps there, provided one has not relinquished [the robe] and does not reach the place where a stone thrown from there would land, then at the appearance of the first light of dawn, one commits an offense for each [instance].

Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* [offense]: if there is a man within the boundary who holds the robe, it must remain close to the body; otherwise, when the dawn light appears, one commits the offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*), because there is no sphere of influence (*prabhāva*).
Furthermore, according to other schools, there are four types of robe-boundaries (*cīvara-sīmā*): first, for a traveler on a road.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that if one carries a robe with a teacher while traveling on a road, the robe is not lost as long as one remains within forty-nine *vyāma* (fathoms) behind or ahead. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: "Even if..."
Within forty-nine *vyāma* across, one does not lose one's robe. Regarding the two continents and the upper realms, the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Observations) states:
"On a water-continent, within fourteen *hasta*, one does not lose one's robe; if someone comes and goes, the robe must remain close to the body, otherwise one loses it.
Regarding the water realm, the *Jianlun* states: "If a bhikṣu is in a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*) and enters a pool at night to bathe..."

Regarding the rule on the "transgression of losing [the robe] at dawn," the *Śamathadeva-śāstra* states: "If one foot is on the bank and one foot is in the water, even if the dawn has passed, the robe is not lost.
Regarding the four types of well-boundaries (*udapāna-sīmā*), the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"When traveling on a road and staying overnight beside a well-railing in the open air, if all the robes are within twenty-five cubits (*hasta*) and one stays overnight outside that area, one loses the robe; or if one places the robes inside the well and stays outside..."

If one stays overnight in an elevated place without securing oneself with a rope, or if one’s hands and feet hang down until the light of dawn appears, one commits an offense in each case (as do other instances such as staying in pits or cellars).

The *Mingliao lun* states: "When traveling on a road and staying overnight, if one mistakenly takes another person's robe and leaves while keeping one's own robe, one loses one's own robe [but does not incur an offense regarding the other's]."

The precept against hoarding precious objects is violated through four conditions: first, it must be money or treasure; second, one must know it to be such; third, it must be for one's own sake; and fourth, one must take possession of it. (This precept is violated by the act of hoarding;

the mention of "handling" in the text indicates the intent at the moment of possession. Handling itself is covered by the separate precept against handling treasures. Treasure is counted as one of the eight types of impure wealth.

A comprehensive enumeration of the names of these eight impure items is found throughout the sūtras and śāstras: first, fields and houses; second, planted orchards and groves; third, [servants]; fourth, [cattle]; fifth, [grain]; sixth, [gold and silver]; seventh, [uncooked grain]; and eighth, [raw silk].
1. Accumulating salt and grain; 2. Keeping the four types of domestic animals; 3. Keeping male and female slaves; 4. Raising herds of livestock; 5. Storing gold, silver, and coins; 6.

Possessing beds inlaid with gold and silver, brocade mattresses, and woolen carpets; 7. Possessing copper and iron cauldrons and pots (except for sixteen vessels, which do not constitute an offense); 8. [Possessing] items made of gold and silver.

To keep these eight things is to perpetuate greed, destroy the Path, and defile the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*); furthermore, it results in impure fruits. Therefore, they are called "impure. Next, the exceptions are explained.

Regarding whether or not one may possess [property]: first, as for fields and houses, there is no opening [of acceptance] whatsoever; only a single small room for the sustenance of the body is permitted, and if it belongs to another person, accepting it is not an offense.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If someone offers a field, house, or shop to the Saṃgha, the Buddha said:

'I allow you to accept it, provided that a *karmadāna* (pure attendant) manages it. Second, regarding gardens and ponds, others do not permit their acceptance. The *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: "A layperson..."
If one gives a pond as a gift to the Saṃgha for the purpose of providing washing and irrigation, as well as for the drinking water of sentient beings, one may accept the third type of stored goods:
salt and grain. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu, when purchasing [grain], forms this thought: 'In the future, it will likely become expensive;

I shall purchase this grain now so that those who recite sūtras, practice dhyāna, and cultivate the Path may rely upon it,' he may do so. Furthermore, there is no restriction on the quantity; whether three or five *shí*, he should be permitted to store salt."

Following the above exemptions, these are medicines for life; there are no other exemptions. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu obtains grains, rice, and so forth, he should perform the ritual of purification (*kalpa*) on that very day.

If no layperson is present, he may perform the purification before the fourfold assembly. If he does not perform the purification, by the time the night has ended, he must perform a confession for an offense of transgression (*duṣkṛta*).

The method of purification is as stated above. Fourth, regarding the keeping of male and female slaves: The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If someone offers a woman to the Saṃgha to provide service..."
The *kappiya-kāraka* (purifier) may accept [the gift]; however, if it is given to an individual, nothing at all may be accepted.

If it is given to the *kappiya-kāraka* for the purpose of providing for the Saṃgha, an individual may accept it. Fifth, regarding the raising of livestock: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that one should not accept any living beings.
Regarding other wild birds and beasts, if they are not accepted, one should say: "I shall kill them; you must find your own way."
Guard aquatic plants so as not to harm them; one must not clip their wings or tether them in cages.

If they are capable of flying and sustaining themselves on their own, release them and do not bind them. The *Dīrghanakhaparivrājakaparipṛcchā-sūtra* states: The Buddha said, "Great King, within my Dharma there are bhikṣus;
even if they act in accordance with the Dharma, starting from one person up to four persons, I do not permit [the following]."

Regarding the acceptance of fields, houses, gardens, elephants, horses, slaves, and other such property belonging to the permanent community of monks (*saṃgha*), it may only be accepted if five or more persons are present.
The *Yījiàofǎlǜ* (The Law of the Bequeathed Teachings) states: "Riding in vehicles or on horseback for one day eliminates the merit of five hundred days of fasting;
for one year—three hundred and sixty days—it eliminates the merit of one hundred and eighty thousand days of fasting. This is from the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*.

Therefore, regarding monks riding on vehicles—excluding the merit of a five-hundred-day fast—the Buddha said: "A monk who knows the prohibitions and the Vinaya may be slandered by others upon being seen [riding], causing them to incur sin;
however, this does not apply to those who temporarily ride due to old age or weakness. Regarding the sixth [prohibition], the keeping of gold, silver, and money:
the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that if a layperson offers gold or silver as the price for robes, it is permissible to accept it, but one must not take it with one's own hands.

If one has a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle things), one should have them know [the location]; if there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, one should point to the ground at one's feet and say, "Know that it is here.
Having placed it on the ground oneself, one should use grass, leaves, bricks, tiles, or the like to cover it from a distance so as to let people know it is being taken away.
If one knows that the Buddha possesses gold or silver and wishes to remove it, if it is on native soil (*jātā bhūmi*), one should instruct a *kappiya-kāraka* to dig a pit and place the coins inside.
If [coins] are placed inside or scattered about, one may personally carry bricks or tiles to throw the coins in, or fill them up oneself.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, and the *Samantapāsādikā* state: "If a sick child possesses gold, silver, or coins, one may have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure attendant) keep them for the purpose of trading for medicine.
If many people provide the price for medicine, it is permissible to place it under a woolen rug; when the eyesight is dim and one seeks it by touching with the hand, there is no offense."
Regarding the seventh [prohibition], the *Mātṛkā-vinaya* states: "An individual is permitted to accept an intricately carved large bed, provided it is not made of gold or silver;
this does not constitute an offense under this Vinaya. Regarding the *khuśu* (carpet), it is three *hasta* wide and five *hasta* long, with a pile three finger-widths high;

its acceptance is permitted, provided it has been purified through formal dedication (*pariṣkāra-dāna*) before being kept. Regarding the eighth [prohibition], copper and iron cauldrons and pots—the *Mātṛkā-vinaya* states that earthenware jars are permitted.
The Buddha permitted individuals to accept various vessels such as copper basins and copper helmets. This treatise states: "If one gives vessels to the Sangha, they should be broken;
they must not be sold. As for musical instruments, they must not be kept [by individuals], but may be sold. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"On the occasion of the Great Assembly on the eighth day of the fourth month, when making offerings, [one may offer] gold and silver stupas, images of Bodhisattvas, banners, and offering implements."
If there are items such as gold or silver that have been gilded, one must have a *karmadāna* (pure attendant) hold them; if they fall to the ground, one should assist in picking them up.

In places where there is no gold or silver, if the gilding is extensive, one may hold them by wrapping the hands with a cloth. One must not first lift them and then let go. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"Regarding those who receive precious objects, if they are attached to any part of the body—even down to the hands or feet—or if they are tied within the *saṃghāṭī* robe or the alms bowl, all constitute an offense according to this Vinaya."
One who accepts gold and silver certainly does not follow the Dharma of our Śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"It should be known that such a person will certainly have no faith in my Law and Discipline.

Regarding the precept against trading for valuables, there are five conditions for its violation: first, it must be money or treasure; second, there must be an exchange; third, there must be a fixed price; fourth, it must be for one's own sake.
The fifth [offense] is incurred upon acceptance, because one exchanges wealth for money or precious gems; this offense is not contingent on whether the items are food or clothing.
This precept is violated by the act of bartering itself, which differs from selling for profit, as it involves buying with the intent to resell.
One may give to a lay attendant (*śrāmaṇera*) who is pure, but one must not give to a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), because they would commit the same offense.

Regarding the offense of trading monastic requisites, there are six conditions for its commission: (1) being a layperson; (2) engaging in mutual trade; (3) fixing a price; (4) doing so for one's own sake; (5) trading with one's own hands;

and (6) accepting the goods, at which point the offense is committed. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one trades items that should be relinquished—such as food—the offense is a *duṣkṛta* for every mouthful consumed;
if one makes clothing from them, the offense is a *sthūlātyaya* for every piece worn. If one requires such items, one should deliberate carefully and say: 'I shall [give] this much...'"
If the person from whom one intends to buy an object refuses, one should speak to them a second time; if they still refuse, one should speak a third time.

If it cannot be obtained after these attempts, one should seek out a *kappiya-kāraka* (a "pure" person) and have them purchase it. If the *kappiya-kāraka* does not know how to bargain in the marketplace, one should instruct them:

"With such an amount of goods, purchase this item. One should deliberate carefully and instruct them on how to buy it. If it is purchased in this manner, there is no offense. If the purchased item is cheap here but expensive elsewhere...

Regarding "not committing an offense for profit" (although there is no offense if one instructs a *kappiya-kāraka* to purchase [an item], one must not take it from before the owner; if one instructs [the *kappiya-kāraka*] regarding the upper or lower parts of a *nikāya* [robe] in a secluded place, one commits an offense):

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that when clothing at a marketplace has a previously established price, if a *bhikṣu* brings the price and purchases it, placing it on the ground, he should say: "Know this price to be for this garment.
If he does not say this and silently takes it away, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense. In certain countries, there is a customary law regarding the purchase of goods.
If a person first comes with a fixed price to purchase an item, and the owner shakes his head [in refusal], it should be understood that this is being compared to the case of the bhikṣu.
One should also speak to him, saying: "Know this price for this item.

If the person understands and must speak to oneself before taking it away, yet takes it away in silence, one commits a *vinayātikrama* offense. For example, if a merchant’s goods are worth fifty coins but he demands a hundred coins.

The Master [Kāśyapa] said that one who attains knowledge at fifty does not commit offenses. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one sells or buys privately and the other party regrets it and wishes to reclaim the original object, it is permitted to return it within seven days;
if more than that time has passed, it should not be returned. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: "If the robe of the Saṃgha has not yet been formally offered three times, one may receive a higher price;

once the three proclamations have been made, one should not regret the transaction, and even if one regrets it, it should not be returned. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "One should cause a pure person (śuddha)..."
When people encounter changing times, one should maintain mindfulness in the mind, ensuring that they may obtain benefit for oneself while not depriving others of their benefit.

The *Three Thousand Codes of Dignified Conduct* states that there are five matters regarding teaching others when entering the market to purchase goods: first, one should teach them not to quarrel with others;

second, one should teach them to buy what is pure; third, one must not allow them to encroach upon others; fourth, one must not run about or urge others to hurry; and fifth, one should protect the feelings of others.
The *Five Hundred Questions* states: "There are those who seek profit by selling [merit] to perform acts of merit;

such people cannot even avoid hell, let alone obtain merit, because they do not follow the Buddha’s words. As for those who receive food through invitations from others, if they accept it while violating the precepts, they will fall into poverty and destitution where there is no food.
In such cases, they should have laypeople prepare the food and manage their livelihood. A nun informed the Sangha, saying: "This is so."
If it is white clothing, two or three people may eat it provided they have made the announcement (*ārocana*); if they do not announce it, they commit a *pāyattika* offense.

If one says to the person [handling the food], "This is not my property," it may be eaten. The *Upāliparipṛcchā* states: "Of all the *pāyattika* offenses, this precept against buying and selling is the most serious.
Rather than being a butcher, one should not engage in trade. Why? A butcher harms only one lifetime, whereas a trader..."

They harm all equally, regardless of whether one is a monastic or a layperson, wise or foolish, observant of precepts or a breaker of them; there is nowhere they do not deceive, always harboring evil intent.
Even if they live on grain, they constantly hope for famine and scarcity throughout the world, as well as calamities such as frost and hail.

If they live on salt or other goods, they desire to cause rebellion and disorder in the distant regions and block the royal roads. For these reasons, their offenses are even more grave than those of a butcher. This is how they act.
One must not perform prostrations toward stūpas or images (though one may still receive merit by performing prostrations with the mental intention directed toward the Buddha).

If food is prepared for the Saṃgha or if a monastic cell is built for the Saṃgha, a bhikṣu who maintains the precepts should not consume it or dwell within it; to do so constitutes an offense. Question: If [the donor] dies, can one receive a portion through formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*)?
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One should not engage in contentious speech with any of the ninety-six types of renunciants when purchasing [items from them]."

Regarding this offense, although this Vinaya permits the five groups of monastics to exchange items with one another, it does not permit them to do so according to the methods of the marketplace by allowing prices to fluctuate up or down.

The precept against diverting property belonging to the Saṃgha into one’s own possession consists of four conditions: first, it must be property generally given to the Saṃgha; second, there must be the perception that it is such property; third, [the intent] to divert; and fourth, the act of diversion.

Regarding "entering one's own possession" (svīkaraṇa): as soon as it enters the hand, one commits this offense. This Vinaya states that there are three types of monastic property (*saṃghika-vastu*): 1. **Property already assigned to the Saṃgha**:

This refers to property belonging to the general community of monks (*sarvasaṃgha*) that has not yet been divided into specific portions for individual monks. To divert such property for oneself constitutes an offense requiring forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). 2. **Property not yet assigned to the Saṃgha**: To divert such property into one's own possession does not constitute an offense. How is this known?

Because the Vinaya states that even if one perceives property as not yet assigned [to the Saṃgha], one still incurs a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*). Thus, we know that if it is indeed not yet assigned, one may take it back.

If one has not been granted permission, how could the perception [of ownership] justify committing an offense? Third, having already relinquished it to the Saṃgha, this object certainly belongs to the Saṃgha;

to urge its redirection into one's own possession constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "To redirect it toward other individuals constitutes a *thullaccaya*; to direct it toward a larger group of monks within the Saṃgha constitutes a *duṣkṛta*. Regarding the redirection of property belonging to the animals, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If one wishes to make an offering to this image and redirects [the funds]..."
Regarding the transgression of giving this [monastic] property to that [stupa], according to this Vinaya: if one permits the diversion of monastic property to a stupa;

if one permits the diversion of property belonging to the *saṃmukhībhūta-saṃgha* (the local assembly) to the *cāturdiśa-saṃgha* (the universal assembly); or if one permits the diversion of monastic property to nuns—in each of these cases, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrongdoing). Therefore, the text states "permitting [it] for another place.
If [property] has entered a stupa, it should not be taken back; it belongs to the stupa for use, as its merit is shared. This applies even unto [property] entering among nuns; it is the same. 10.

The *Sòngbālùn* (Commentary on the Vinaya) states: "If a donor gives property intended for the *pravāraṇā* (self-indulgence/invitation) monks and it is diverted to other *pravāraṇā* monks, the goods should be divided among those [intended] monks.
If a bhikṣu does not return them to this [original] sangha, he commits a grave offense (*pārājika*) based on the value of the money;

even diverting the property of a single individual from one person to another constitutes a grave offense. (According to this principle, if property definitely belongs to the Sangha—such as items for the sequence of the assembly, offerings for recitation, or ritual provisions—and one diverts private items to share with others, one commits an offense.)"
Regarding grave offenses: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that it is a grave offense for a nun to solicit offerings, or even to accept them with partiality or bias;

it is also a grave offense to solicit items on behalf of the Saṃgha and give them to one's own relatives. According to this Vinaya, if one diverts property belonging to the Saṃgha, once the diversion is complete, one incurs the offense of "mutual use" (*anyonya-paribhoga*).
Regarding the offense of begging for ghee and oil, there are five conditions for its commission: first, it must be from a householder who is not a relative;

second, one must request ghee in person; third, one must not return it if it is not used; fourth, one must subsequently request another item; and fifth, the offense is committed as soon as the other item is received into one's hand.

The underlying principle is that if one begs for ghee but receives something else, there is no *pratideśanīya* (offense requiring confession). Since the offense arises from the consumption of food, if the food is not eaten and is returned to the owner, there can be no transgression.

If there is indeed an offense involving a transgression and the four permissible conditions—namely, a formal invitation, a repeated invitation, a lifelong invitation, and the permission to request medicine—then there is no fault in requesting it directly.
If there were a fault in requesting it directly, why would it be necessary to establish the separate transgression of mutual solicitation?
The rules regarding diverting food intended for the assembled Saṃgha to instead provide the five robes and requisites are understandable.
However, if a layperson sincerely offers food, or if one obtains food through begging, it is a transgression to divert its value for other uses.
The precept against keeping an extra bowl is violated when five conditions are met: (1) one already possesses and maintains a bowl; (2) one further acquires another vessel;

(3) one does not perform the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification/declaration); (4) one is not subject to causes such as insanity; and (5) the dawn breaks, at which point the offense is incurred. The sixteen types of vessels are:
a large cauldron, its lid, a large basin, a large ladle, a small cauldron, its lid, a small basin, and a ladle; a water jar and its lid.

There are two large water basins with ladles, two washing bottles with bottle lids, and two small basins with ladles; in total there are two cauldrons, four basins, two bottles, and four ladles, making sixteen items including the lids.
If these exceed the prescribed length and have not been formally purified (*paryavadāpana*), one commits an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

The *Mātṛkā-vibhāṣā* states: "Among these sixteen items, if any one exceeds the length, it must be given away that very day, either to a layperson or to a nun. Otherwise, one commits an offense of falling (*pāyattika*)."
Regarding the offense of forcibly seizing monastic robes after having traded for them, there are five conditions for its commission: first, a mutual exchange; second, the determination of the price;

third, the equivalence of value; fourth, the act of forcible seizure with a mind of anger; and fifth, the acquisition of the object, at which point the offense is incurred. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"If a nun has finished trading robes with the Great Assembly (the monks) and subsequently regrets it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a nun discards her old *saṃghāṭī* robe and someone [offers a new one]..."

Regarding the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* for giving away, taking back, mending, or reclaiming [an item], and the offense of *pāyattika* for reclaiming other minor miscellaneous items after having given them to another:
these are now briefly explained as follows. (From the *Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya*, Chapter One Hundred and Eighty-Eight). (Note: "大僧" refers to the *Mahāsāṃghika*).
There are ninety precepts, and there are twenty-one precepts that differ from those for nuns.

Regarding the precept against minor lying (*anṛtavāda*), it is committed when six conditions are fulfilled: first, a person; second, the perception of them as a person; third, speaking in contradiction to that perception;

fourth, knowing one is speaking in contradiction to that perception; fifth, the completion of the speech; and sixth, the listener’s understanding—upon these, the offense is incurred. The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Lying, divisive speech, and harsh speech..."
These characteristics are combined to form four permutations: first, there is false speech that is not double-tongued or harsh speech. One transmits these words from one person to another;

because it is untrue, it is called "false speech," but because there is no intention to cause separation, it is not "double-tongued," and because it is spoken with gentle words, it is not "harsh speech.
The presence or absence of the remaining permutations can be understood by analogy with the above. The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "The other three types of verbal karma..."

Whether combined or separate, the single category of frivolous speech (*sambhinnapralāpa*) is necessarily never dissociated from them. The *Upāliparipṛcchā* states: "Regarding one who does not speak falsely:

if one explains the Dharma, engages in debate, or transmits messages—regardless of whether they are right or wrong—one must never claim for oneself that 'this is correct. One should always ensure that [one's words] are traced back to their source;
then there will be no fault. Otherwise, this axe shall be in one’s mouth. According to this Vinaya, when the Saṃgha recites the precepts... the third [case].

Question: If one remembers that an offense has been committed but does not declare it, or if one speaks otherwise than the truth, or if one speaks perversely, or if one speaks in a loud voice such that the meaning is not understood, or if one says something and the person before one does not understand—it is stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* that these all constitute offenses.
Specifically, if one addresses a person of high caste as being of low caste, it is a *pāyattika*; if one addresses a two-eyed person as being one-eyed, it is likewise a *pāyattika*.

Committing a *pāyattika* offense for lying, and another *pāyattika* for intentionally annoying a bhikṣu; speaking to a one-eyed person, saying, "You are a blind person," constitutes a *pāyattika* for annoying others.

Regarding the precept against abusive speech, there are six conditions for its transgression: first, it must be a bhikṣuṇī; according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, abusing those in the three lower assemblies also constitutes an offense.

1. Regarding the offense of self-deprecation: the *Vinayavibhaṅga* states that it is an offense of expiation (*pāyattika*) to speak in such a way as to disparage oneself. 2. Regarding the offense of repeating the words of others to insult: it is an offense of expiation to repeat the words of another to insult someone.

3. One must know that this constitutes disparagement. 4. One must act with the intent to humiliate the other person. 5. The speech must be completed. 6. The person addressed must hear and understand it; only then is one guilty of this rule.
The *Vinaya* defines "insulting speech regarding class" (*jātivyabhicāra-vāda*) as follows: "Born into a low-caste family, your occupation is low, and your craft and skill are also low. If one says:
"You are a person who has committed an offense. Even if one speaks according to the facts, it constitutes an offense against the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa*. The *Vinaya* states:

"If one reviles a *bhikṣuṇī*, one’s parents, or others by means of grave and evil speech—saying 'Your parents are such-and-such,' you incur a *Thullaccaya*; saying 'Your preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or teacher (*ācārya*) are such-and-such,' you incur a *Dukkaṭa*;

saying 'Your companions are such-and-such,' you incur a *Viniyatika*. The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "Although these are words of truth, because they are spoken at an improper time, they constitute frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*)."

The precept against divisive speech (*paiśunya*) is violated when six conditions are met: first, it must be a nun; second, she speaks of base and evil matters; third, one knows these to be evil matters;
fourth, one transmits them from one party to another; fifth, the words are finished; sixth, the listener understands them—only then is there an offense.

According to this Vinaya, "divisive speech" means causing strife between parties and leading to their separation. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "To report evil matters by saying, 'So-and-so says you are [such-and-such]...'"
Regarding the superior, middling, and inferior dharmas, if one desires to cause others to turn away from oneself, whether they actually turn away or not, the *Devī-sūtra* states:
"If, after having spoken, one speaks again, and if this speech is not transmitted [to others], but causes both sides to become estranged, all such cases are auspicious."
The precept against sleeping in the same room as a man involves five conditions for its transgression: first, it is a man; second, the characteristics of a "room" (*śālā*) are present;
third, they sleep together; fourth, one knows they are sleeping in the same room; and fifth, the transgression occurs with every turning over. According to this Vinaya, there are four types of rooms:

first, those enclosed on all four sides and covered above (meaning if they are in the same hall but separated by partitions, this does not conform to the *Śāstra*); second, those open at the front and without... [text truncated].

1. A room with walls (referring to a hall with screens at both ends under the eaves); 2. One that is covered but not completely (referring to one surrounded by walls with its top fully covered, yet having a skylight in the center); 3. One that is completely covered but has openings (referring to one that is generally covered but has gaps or holes above); 4.
One that is completely covered but has open spaces (referring to one that is fully covered but has fissures or apertures in the ceiling).

In these four types of rooms, if a *bhikṣuṇī* sleeps together with a man—regardless of who arrived first or last, and whether they merely lie side-by-side or turn over against each other—she commits a *pāyattika* offense for every instance. This applies equally if she sleeps with an animal.
Regarding those such as eunuchs and those with both sexual organs, [if] a bhikṣuṇī who has been ordained for many years lies down during the day while a man stands, it is permissible;
however, if the man sits, it constitutes an offense. The *Tiānpó lùn* (Devadatta-śāstra) states:

"If people gather together within the same enclosure, even if there are various small rooms inside the hall, because the chambers share the same space, they still constitute a single room. If there are many... [the text continues].

If one shares a single door with another room and conceals [the offense], it is an offense; this applies even if the wall of the house is made of cloth partitions, or if one sleeps together for as long as half a cubit in height—it is all an offense.
If one sleeps together with ten men, there are ten *pācittiya* offenses;

for every time one gets up and lies down again, one incurs ten *pācittiya* offenses; for every time one turns over, one incurs ten *pācittiya* offenses. This same rule applies if [one stays] in the house of a layperson (*avadātavasana*).
If a man shares a room with another and does not close the door, it is auspicious.

Regarding the precept against staying overnight with one who has not received full ordination (*upasampadā*), the offense is established through five conditions: first, the person has not received full ordination;
second, they are either male or female; third, the rooms are connected; fourth, one stays together with them; and fifth, the stay exceeds three nights. These constitute the offense.
The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* states: "If one has already stayed overnight with a śrāmaṇerī for two nights and stays overnight with a male on the third night, one incurs two *tissa-āpatti*s.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "On the third night, the offense is complete. If one does not repent before staying overnight again later, the offense increases further; there is no allowance for a second night.
Once the repentance has been performed, one should stay in a separate room, after which one may obtain [the allowance] for two nights again. This is according to this Vinaya.
If there is no further place to stay, one may have a śrāmaṇera or a layperson leave before the dawn of the third night has appeared, or one may leave oneself;

this is also permitted for the sake of protecting against the appearance of dawn. However, regarding the fourth night, whether one leaves oneself or sends the other away, there is no further allowance.

To recite the precepts together with one who has not received full ordination (*upasampadā*) entails an offense when five conditions are met: (1) the teaching spoken by the Buddha; (2) two words or phrases;

(3) the person who has not received full ordination; (4) reciting in unison; and (5) the completion of the utterance. The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If the voice and the phrases coincide, it is a *thullaccaya*;
if the voice coincides but the phrases differ, it is a *duṣkṛta*."
The precept against speaking of another’s grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) to one who has not received full ordination involves seven conditions for its transgression:

first, being a *bhikṣu* or *bhikṣuṇī*; second, having committed an offense of the first two categories; third, knowing [of the offense]; fourth, there being no legal exemption (*anāpatti*) granted by the Saṃgha; fifth, addressing someone who has not received full ordination; sixth, the verbal expression being clear;
and seventh, the person addressed understanding it—then the offense is incurred. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that a *bhikṣuṇī* may speak of a *bhikṣu* to a layperson (*avadātavasana*).
The *Devānuśāsana-śāstra* states generally regarding minor transgressions (*duṣkṛta*): "It is better to destroy a stūpa or damage an image than to speak of the gross offenses of others;

if one speaks of them, one destroys the Dharma-body. This rule applies regardless of whether the person has committed an offense or not; whoever speaks in this manner commits a *duṣkṛta*. This Vinaya further states:
"If one mentions another's name, their clan, their physical appearance, their clothing, or their dwelling, or if one speaks of oneself..."
All such offenses constitute *thullaccaya*.

Regarding the precept against teaching the Dharma to a man for more than five or six words, the offense is complete when six conditions are met: first, there is a person who is a man; second, one knows him to be so;
third, he has not requested instruction; fourth, there is no wise laywoman present; fifth, the words of the discourse are completed; and sixth, it exceeds five or six words.

Regarding the rule concerning speech, it is stated that one who is invited may speak no more than five or six words. If one speaks without being invited, it constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense) for every phrase according to its meaning.

"Five words" refers to: form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all non-self (*anātman*). "Six words" refers to: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are all impermanent (*anitya*).
If one adds even a single further phrase, it becomes an offense under the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, which states: "If one speaks six phrases..."
It has already been stated that one should say, "May you quickly reach the end [of your life]. If one obtains the *Devī-śāstra*, it says:
"A wise woman—one who understands human sentiments—may serve as a witness; there is no offense. If one speaks to a young boy, it is auspicious.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Whether blind or deaf, they are also called 'non-persons. One blind person and one deaf person count as one person. If [the other] is also asleep..."
It is said that if one speaks to a man who is like a father or a brother, one commits an offense of the fivefold division (*pañcāpatti*).
However, if one recites a sutra for oneself and a man comes to listen, or asks about essential points and one explains them for the sake of resolving his doubts, there is no offense.
The offense of digging the earth requires five conditions for its commission: first, it must be native soil; second, one must perceive it as native soil; third, one digs it oneself;
fourth, when causing another to dig, one does not utter the "purifying speech" (*jñapti-vākya*); fifth, the damage is as much as the tip of a mosquito's leg, at which point the offense is incurred.

According to this Vinaya, if one instructs another to dig without uttering the purifying speech, it constitutes a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), regardless of whether the person being instructed is present or absent. If one digs it oneself, [the same applies].

If one digs up one *pācittiya* [offense] and stops midway, for each [subsequent] *pācittiya*, if one causes another person to dig up one *pācittiya*, or if one speaks with heavy words or digs rapidly, word for word it is a *pācittiya*.

The *Saṃghāṭi-vinaya* says: "Running back and forth, desiring to cause the ground to collapse, or even throwing objects so as to injure [beings] down to the size of a mosquito's leg—all these are *pācittiya*.
If one nails a wall inside a room and damages it, it is a *pācittiya*."
One who commits this incurs a *vinaya-āpatti* of transgression; however, there is no offense if there was a pre-existing hole, nor if the ground contains sand or stones.
The *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing) states: "If a wild fire approaches the monastery, one may clear away grass or dig the earth to protect the dwelling and cut off the fire's path;
even if one holds fire in the hand and throws it to the ground, there is no offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "There is no offense if the ground is covered."

The precept against destroying living seeds is violated when five conditions are met: first, it must be one of the five types of living seeds; second, one must perceive it as a living seed; third, one destroys it oneself;
fourth, one does not employ the "pure speech" (vāk-karaṇīya) that acknowledges its purity; and fifth, the object is actually damaged, at which point the offense is committed.

According to this Vinaya, there are five types of living seeds: first, roots; second, branches; third, joints; fourth, bulbous roots; and fifth, seeds from seeds. Furthermore, there are five methods for rendering these seeds pure: first, fire; second, [wind]; third, [salt]; fourth, [frost]; and fifth, [the hand].
1. Cutting with a knife; 2. Wounding with a finger-nail; 3. Breaking with a blade; 4. Piercing with a bird’s beak; 5. Unfit for sowing.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Roots and stalks are purified by cutting with a knife; joint-seeds are purified by cutting with a knife or by removing the sprouts and eyes;
heart-seeds, such as those of the radish, ginger, and dock, should be purified by crushing; and seed-pods, such as rice and wheat, are purified by removing the husks. If...

In general, purification by fire (*tejovisodhana*) applies to all five types [of fruits]. Among the five kinds of fruits, those with seeds inside the rind—such as dates, apricots, and the like—should be nicked with the fingernails for purification;
once purified, they may be eaten after the pit has been removed, though if purified by fire, they may be eaten with the pit intact.

Those with seeds in the skin—such as *bījapūra*, pears, crabapples, and the like—all require purification by fire. However, if any ripe fruit falls naturally, it does not require further purification.
If one is wounded by wood or stone as slightly as a mosquito's leg, it becomes pure; one should remove the seeds and eat the husks.
Regarding fruits whose seeds are the fruit itself, such as coconuts, walnuts, and pomegranates, these all require purification by fire.

Regarding grains whose seeds are the fruit itself, such as coriander, sesame, and linseed, those that are seedless should be purified by crushing and rubbing, while those with seeds should be purified by fire. Regarding horn-fruits whose seeds are the fruit itself, such as large and small beans: [the same applies].
If these seeds have not yet been processed, they should be purified by crushing; once processed, they should be purified by fire.
Regarding the *māmāte* (storehouse), if it has not been purified and one fears that young nuns who do not know the Dharma might [handle them], one should have someone purify them with fire.

Even if, at a later time, one constantly says "thresh them away," there is no offense (other cases should be understood by analogy). If one throws five types of living seeds into a pond, a well, or into water containing excrement or urine...

If one steps on excrement from a refuse heap, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*; if it causes death, it is a *pārājika*. If one steps on grass or wood with the intent to cause death, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*;

if it injures [the victim] as little as a mosquito’s leg, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). This applies equally whether standing, sitting, or lying down. Regarding moss growing on stones or hair growing on cakes, these must be handled by a lay attendant (*karmadāna*);
otherwise, one commits an offense. If they have been dried in the sun, they may be stripped away; however, floating duckweed in water may not.

If one finds a place where cattle or horses have passed, one may take water for use. If there is no such path, one should seize a clod of earth or a stone and throw it upward, saying, "Go up to the Brahma-heaven!
When it falls back down, one may take water from the opening it has made. If one overturns duckweed in the water, it is a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense.

If it lands on the bank, it is a *thullaccaya* offense. When entering the water to wash, [if the water is... (Note: The source text appears to be a fragment of a monastic disciplinary code (*vinaya*), likely from a Chinese translation of a Sanskrit text. The final phrase is incomplete.)

If grass touches one's body, one should douse it with water or enter the water. Regarding the violation of the *vinaya* concerning the "morning fungus" (*cāojùn*), the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing) states:

"If one requires flowers or fruit, one may climb the branch oneself and have a *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) take them; it is also permissible to embrace the *kappiya-kāraka* while they take them. The *Wufen* (Five-Part Vinaya) states:
"In all matters concerning plants and trees, if there is a need for something, one should say to the *kappiya-kāraka*: 'You know this.'"
If he does not understand, one should speak again, saying, "Look at this. If he still does not understand, one should speak again, saying, "I must have this.

This Vinaya does not say that looking at it constitutes an offense; the same applies to the destruction of ground. If grass grows covering a path, and one clears a way by tying it up, breaking branches, or stripping leaves, there is no offense, because it was not done intentionally.

The precept regarding the spreading of monastic bedding in an open space involves six conditions for an offense: first, it is a bed belonging to the Saṃgha of the four directions; second, one knows [it belongs to the Saṃgha]; third, it is an open space; fourth, one spreads it oneself or causes another to spread it;
fifth, upon departing, one neither picks it up oneself nor causes another to pick it up; sixth, as soon as one passes through the gate, the offense is incurred.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, because he did not sit or lie down but failed to pick it up, the Buddha declared it to be a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation) even in the case of a layperson’s house.
If one borrows monastic bedding and does not put it away after eating, it is also a *thullaccaya* offense.

If a person in charge of monastery affairs has left monastic bedding out in the sun to dry, and a monk sits or sleeps beside it [without moving it]—this is considered a minor fault (meaning that because a strong wind blew, he was unaware of it). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

if a statue is placed upon a monastic bed and a bhikṣu touches it with his hand while prostrating, and does not move it, it is also a *thullaccaya*; this applies even if many people are prostrating and all touch it with their hands.
Regarding "contact" as the final factor, this rule constitutes an offense upon exiting [the boundary] (because one has formed the intention not to return).
The precept concerning the spreading of monastic bedding in a secluded place involves six conditions for an offense: first, it is monastic property; second, one knows it is monastic property;

third, it is a secluded place; fourth, it is used for one's own sake; fifth, one neither picks it up oneself nor instructs another to pick it up; and sixth, one either crosses the boundary or passes beyond [the designated area].
The offense is committed after three nights.

Regarding the precept against forcibly spreading out monastic bedding to disturb others, the full offense is established through five conditions: first, having previously borrowed a dwelling and already settled within it;

second, knowing that another has already been residing there; third, intending to cause them disturbance and annoyance; fourth, forcibly spreading one's bedding in the midst of their space; and fifth, [the act being completed].

Regarding sitting or lying down [inappropriately], the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If, for the purpose of annoying others, one opens a door and then closes it, makes a sound when opening and a sound when closing, kindles a fire, lights a lamp, performs incantations, continues the recitation of sutras, or preaches the Dharma—whenever such acts cause another to be displeased—one commits a *pāyattika* offense."
The precept regarding water containing insects involves four conditions for its violation: first, the water contains insects; second, one knows that it contains insects;

third, one does not employ the method of filtering; and fourth, one uses the water as intended. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If the insects are minute, one should construct a triple-layered filter.
If insects still remain, one should separately dig a well. If, upon careful inspection, insects are found, one should abandon the place where one resides and depart."
When using water containing insects as a skillful means for sprinkling, one should lift the bowl once with each exhalation; according to the number of breaths, there shall be as many lifts.

If one causes another person to sprinkle it, one should lift once for every word spoken. If one causes another to sprinkle rapidly, one should lift once for every word. Insects represent impermanence:

they may have existed before and now not exist, or they may have not existed before and now exist. Therefore, one must examine the water carefully every day and use it only when no insects are present.

The precept against eating in a group consists of seven conditions for its transgression: first, there is a donor; second, there is an invitation by the Saṃgha in order, or a separate invitation, or a separate request;
third, it concerns the five types of formal food within the proper time; fourth, the place of eating constitutes a group; fifth, one knows that bhikṣuṇīs within the boundary have not assembled;
sixth, there is no valid reason; and seventh, each swallow constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. This Vinaya makes no distinction between laypeople and monastics; all are subject to the same rule.
The *Śiṣyānuśāsana-śāstra* (Treatise on the Views of the Almsgiver) states: "It is necessary to separately invite four people so that together they constitute a formal assembly (*gaṇa*).

If, at the same seat, one person covers his bowl and does not eat while waiting for the other three to finish eating, and he eats afterwards, there is no offense. Thus, it is known that receiving [the meal] together constitutes a formal assembly.
This Vinaya states: "If two or three people eat according to their own wish, those from four people upwards should divide themselves into two groups."

The various sections enter the meal-taking area alternately. (If the distance between the monks outside the gate and those inside the house is sixty-three paces or more, it is not termed a "separate assembly," because they naturally belong to a single boundary.

The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: If within a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) there are two locations for the Saṃgha, and on a single day both have donors providing food—one being a place where the *poṣadha* is observed and the other a place where it is not—then if no one from the latter is invited to the *poṣadha*, nor does anyone send even a single portion of food [to the former], [it constitutes a fault].

This monk commits a *thullaccaya* offense; however, according to this Vinaya, one who is ill does not commit an offense, even down to the case of being lame in the heels, and thus it is not an offense. The *Jianlun* (Treatise on Views) states:
"It means that when sand and dust enter [the wound], one is unable to walk."
The precept against eating at improper times (*vikāla-bhojana*) is violated when four conditions are met: first, it is an improper time; second, there is the perception that it is an improper time;

third, one is consuming food at a proper time; and fourth, with every swallow, one commits the offense. This Vinaya states that "proper time" refers to the period from the appearance of the dawn light until midday;
according to this rule, the same applies to all four continents. The *Vīra-samādhi Sūtra* states that the Buddha spoke on the matter of eating for the Bodhisattva Dharmamati.

There are four types of eating times: the time of the gods (*deva-bhakta*), the time of the Dharma (*dharma-bhakta*), the time of animals (*tiryag-yoni-bhakta*), and the time of hungry ghosts (*preta-bhakta*).

Of these, the latter two types of food frequently cause illness. Monastics should consume food at the time of the gods or the time of the Dharma; therefore, it is called "timely food" (*kāla-bhojana*).
That which occurs after midday is not one of these two superior times, and is thus called "untimely" (*vikāla*). As the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing) states:
If food is vomited but has not yet passed the throat and is swallowed back again, there is no offense. If it has passed the throat, it is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The disciple of Anuruddha was ill and took emetic medicine. After midday, he felt faint. The Buddha said: 'Give him rice gruel squeezed from a bag after straining the juice of paddy, millet, or bamboo shoots.
Even so, he did not recover. The Buddha permitted him to eat rice gruel in a secluded place. (Although this exception exists, one should resort to it only in cases of urgent necessity.)

Regarding the precept against eating leftover food from the previous day, three conditions must be met for an offense to occur: first, it must be leftover food from the previous day; second, one must know it to be so; third, upon swallowing it, the offense is incurred.

According to this Vinaya, if one receives food on the current day, stores it within the boundary, and keeps it until the next day to cook and eat oneself, one incurs seven offenses with every swallow:

namely, three *thullaccaya* (grave offenses) and four *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing offenses). The three *thullaccaya* offenses are: first, not having received [the food formally]; second, eating at an improper time; and third, eating leftover food from the previous day.

The four offenses of *pācittiya* (transgressions requiring expiation) are: 1. cooking for oneself indoors; 2. storing food indoors overnight; 3. cooking for oneself; and 4. receiving food from one who has been touched by an impurity.

Regarding the precept against accepting food [from improper persons], its full conditions can be understood by consulting the *Śāstra*, which states that gods, humans, ghosts, spirits, animals, and even birds can all constitute those from whom food is accepted.
Furthermore, the *Pāśa-śāstra* states that non-humans, animals, and ignorant small children are excluded because they cannot serve as witnesses.

In all cases, one does not perform the formal reception [of the food]. (According to this, when receiving food from an animal, one must understand human speech before it may be received. This Vinaya excludes water and tooth-sticks, as these do not require formal reception.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If dust is blown by the wind, or if a camel shakes its body and dust arises, or even if birds, women, or walking garments drag along the ground and dust arises—if such dust falls upon the bowl, but does not fall upon the food, [it is permissible]."
If one has already completed the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) of food, it must all be accepted again;

however, when an animal shakes its body and food falls [into the bowl], it is considered accepted if one forms the intention (*manasikāra*) to accept it, whereas if one does not form the intention, it is not considered accepted.

Furthermore, when walking with a vessel of roasted flour (*piṣṭaka*), if the flour shakes out and falls into the bowl, it is termed "accepted" if one forms the intention to accept it, but it is not so termed if one does not form the intention.
The same applies to receiving food with other parts of the body. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "A monk with impaired vision may receive food by pressing it [with his hand].

(This implies that when many monks and nuns currently receive food by pressing it against the ground, how does this differ from the blind? The *Samantapāsādikā* states: "If sweat from the forehead flows into the bowl, one must receive the food again;
