If he obtains food, the offense is calculated as a *pārājika* (grave offense). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that coming uninvited is a *duṣkṛta*.

The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states that because of famine, if one invites only one or two people and thereby causes distress to many others, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension from the community). [This applies] regarding the matter of providing for a sick monk or making robes.

Regarding the matter of not committing an offense: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that one may set up canopies and prepare ritual implements for a lay household’s assembly, provided one does not lift objects together with a man.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that a layperson (*avadātavasana*) should borrow bedding from the Sangha (this likely refers to cases where it is mutually beneficial for cultivating merit;

other matters should be prohibited). The *Samyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states that although a śrāmaṇera has not yet received full ordination, he is included in the count of bhikṣus according to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

The Sūtra states that even those who have not yet received the ten precepts may accept an invitation (the aforementioned nuns, śikṣamāṇās, and śrāmaṇerīs are all to be treated according to this precedent).

Third, regarding the notification for the assembly: this Vinaya states that if one wishes to accept an invitation, one should go and stay at the place where the community of monks regularly takes their small and large meals.
When the donor announces that the time has arrived, the elder (upādhyāya) should lead the way, proceeding in a formation like a flight of geese.

When departing, the bhikṣus should walk behind with their right shoulders bared. If there are matters concerning the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, or a sick bhikṣu, they should inform the senior elder (*upādhyāya* or *sthavira*) and proceed ahead.
If there are dangers to life or to the holy life (*brahmacarya*) within the assembly—whether such dangers are announced or not—they are permitted to depart.
If the senior elder must attend to the needs of nature while traveling on the road, the others should wait for his return before proceeding as they did previously.

Furthermore, regarding the fourth point concerning visiting a house for a meal, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Upon arriving at the place of the meal, one should remain silent and single-minded, maintaining pure deportment to inspire wholesome thoughts in others;
one should remove [one's shoes] before entering and sitting. The *Yi* (Commentary) explains: "If one has arrived at the house of the host, but the Buddha’s seat has not yet been set out..."
The nuns must not sit before the seat of the Holy Sangha; rather, one should first install the various scriptures and images in a high and prominent place, ensuring they are extremely pure.
Only thereafter should the seat of the Holy Sangha be spread out. This ritual has five fascicles, which was produced by Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty based on the Chinese Tripiṭaka;
as the text is extensive, it is not recorded here. Now, following the *Pinvilou Jing* (Sūtra on Inviting Piṇḍola), it says: "In advance..."

When making an invitation for the night, one should prepare a seat by spreading soft materials in a high and prominent place; if, when I arrive, there is a sign at the seat, it indicates [the presence of the Sangha].
Nowadays, monks and nuns are mostly arrogant and treat this dharma with contempt and insult, which is particularly contrary to the Buddha’s teachings.

Since they themselves lack reverence, they also cause laypeople to be irreverent toward the Triple Gem; this is the source of the extinction of the Dharma. From now on, the Elder [should act accordingly].

Below, I have further consulted the *Sūtras* and *Vinaya* to supplement the preceding text. Although the arrangement here does not follow the original sequence, it does not deviate from the underlying principle.

When the seat for the Noble Sangha is prepared, it must be large enough to accommodate one person sitting cross-legged; furthermore, the patron should issue an invitation for that night according to the proper time.
The seat itself must be cleaner and more excellent than the seats of the monks, yet one must not scatter thorns or flowers upon it. Furthermore—
If one obtains a seat painted or carved to resemble that of the Buddha, its height must not exceed one chi and six cun;
otherwise, it is no different from an ordinary seat. Furthermore, one must not use the permanent property (sthavira) of the Sangha, such as bowls or basins, to place food before it;

one may only offer flowers. If one uses alms bowls or copper basins, this applies to both the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) and the reward body (saṃbhogakāya), and is in accordance with principle.

Regarding the point that he is the same as ordinary people: although this Piṇḍola is a holy monk whose *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) still endures, the Buddha’s regulations require that he be provided with offerings every day throughout the three continents.
Furthermore, when observing the precepts, he is no different from ordinary monks; how could he break the precepts by occupying a high seat?

Moreover, if he touches the pure vessels of the monastic community, the money belonging to the holy monks must be returned for the use of the holy monks. If there is any surplus remaining, it should be... [taken].
When entering to perform offerings, one may bring items such as the noble seat, alms bowls, bronze basins, spoons, chopsticks, food cloths, temple buildings, lamps, and candles;
however, these must not be brought into the permanent property of the Sangha nor used for private personal ends.

Furthermore, one must not fashion images of the Noble Sangha and place them upon the head of the Sangha hall. If the *saṃbhogakāya* of Piṇḍola himself were to come to receive offerings, how could [an image] possibly suffice?
If one sets aside the original form and sits [in its place], one must not use the property of the Holy Monk (Śāstṛ) to create other forms such as those of Ānanda or Kāśyapa.
Why? Because items belonging to specific individuals may not be used interchangeably; thus, the Vinaya states that what is permitted for this location may not be used for anything else.
Fifth, regarding those who take their seats: this Vinaya states that when Prince Bodhi invited the Buddha, he requested the Buddha to step upon a cloth spread from the foot of the stairs;
the World-Honored One did not accept it and had him remove it for the sake of future bhikṣus. Furthermore, when going to the place of eating, one should not stay in a disorderly or crowded cluster;
rather, one should sit according to the proper order. Once the senior monk (upādhyāya) has taken his seat, [the others] should likewise do so.
When observing those seated in the middle or lower sections, do not allow them to sit improperly or fail to properly cover their bodies. If anyone is so negligent, snap your fingers to alert them;
if necessary, send someone to speak to them so they may sit well and according to the Dharma. Those seated in the middle and lower sections should likewise keep watch over one another.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that "sitting with improper covering" refers to wearing fine, thin, or coarse clothing such that the body is exposed. This is called *mahā*.

Regarding sitting on a low seat (meaning sitting improperly): if a nun sits improperly and does not wait for one to speak, fearing she may feel shame or embarrassment, one should employ a skillful means to have her take some object.
If a courtesan intentionally acts in this manner, one should withdraw from the place oneself.

According to this Vinaya, when visiting a house where an invitation has been received, after the mutual inquiries regarding seniority and age are completed, if one fears that the time for the meal is about to pass, it is permitted for eight senior monks to [invite] the nuns.
Regarding the sequence of seating for those remaining, they sit according to their rank. The *Five Hundred Questions* states:
"If one sits alongside the teacher and there is no other place, may one eat from the same dish? The *Śrāmaṇera-Ācāra-sūtra* states:
"When eating while sitting in a row with the teacher, one should remain six feet away from the teacher. This Vinaya states: "One should not intentionally go to the meal later than the other bhikṣus."
If one sees [something] arising, there is no need to arise; if it is something that has not yet arisen, one should remain seated in the open space (the *bhikṣuṇī* should act likewise).

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If there is something laughable, the elder (*sthavira*) should say: 'How can you show your gums and teeth and laugh "ha-ha" within the Noble Vinaya? You should endure this.
One should arouse the perception of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and death. If it cannot be stopped..."

One should cover the mouth with the corner of one's robe and gradually restrain oneself; if the body is unsteady, one should move the hands and feet, even to the point of breaking off blades of grass, until one gradually attains self-control.
The meaning is that if one arrives at a house where someone has died, one must strictly avoid noisy laughter and must not engage in idle worldly talk that would provoke the derision of the laity.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one arrives at a place of invitation and there is a visiting bhikṣu outside..."
If one is not permitted to enter, one should ask the host, "May I enter? If permission is not granted, one should say, "Give me my share of food;
we shall eat together. If this is still not permitted, one should personally inquire whether there is food available in the *saṃghārāma* and go there to eat.
The *Pāli Vinaya* states: "All [monks] gather outside the gate in one place; call in one senior [monk], and the rest remain behind."

Even those who have not gathered should be summoned; although one may strike the *kanda-ti* (wooden gong), one must ultimately not exclude anyone, for only then is purity attained. (The same applies to *bhikṣuṇīs*).

Nowadays, at places where the *poṣadha* is observed, the presiding elder (*sthavira*) worries only about his own food and new offerings, yet does he ever worry about the transgressions of guests outside the gate, *bhikṣuṇīs*, or those who have separated from the assembly? The entire community incurs guilt [for such negligence]. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
"The World-Honored One, when deliberating, always sits in the midst of the assembly, with the *bhikṣus* on his left side and the pure laymen (*upāsakas*) on his right side."
Regarding the sixth point, pure food: this Vinaya states that the elder should ask whether the fruits and vegetables have been purified (*pariśuddha*).

If they say they have not been purified, he should have them purified. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that the elder should know who is tending the rooms or tending the sick and should tell them to give the food.
If the donor is stingy, one should say, "Long-lived one, according to the Dharma it should be given; you must not refuse to give. This applies if it is already late in the day.
One should first dismiss them and send them away.

Regarding the seventh practice, the *Zengyi Ahan Jing* (Ekottarika Āgama) on incense-offering and prayers states: "When there are those who provide offerings, they hold incense burners and announce that the time has arrived.

The Buddha said: "Incense is the messenger of the Buddha; therefore, it is required. This is also recorded in the *Wubai Wenshi Jing* (Sutra of Five Hundred Questions) and the *Sanqian Wei yi Jing* (Sutra of Three Thousand Dignified Manners).
It is said that one must not stand while receiving incense. Once a bhikṣu received incense from a woman, she touched his hand; lustful thoughts arose and he fell away from the Path. The Buddha said:

"If one stands while receiving [incense], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. (The case of a bhikṣuṇī receiving incense from a man is analogous; however, if the incense is held suspended while standing to receive it, it should be permitted. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that chanting is permitted so that the various devas may hear the hymns and rejoice.
In this Vinaya, after the Buddha had accepted the roasted flour (*maṇḍa*) from the merchants, he then performed the *praṇidhāna* (dedicatory prayer), as in the case of Bianyi.
The *Sūtra on the Son of a Householder* states: "Before eating, one should perform a prayer of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"The senior monk (*sthavira*) should know that he ought to perform a timely prayer of dedication for what has been offered by others; if he is unable to do so, the next seat in rank should speak; if he also cannot, it should continue down to the lowest seat.
If no one does so at all, all incur an offense. The *Saṃyukta-ratnapiṭaka-sūtra* states: "If the bhikṣus preach the Dharma or recite mantras..."

When it comes time to explain, one should appropriately express sorrow, grief, joy, and pleasure; yet now the Teacher speaks falsely, his mouth flowing with flowery words and musical modulations as he greedily pursues worldly matters.
Eighth, regarding the recipient of food: if one wishes to receive food, one should first weigh one’s own virtue and conduct—whether superior or inferior—and only then accept it;
one must not be arrogant, lest one fall into the error of the donor. The *Pō-lùn* (Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya) states:

"That which is produced by a farmer is a fruit of effort (*prayoga-phala*), not a fruit of sovereign power (*adhipati-phala*); whereas eating the flesh of one's own child is a fruit of sovereign power, not a fruit of effort. [The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* also says:]...
The Cloud Sūtra says: "I tell you, monks: suppose this single grain of rice were produced by a hundred days of labor; it represents the share of one's wife and children.
Since it is given for the sake of seeking merit, how can you discard it? The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says: "One should contemplate that this food is difficult to digest and difficult to procure.

The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* says: "Whenever one receives food, one should give rise to a sense of revulsion, [thinking: 'This is for the sake of preserving my physical life,' and furthermore, 'It is a gift of faith received from others.'"
If one uses [offerings] contrary to the Dharma, one will enter the three miserable realms (trāya) and undergo great, heavy suffering.

If one does not undergo the retribution of suffering, yet consumes the offerings of others' faith, then one’s belly shall burst open and the robes shall fall from one’s body. If the donor lacks merit yet still gives, both the giver and the recipient will fall together into the realm of the gift.
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "Food is for the sake of practicing the Path, not for the benefit of the body."
Raising horses and raising pigs are no different. The *Gāthā-śāstra* says: "When receiving food, one should form a thought for every mouthful;

when receiving clothing, one should form a thought for every garment; when entering a room, one should form a thought for every entry. For those of dull faculties, they should form a single thought at the outset regarding food, clothing, and housing.
The commentary states: "At the very beginning, when about to eat, one first offers [the food] to the Triple Gem and to the sentient beings of the six realms."
When eating thereafter, one should maintain mindfulness at every mouthful with the intent of taking refuge in the Triple Gem. When first placing the first spoonful of rice, one should vow:
"May all evil be severed and exhausted. When placing the second spoonful, one should vow: "May the cultivation of all wholesome dharmas be fulfilled.
When consuming the third spoonful of sauce and vegetables, one should dedicate the merit performed toward all sentient beings so that they may together attain Buddhahood. This is...
Is it not of great benefit to receive the Bodhisattva’s Threefold Pure Precepts (tri-śikṣā-saṃvara) with every morsel?

If one cannot maintain this mindfulness for each individual mouthful, one may first form a single collective thought before eating; this is also permissible. As the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing) says:

"If someone offers food to the Buddha, who is entitled to eat it? If there are monks attending upon the Buddha, they should eat it. If there are no monks, even a layperson attending upon the Buddha may eat it."
Regarding the permission to eat [the food]: the *Vinaya* states that those who offer to or repair a Buddha-stūpa may eat [the food].

The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Among all forms of giving, there is none superior to the gift of Dharma; among all karmas, there is none superior to the karma of Dharma; and among all forms of gratitude, there is none superior to the gratitude for the Dharma.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Giving to an animal yields a hundredfold merit; giving to one who has violated the precepts yields a thousandfold merit."
It is said that after [the Buddha] had caused the *āṭavika* yakṣa to receive the precept against killing, he addressed the yakṣa, saying:

"I shall now command my śrāvaka disciples that wherever the Buddha-dharma exists, they must all provide you with food. If there is a place where this cannot be provided, those are merely the followers of Māra and not my disciples.
The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states: "If one gives to beggars, birds, dogs, and the like, it should be..."

One should give according to one’s own means and must not take what belongs to others. The *Sūtra on the Nun Vāsantī* states that when food is given to sentient beings, it increases a hundred-thousandfold.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that when a spirit receives a single mouthful of human food, it increases ten millionfold.
The *Madhyama Āgama* states that if one performs offerings and sacrifices for the deceased, they will enter the realm of hungry ghosts if they were born there.
Those in the intermediate state attain other realms of existence because each has its own means of livelihood and sustenance.

If one’s kinsmen are not reborn within those entry points, then by merely giving, the donor alone obtains the merit. Even when the donor is reborn within the six realms of existence, the merit of the gift constantly follows them.

By maintaining the precepts, one may obtain only a human body; however, this must be assisted by further merit for the retribution to lead to a favorable rebirth. As the Sūtra says: "By means of [the merit of] the deceased..."

Regarding the clothing and belongings of a deceased person used for making merit, the deceased receives one-seventh of the benefit. (According to this scriptural passage, all clothing and belongings possessed prior to death that have not yet been distributed to the body must have merit performed with them early on;

these then belong to those present. This Vinaya states: when a bhikṣu obtains food and eats it immediately, he is censured by the laity. The Buddha ordered that the "equal distribution" (saṃbhojana) be announced before eating.
According to the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya, one waits for the announcement of the equal distribution before eating. If the time [for the meal] is about to pass, one should act accordingly.
Regarding eating without fault, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "From now on, the *upādhyāya* shall wait for the sound of the announcement, 'The meal is served to all,' and so forth;

only then may the entire Saṃgha eat together. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "When a *bhikṣuṇī* arrives at the place of invitation, if she eats before the formal announcement [of the meal], there is a *pāyattika* offense for every mouthful;

for the two other assemblies [the *śrāmaṇera* and *śrāmaṇerī*], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. The *Ekottarika-āgama* states: "When kings provide offerings, they serve the food with their own hands, and commoners do likewise. If this is according to the present *vinaya*:
Request that the Saṃgha of both divisions first grant [the food] to the bhikṣus, lest the time should pass; they should be granted all at once. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"At the time of eating, one should protect the right hand; one should receive the food vessel with the left hand. One must not deeply press the lips against the rim of the bowl, nor touch the forehead or nose with it.
Furthermore, when drinking, one must not finish the contents entirely, leaving a small amount in the mouth. As for rice grains, one should discard them after spitting them out."

If one washes with water those who are noisy and disruptive while eating in the sequence following the lower-ranking *śrāmaṇeras*—fearing that it might damage the faith of the laity—one does not incur the offense of playing with water.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "When food adheres to the hand, one must not shake it off;
one should pick it up. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One must not make a smacking sound with the mouth. The *Naiyāyika-vinaya* states: "One must not eat by snorting through the nose."
Regarding the ninth rule on the method of eating: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that the senior monk (*sthavira*) should eat slowly and must not finish quickly;

he should remain and watch the junior monks so as not to let them eat in a disorderly manner or fail to eat their fill. He should keep a mutual watch over them until the distribution of water is completed and the prayers for blessings (*svastyayana*) have been performed, after which he may then stop.
It further states that when a lay devotee has finished providing a meal for the Saṃgha, he should leave behind some of the remaining food.

The *Liyu Bishapuo Lun* (Treatise on the Li and Bishapuo Schools) states that when monastics—whether monks or nuns—and laypeople have finished their fast, they do not use soap powder, ash, or *kumuda* (gymnema) to rinse their mouths;
otherwise, the fasting rite is not perfected. For example, in the past there was a bhikṣu named Lien-ti who was sixty years old.
He observed the fast precepts without omission, yet on one single day he used *kumuda* and bean flour to complete the rite.
If it were otherwise, none would constitute the fast. According to this Vinaya, it merely states that one knows the time of standing, knows the time of sitting, and knows the time of lying down;
if, during any one of these four modes of deportment, one eats the five kinds of staple food to satiety, the fast is accomplished, regardless of whether one has washed with soap powder.
Regarding the tenth [topic], *dakṣiṇā* (the giving of thanks): The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states that after the Buddha and the bhikṣus had finished eating, they departed in silence.
The donor became suspicious, so the Buddha instructed the elder (*sthavira*) to recite a great *dakṣiṇā*, even if it were only a single verse, which said:

"If one gives for the sake of profit, this profit shall surely be obtained; if one gives for the sake of happiness, one will surely obtain happiness later. This rule first appeared regarding the serving of rice gruel.

If characters cannot be formed on the surface of the rice pot, there is no offense. "Thick" refers to a proper meal; once one has eaten their fill, to eat again constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* for the monk and a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* for the nun.
Furthermore, there are five benefits in receiving a gift of gruel: first, it removes hunger; second, it removes thirst; third, it digests food remaining from the previous day;
fourth, it regulates the large and small excretions; fifth, it eliminates ailments caused by wind. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that there are ten benefits in giving gruel.
Pure in the observance of the precepts, one is honored and respected by others. By offering gruel at the appropriate time, ten benefits accrue to the practitioner:

physical beauty, strength, longevity, happiness, eloquence in speech, the elimination of undigested food and wind-disorders, and the alleviation of hunger and thirst. This is called a "noble medicine" as taught by the Buddha.
Those who desire long life and happiness among gods and humans should offer gruel to the Saṃgha. This is according to the Vinaya, as found in the *Upāliparipṛcchā*.
If the presiding elder (upādhyāya) is unable to preach the Dharma or offer blessings for the donor, he may request another who is capable to do so; if he does not speak, he incurs an offense.
When the great offering (mahādakṣiṇā) is being recited, the four senior monks must remain present while the others are permitted to leave.

The *Sāhasrika-vidhi-sūtra* states: "One must not preach the Dharma for others before having eaten, for fear of falling into wrong livelihood. Therefore, at the beginning of a vegetarian feast, if the monastics have not been invited by the patron (dānapati), [they should not preach].

To have many deceitful intentions and forcibly demand that scriptures be read before one’s meal is also a form of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*). The *Pāramitā-śāstra* states that there are four benefits to preaching the Dharma after one has eaten:
first, to digest the offerings of the faithful; second, to repay their kindness; third, to cause them to give rise to a joyful mind so that their roots of goodness may be fulfilled;
and fourth, because laypeople should practice the giving of material wealth while renunciants should practice the giving of the Dharma. Thus it is seen in the treatises.
It is said that when listening to the exposition of the meaning, one must synthesize the five divisions of the texts. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"When various bhikṣus invited those who had broken the precepts, held wrong views, or possessed impaired faculties to recite hymns (*geya*) and preach the Dharma, these evil persons gained influence and were able to insult the Saṃgha. The Buddha said:

"Invite a Dharma Master who is proficient in the Tripiṭaka and possesses all intact faculties. The *Saṃyuktāgama-śāstra* states: "If there is no one capable of chanting or reciting [the scriptures]..."
In such cases, they should be assigned in order; if there are none at all, each person should recite one verse. One capable of this does not incur a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
This Vinaya prescribes that one should recite the verse: "Commit no evil. The *Ekottarika Āgama* explains:
"To commit no evil" means to be fully endowed with the precepts and pure conduct. "To practice all good" means to have a pure mind; purify your own mind.

This means that the removal of perverse delusions refers to all the Buddha’s teachings; that is, because deluded perceptions are extinguished through the purity of precepts, the purity of intention, and the purity of mind, there is no perversion;
and because there is no perversion, deluded perceptions are extinguished.

Regarding the eleventh point, "Returning to the Monastery": The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that when returning to the monastery, eight senior monks (*sthavira*) wait for one another while the others proceed ahead.
The *Saṃyukta-āgama* states that after the bhikṣus have finished their meal, they all enter the meditation hall to practice dhyāna;

at the third watch (the afternoon), they arise from meditation and preach the Dharma. In these current times of the Final Dharma (*mofa*), monks and nuns, having finished their meals, extensively engage in secular affairs, wandering through marketplaces and streets, filling the thoroughfares and stalls, seeking only profit—how can this be called [the true monastic life]?
[The monk who has left the household life and stilled evil].
Chapter Twenty-Six: Arriving at the Temple.
This chapter has two main sections: first, entering the temple; second, the ritual procedures.
First, regarding entering a monastery: this Vinaya states that when an *āgantuka* (guest) monk hears that others have arrived, he should go outside to welcome them.

He should receive their robes and bowls, arrange them in the *jantāghara* (warm room), the multi-storied pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*), or the walking path (*caṅkrama*), and provide them with water vessels and other requisites.

or she committed the offense of speaking of others, incurring a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, the number of which she does not recall; or she committed the offense of crossing water alone, entering [a village] alone...
I stayed alone in a village; I walked alone at the rear [of the procession], and thereby incurred a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, though I do not recall the number of times.

Or, I accepted food and clothing from a man with a lustful mind, and thereby incurred a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, though I do not recall the number of times. Now, I beg the Saṃgha for fifteen nights of *mānatva*.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience. The Saṃgha grants the fifteen-night *mānatva* to the bhikṣuṇī [Name].
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen: this bhikṣuṇī [Name] intentionally committed the offense of acting as a matchmaker between men and women, thereby incurring a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
I do not recall the number of times I committed offenses resulting in *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meetings of the community) when accusing others of such offenses;

I do not recall the number of times I committed offenses resulting in *saṃghāvaśeṣa* for crossing a body of water alone, entering a village alone, staying overnight alone, or walking behind someone alone;

I do not recall the number of times I committed offenses resulting in *saṃghāvaśeṣa* by accepting food or clothing from a man with a lustful mind. Now, I beg the Saṃgha for fifteen nights of *mānatva* (probation).
[The motion: "The Saṃgha now grants a fifteen-night *mānāttā* to the bhikṣuṇī [Name].
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha granting a fifteen-night *mānāttā* to the bhikṣuṇī [Name], let them remain silent;
whoever does not consent, let them speak. (This is said three times. The Saṃgha has consented and has finished granting the fifteen-night *mānāttā* to the bhikṣuṇī [Name]. The Saṃgha...
Because she has consented by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Regarding the third matter of deprivation: once the *karmavācanā* master has performed the ritual procedure, he shall issue this admonition: "Listen, virtuous woman!

This is a formal motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), a noble teaching and a wholesome medicine; keep it in your heart. Thirty-five matters are hereby deprived. This is the refutation.
One must not violate the rules of subjugation (*vinaya*) by persisting in communal toil; rather, one should further serve pure nuns—this is the method of subjugation.

One should practice each of the eight matters, such as the formal announcement (*jñapti*), in accordance with the Dharma—this is the method of disclosure (*āviṣkaraṇa*). One should increase self-reflection and shame, deeply reproaching oneself, and recollecting and relying upon the practice, making the formal announcement every day so that no omission occurs.
Should there be an omission, one loses the previous day’s merit. If one is arrogant toward oneself and others, having already manifested [one's faults], [one shall be disciplined].
Having finished the instruction, when the Saṃgha has assembled, she shall immediately make this formal declaration:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], have intentionally committed the offense of acting as a matchmaker between a man and a woman, thereby incurring a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense."
I do not recall the number of times I committed an offense and was told by others that I had incurred a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense;
I do not recall the number of times I crossed a body of water alone, entered a village alone, stayed overnight alone, or walked behind someone alone, thereby incurring a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense;

or I do not recall the number of times I accepted food or clothing from a man with a lustful mind, thereby incurring a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. I have already requested from the Saṃgha fifteen nights of *mānatva*. The Saṃgha...
I have already been granted fifteen nights of *mānāpya*. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], from this day forth shall practice *mānāpya*;
I inform the two assemblies of the Saṃgha so that they may know I am practicing *mānāpya*. (Three such announcements.)
If one night has already been completed, the remaining wording is as above, up to:
"The Saṃgha has granted me fifteen nights of *mānāpya*. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], have completed one night;

fourteen nights remain. I inform the two divisions of the Saṃgha so that they may know I am practicing *mānāpya*. (For subsequent days, the procedure is similar, with the number of remaining nights being reduced accordingly.)

The same may be understood by analogy. If the monks and nuns are in separate locations, one should first go to the place where the monks are and announce: "Venerable Sirs," and so forth; the subsequent phrases are the same as those used before and after. Then, one goes to the place where the nuns are and announces: "Sisters, may the Saṃgha listen," and so forth; the subsequent phrases are the same as above.
Fearing that making such announcements separately might be cumbersome, it is better to assemble the two divisions of the Saṃgha in one place and announce them collectively.

When visiting monks or nuns enter the boundary, one should all make the following formal announcement (*jñapti*): "Venerable Sirs, please attend to me with one mind" (the subsequent phrase is the same;

for a senior nun, say "Sister"). This is to inform them that I am practicing *mānatva*. (The intermediate words of the announcement are all the same as the monastic rules. If there are many visiting guests, one should announce:
"All Venerable Sirs (or Sisters), please attend to me with one mind," etc., the rest being the same as above. If the visiting monks or nuns are elderly and advanced in years...
Once the visitor has arrived and been seated within the room, one may then perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*).

At the time of making the announcement, one should always maintain a sense of shame (*hrī*), compassion, and self-reproach, refraining from jesting. The visiting guest, upon receiving the announcement, should likewise feel shame and must not treat it with levity.
Such is the method of practice; both host and guest should instruct visitors on wholesome conduct.

Regarding the fourth case, the *Vinaya* states that when one has obtained *mānatva*, one also practices the method of concealment (*paryavasthāna-dharma*), with the sole exception that one must announce [one's status] daily to the Saṃgha while staying among them.
One should visit pure monks three times each day and perform all actions according to the Dharma without opposition.
On the day of the *poṣadha*, one should sweep and sprinkle the *poṣadha* hall and provide water and utensils.
Śarā and others who reside in small rooms should not sleep together; (however, for nuns on a journey, two may sleep together).
If there are robes or requisites belonging to the Saṃgha, they may take them according to their order of seniority, sitting below the great bhikṣuṇīs and above the śikṣamāṇās.
They must not engage in walking meditation with pure bhikṣuṇīs or share the same bed or plank; a partition must be made between them.

Thereafter, while seated, one should provide service to the pure members of both divisions of the Saṃgha. Upon seeing a guest arrive, one should take over the carrying of their robes and bowl, even down to washing away the latrine;
one must not be negligent or indolent. One should not remain in a secluded room because the guest might not see one;
rather, one should go to a small hut or sit upon a rope bed at the entrance to wait for outside guests, ensuring they do not enter silently.
If one knows that the great assembly is difficult to assemble, or if one does not wish to go, or if that person is weak and possesses much hesitation or shame,
one should go to the Saṃgha and say:
"Venerable sirs, today I relinquish the command and shall not carry it out" (recite this once).
If one wishes to travel, one should return to the Saṃgha and announce:
"Venerable Sirs, today I shall act according to your instructions" (this is stated once).
The *Jianlun* states that for one practicing *parivāsa*, if someone invites them or requests that they confer the precepts upon another, they may suspend their practice of the *parivāsa* method.
When the business is concluded, one may continue traveling; however, if there are many bhikṣuṇīs in the monastery, it is difficult to announce [one's departure].

During the daytime, one may practice the "method of leaving" (*śeṣa-cāra-dharma*), but once the dawn has not yet appeared, one must return and announce the journey again. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that even by night, through announcing to the Saṃgha, one may stay for twenty-five nights.
This Vinaya states that regarding the confession of bhikṣuṇīs, they may perform it alternately with one another, having them perform prostrations and go out to meet [the preceptor].
One may also receive the prostrations of śrāmaṇeras and others; however, there are eight matters that constitute the "loss of the night" (*rātriparihāṇi*) which one must carefully guard against:

first, going to another monastery without informing [the preceptor]; second, not informing [the preceptor] when a visiting bhikṣuṇī arrives; third, not informing [the preceptor] when one goes outside the boundary for a necessary reason;
fourth, not informing [the preceptor] when walking slowly within the boundary; fifth, not sending a messenger when ill; sixth, failing to inform the six great monks.
One must not stay overnight in the same room as another person (for nuns, this refers back to the preceding rule); seven, one must not reside where no bhikṣuṇīs are present;

eight, one must not fail to announce [one's presence] during the fortnightly recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* (for nuns, when performing the confession, such an announcement is unnecessary). Regarding these eight matters, they must not be violated or omitted;
should one violate even a single item, one loses the right to stay overnight.

Fifth, regarding the expiation of offenses: after this nun has completed the sequential performance of the fifteen-night *pārivāsika* rite, she should shave her head cleanly, don the seven-strip robe (*saptaka-cīvara*), wear the shoulder-covering garment (*aṃsa-vastra*), and put on clean leather sandals.

Having fully cultivated dignified deportment, she should come before the two assemblies of the Sangha, prostrate toward the four directions at the feet of the monks, and with earnest and sincere devotion, acknowledge and repent for her prior transgressions, reflecting deeply upon her own faults.

"Having been born as a woman, I have committed many grave offenses by defiling the monastic community. Now, having received the compassionate instruction and admonition of the Venerable Ones, I am freed from these various obstacles;
my joy is beyond measure. Having thus offered thanks, one then requests the removal of the offense, saying: "I beg for the purification of my transgression."
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], intentionally committed the offense of acting as a matchmaker for men and women, incurring a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense;
I do not recall the number of times this was done. Or I committed the offense of speaking of others, incurring a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense; I do not recall the number of times this was done.

Or I committed the offenses of crossing a body of water alone, entering a village alone, staying overnight alone, or walking behind someone alone, incurring saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses; I do not recall the number of times these were done. Or I accepted [the advances of] a man with a defiled mind...
I, [Name], a bhikṣuṇī, committed the saṃghāvaśeṣa offense of providing food and clothing for my child; I do not recall the number of times it occurred.
I have already requested from the Saṃgha fifteen nights of *mānatva* penance, and the Saṃgha has already granted me fifteen nights of *mānatva*.

I, bhikṣuṇī [Name], having completed the fifteen nights of *mānatva*, now request from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karma*) of rehabilitation from the offense. May the Saṃgha grant me rehabilitation from the offense.
The *karmavācanā*. Out of compassion [this is said] three times.
The one performing the *karmavācanā* asks the Saṃgha:
"The Saṃgha is now in harmony; what is to be done? They reply: "Perform the *karmavācanā* for the removal of guilt (*āpattivyutthāna*)."
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣuṇī [Name] intentionally committed the offense of acting as a matchmaker for men and women, incurring a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense;
she does not recall the number of times it occurred. Or she committed the offense of speaking of others, incurring a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense; she does not recall the number of times it occurred.

Or she committed the offenses of crossing water alone, entering a village alone, staying overnight alone, or walking behind alone, incurring saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses; she does not recall the number of times these occurred. Or she accepted a man with a lustful mind...
[She] provided clothing and food [to a monk], thereby committing a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. She does not recall the number [of times she committed it].
She has already requested from the Saṃgha a fifteen-night *mānatva* penance. The Saṃgha has already granted a fifteen-night *mānatva* to this nun, [named] So-and-so.
This nun, So-and-so, having completed the fifteen-night *mānatva*, now requests from the Saṃgha the *karmavācanā* for the removal of the offense. If...
The Saṃgha, please listen: the Saṃgha now performs the *karmavācanā* for the removal of the offense (*āpattivyutthāna*) for the bhikṣuṇī [Name].
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, please listen: this bhikṣuṇī [Name] intentionally committed the offense of acting as a matchmaker between men and women, thereby incurring a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
I do not recall the number of times I committed offenses resulting in *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting of the Sangha) for claiming that another person had committed such an offense;

nor do I recall the number of times I committed offenses resulting in *saṃghāvaśeṣa* for crossing a body of water alone, entering a village alone, staying overnight alone, or traveling behind someone alone;

nor do I recall the number of times I committed offenses resulting in *saṃghāvaśeṣa* for accepting food or clothing from a man with a lustful mind. I have already requested from the Sangha a fifteen-night period of *mānāpya* (probation).
The *mānatva* has been granted by the Saṃgha to the bhikṣuṇī [Name] for fifteen nights.
This bhikṣuṇī [Name], having completed the performance of the fifteen-night *mānatva*, now requests from the Saṃgha the *karmavācanā* for the removal of her offense (*āpatti-vinodana*).
Which elders approve of the Saṃgha granting the *karmavācanā* for the removal of the offense to the bhikṣuṇī [Name]? Those who consent, remain silent. Who does not...?
The *kṣānti-vādins* have spoken thus (three times). The Saṃgha has consented; the formal act (*karman*) for the removal of the offense for the bhikṣuṇī [Name] is completed.
Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is to be upheld as such.

The sixth admonition: After the *vinayadhara* has performed the *karmavācanā*, he should issue this exhortation: "Sisters, listen attentively! In these times, the Dharma of the scriptures and images is declining;
as the law follows the whims of men, transgressors arise in competition and their remorseful intentions turn toward further corruption.

Although they delight in shaving their heads and donning the dyed robes, worldly sentiments still remain within them. Consequently, they are able to receive the precepts yet break them; they grow weary of the prohibitions and weary of maintaining them, showing no joy in repentance."
Those who commit offenses and enter hell merely seek worldly protection and do not aspire to transcendence; now that you have violated the precepts, your lot is akin to this calamity.
Fortunately, having relied upon repentance and reformed your past errors with diligent effort, you confess your prior transgressions—this is truly a great admonition. Therefore, the Treatise says:
"If there are twenty pure bhikṣus who expel a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, my Dharma shall not perish. Now, O virtuous woman...
If people can cause the True Dharma to flourish so that it is not severed, they are true sons of the Buddha who can repay the profound kindness of the Triple Gem;

furthermore, they cause both the mundane and the holy to rejoice, and both monastics and laypeople to look up to them with reverence. From this day forward, I pray that you will never again commit transgressions, remaining no different from a bhikṣu bound by a grass rope or one who guards a pearl on a goose’s neck.
Even if one were to attempt to perform repentance, the causal conditions would be difficult to discern in these final times.
"Among the Dharma, there are many wicked bhikṣuṇīs whose very names one would not wish to hear, let alone listen to your confession.
Having thus admonished them to cease future transgressions, the bhikṣuṇīs who were confessing all joined their palms at once and replied: "We receive this with our heads bowed and shall uphold it;

we vow that until the end of the future, we shall never dare to commit such offenses. (Thereafter, they chanted the ritual prostrations and dispersed. If there were those who had committed *śaikṣa-dharmas* or *pāyattika* offenses, they were to be purified by collectively confessing them during this assembly.)
