Knowing that this is not easily accomplished, one must inquire which school’s precepts were received; if the origin is obscure and untraced, one must further ask what Vinaya this monastery follows in its practice so that the beginning and end may be firmly established.
The Great Teachings must be distinguished and not allowed to be interchanged, lest one merely delude one’s own mind.

Furthermore, as the customs of the frontier barbarians gradually diverge from those of the civilized lands, and their requisites, vestments, forms, and names differ, these matters must also be treated with lightness [of adjustment].

This section carefully distinguishes between categories rather than treating them as a loose or miscellaneous collection of rules; it relies on the teachings to prevent errors. Herein, the four *parājika* offenses are established as the foundation.
Where this text is insufficient, other sections provide the necessary supplements. This consists of three parts:

first, regarding items that the Buddha permitted monks to possess—such as the five robes and the six requisites—it was because these are essential for supporting the body and the path that the Buddha judged their possession to be minor (*āpatti-dukkaṭa*). Second, regarding items that the Buddha did not permit monks to possess...
Fields, houses, slaves, gardens, ponds, and miscellaneous livestock invite censure and obstruct the Path; their acquisition is judged as grave, and their possession is strictly prohibited.

Regarding the three Buddhas’ allowances for possessing items—such as extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*), alms bowls, money, gems, gold, and silver—although these items may obstruct the Path by fostering greed, they are the necessary requisites for the practitioner’s life.

Therefore, the Buddha permitted their possession provided one performed the ritual of *viśuddhi* (purification/declaration of purity). While there is no fault in using them, the underlying principle contains both light and heavy degrees of transgression, which are distinguished separately into three categories.
"Those of heavy nature" refers to all items such as gold, silver, coins, treasures, wooden or stone basins, jars, cauldrons, pots, carts, and the sixteen types of utensils;
because their substance is heavy and they are unfit to be carried along the road, they are classified as heavy.
"Those of light nature" refers to all the one hundred and one requisites that may be carried with one's person, such as cloth, silk, thread, and cotton; there is no limit to the quantity of these.
Regarding the classification of offenses as light or heavy based on their usage:

there are cases where the object itself is heavy but the offense is classified as light due to its usage, such as a razor, a stone for cleaning bowls, a bowl-casket, a chest for the five robes, a needle-case, or a bowl, cup, spoon, or chopsticks—regardless of whether they are made of iron, ceramic, or wood—all are classified as light.
Conversely, there are cases where the object itself is light but the offense is classified as heavy due to its usage, such as large or small curtains, screens, or pillows.

Fans, felt, mattresses, bedding, curtains, and so forth are all judged to fall under the category of heavy [offenses]; as these do not exhaustively cover all cases, they are further subsumed within seven branches.
Subsequently, lightness and heaviness are determined based on this.

First, regarding those made of silk, hemp, wool, or cotton: according to this Vinaya, a sitting or sleeping mat falls under the category of heavy [offenses] if it is a *k'ou-lu* (carpet) five [units] in length.

The width is three *cubits* and the length of the fringe is three finger-breadths; the Buddha judged this to fall under the category of light offenses (*laghu-āpatti*). By extension of this principle, a single-layered rug (*kaṭhina*) is also judged to be a light offense.

Those exceeding the previous limit of eight feet are heavy offenses. Thin and soft woolen rugs that meet the prescribed measurements fall under the category of light offenses, whereas those exceeding the measurement and made of leather are heavy offenses because they are unfit for use.
Small woolen carpets (*kambala*), brocade, embroidery, and *qi* silk with distinct colors [are also subject to these rules].
Those with patterns of birds or beasts among the various silks and brocades are considered heavy; those without such patterns are considered light.
As for other items such as twilled cloth or raw silk fabric, regardless of their size, they are classified as light by this principle.

Therefore, the Vinaya permits the acceptance of high-priced coarse garments and various fine robes. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that there are two kinds of water-strainers: [the waist-strainer] and... (the bowl-strainer).

Regarding the carrying of bedding and other items: cotton cloth (*karpāsa*) single-layer mats and undergarments for the body, along with needle-cases, thread-bags, alms-bowl bags, and leather sandals, are judged by the Buddha to be light.
Brocade, fine silk, woolen rugs, felt, mosquito nets, and the like are included among the heavy.
According to this Vinaya, those that are soft and small are light, while those that are thick and large are heavy. Needle-cases and thread-bags made of dyed colors are classified as heavy.
Whether it be hemp thread, silk, cotton, or other materials, regardless of the quantity, if they have been personally woven into robes by a relative, they are classified as light;

if they have been woven by one who is not a relative, they are classified as heavy. Bags for storing the three robes (*tricīvara*) are classified as light according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*; bags for miscellaneous items outside of those are classified as heavy.
Miscellaneous threads from laypeople, boots, socks, and clothing for men or women that has been dyed in various colors are also classified as heavy.

Regarding items that are not of heavy weight but are dyed with colors: they are classified as light because they are intended for wearing and maintenance, and because they constitute clothing materials.
Therefore, the subsequent section of this Vinaya states: "From this day forward, one should not wear any clothing belonging to laypeople.

By this principle, if there are nuns who currently make such garments as laypeople's robes, tunics, those with low collars, those worn over both shoulders, or long-sleeved garments, they are correctly judged to fall under the category of heavy [weight] if they are indeed laypeople's clothing.

Regarding those that are torn or damaged: regardless of whether they are made of colored or non-colored materials, if they are fine silk or brocade, even if torn, they are classified as heavy because of their exquisite color;
however, if they have been dyed and subsequently torn, they are classified as light.
Second, regarding those made of copper, iron, pottery, or wood: this Vinaya states these include copper jars, basins, rope beds, water flasks, and wash-basins.

The staff, fan, axe, chisel, lamp-stand, desk, table, carriage, litter, and tools made of iron, leather, bamboo, wood, or pottery—these five types of implements are all considered "heavy" when used for construction.
A razor for shaving is classified as "light," while money, jewels, and the like are classified as "heavy.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "All dyed materials, whether they have been boiled or not, should not be divided; they are to be treated according to the same category as other implements."

Regarding items such as heavy *saṃghāṭī* robes, money, the seven precious gems, pearls, wooden trays, wooden basins, bamboo brooms, and so forth, they are classified as "heavy" according to the *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing).

It is stated that needles and thread are "light. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states that for the purpose of cutting and tailoring the *kaṣāya*, one may keep a four-inch blade with a crescent-moon-shaped edge;

by this principle, it is judged to be a "light" offense. Exceeding the prescribed size for white iron, porcelain, or earthenware bowls is "heavy. This applies when [the items] have already been produced.

Various items prepared for funeral rites and the like are all judged to be "heavy" (grave) offenses. However, if such items were made during one's lifetime for the sake of one's preceptors, parents, or other teachers, they are categorized according to their respective light or heavy status.

As for the mirrors, folding screens, sliding doors, and locks belonging to the deceased, because they obstruct the long-term [use of the monastery], they are judged by principle to be included among the "heavy" items.
Regarding the *kūyara* vessels mentioned in this Vinaya, tradition states that they are copper bowls.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) states that a *kañcī* refers to a small bowl. The *Vinayamātṛkā-uttaragrantha* (Essentials of the Vinaya) states that a *kañcī* is an accessory utensil for eating;

in the language of Qin (Chinese), it is a shallow iron bowl. By extension of this meaning, it includes items such as offering stands, scripture racks, Buddha-beds, desks, tables, fly-whisks, as well as the inner lining of incense burners, the cloth covers for incense burners, and scripture cabinets.
If one acts without a deliberate intention, at the time of doing so, [it is merely...]
Regarding items intended for entry into the Buddha-dharma as offerings: they shall follow the deceased’s intent and be used for the purposes of the Buddha-dharma;
they must not be confiscated and transferred elsewhere because they have been specifically designated for that purpose.

If these items were made with one's own property during life, or were given as a gift by another without a specific designation, then according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Kṣudraka-vastu*, they should be given to whoever is capable of making offerings with them—provided such a person exists.
Items adorned with jewels that cannot be separated [from the body] are included among light valuables;

other miscellaneous items such as incense tables, incense burners, Buddha-beds, curved armrests, knee-clamps, *cintāmaṇi* staffs, fans, and scripture cabinets follow the status of the deceased while they were alive.

If these items did not belong definitively to the Buddha-dharma during the person's lifetime, they are classified as heavy after death; if they did belong definitively to the Buddha-dharma, they follow that classification.

The spittoon of the deceased, heavy wooden *muhua* beads, *mulan* wood, bamboo-segmented rosaries, cleansing powder, flour, and gourd vessels shall accompany [the deceased] on the long journey because they are essential.
Regarding the determination of light items such as bells, coins, and residual property: if the donor has designated them specifically for the bell, they shall be returned to the use of the bell;
if the donor’s intention was general, the residual property shall enter the common property of the monastic community (*sāṃghika*).

Third, regarding fields, houses, gardens, and groves: according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, entering heavy red earth constitutes a grave offense; entering heavy yellow arsenic or white plaster also constitutes a grave offense.
Fourth, regarding leather goods: the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that "leather goods" refers to oil-sacks with a capacity of half a *dō* or less.
Regarding the binding of leather sandals, hide, and so forth: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that it is permitted to divide leather sandals;

by this standard, flat boots and socks are classified as light [offenses], while high boots and the like are classified as heavy, because they resemble secular dress. Thus, this *Vinaya* states that no leather garments whatsoever may be worn, as they constitute a heavy offense.
The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "If there is a prior entrustment in the Sūtras or Vinayas, one should rely upon that specific entrustment."

Regarding those works that have not been formally entrusted [to the Sangha], they may be given to whoever is capable of upholding them. As for secular books, plain paper, paintings, silk, and the like, these are categorized as grave offenses;

however, works such as Master Zhaolun’s *Five Treatises* and Master Jiao’s *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, as well as those containing internal (Buddhist) terminology, are categorized as light offenses.
It is also permissible for individuals outside the community to read them.
Fifth, regarding domestic animals: according to the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, these constitute a grave offense (*guru*).

Sixth, regarding male and female slaves: according to this Vinaya, these also constitute a grave offense; whatever private property they possess, regardless of its value, shall be forfeited to that person.

If a slave belonging to the permanent monastic community (*sthavira-saṃgha*) dies, their clothing and belongings are given to their relatives; if there are no relatives, they are used for the maintenance of the community.
If a slave or servant who lived with the Sangha dies, their property and wealth shall be divided among those who shared their food and clothing.
If they did not share in the same resources, they shall simply be made to pay their taxes; or, if they served by turns and performed labor, their property and wealth shall go to their relatives.
If there are no relatives, the matter is treated the same as property without an owner.

Regarding the seventh category, the four medicines—whether given at the proper time (*kāla*), at the improper time (*vikāla*), for seven days (*saptāha*), or for life (*yāvajjīva*)—are all classified as heavy offenses.
What has been listed above follows the general principle; where details are not fully provided, they may be inferred by analogy.

However, although the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* classifies items such as the bathing jar, mendicant’s staff, needles, awls, and knives as heavy, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* and the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* classify them as light. This does not contradict the fundamental principle, as it depends on the specific circumstances.
Because it is necessary for the body, it differs from other items that obstruct the path.

Regarding the sixth point, "those who owe a debt": if there are light or heavy items owed by an individual to the Buddha-Dharma, or by the deceased to an individual, or by the deceased to the Buddha-Dharma—if such items exist, they should be returned as equivalent;
if they do not exist, they should be returned through exchange. The reason they must be sought is...
Heavy items shall go to the permanently resident Sangha (*sthavira-saṃgha*), while light items shall go to the present Sangha (*pratyutpanna-saṃgha*).

If one who previously owed light items from the deceased now recovers heavy items, they must exchange them for light items and distribute the latter. If one who previously owed heavy items from the deceased now recovers heavy items, they shall be assigned to the heavy category;
since they were originally heavy items, they remain heavy. If they were originally light items, they shall be assigned to the light category for the Sangha.
Regarding items belonging to the permanent endowment (*sādhāraṇa*) that have been borrowed from the deceased, they need not be reclaimed, as they must be returned to the permanent endowment.

If light items were borrowed, they should be reclaimed for distribution among the present monks (*pratyutpanna-saṃgha*). If an individual has borrowed both light and heavy items, both must be reclaimed;
the heavy items are to enter the permanent endowment, and the light items are to enter the present assembly. The *Daśādhyāya-vinaya* states: "If one dies while in debt, [the debt remains]."

Treasures should be returned; if property belonging to the Three Jewels or the deceased is lost, it must be reclaimed and brought into the presence of the community (*saṃgha*), for it is necessary to demand it back and settle the matter according to the original basis.
This applies even to mutual debts between current residents, guests, and former residents from the four quarters, as explained above.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If someone borrowed wine from another on credit and died before returning the price, the Buddha said: 'Take his robe and bowl and repay the debt.'"
If there is no property belonging to the deceased, one should take the property of the Saṃgha [to pay the debt], fearing that it might bring ill repute upon the bhikṣus.

By this principle, if the deceased owed other goods for which no reproach would arise if not returned, there is no offense in not returning them, because the deceased had no property. However, if the deceased did possess property, it must be returned.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one has previously given the price for a robe to another, and that person dies, one should go and reclaim it; if one has already taken another's robe, one should likewise reclaim it."
If the debt is repaid with interest, but there is no original robe remaining, one should sell the robe and bowl to repay the mother. The *Mātṛkā* states:

"If there is property with interest held outside, send a *karmadāna* (attendant) to seek it out and bring it into this monastery for the permanent use of the Saṃgha. By analogy with this principle, if goods owed are in the house of a layperson, the same rule as in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* applies:
among the five groups of renunciants who were present when [the debtor] died at a place without a fixed residence, those who saw him first shall receive the heavy [portion].

Regarding the matter of objects being handled according to the prior owner's disposition, the *Five Hundred Questions* states: "If a bhikṣu borrows an object belonging to another and that person dies, he must inform the Saṃgha before taking back the original item.

If he does not inform them, he incurs an offense. If the other party refuses to return it and he takes it by force, or if the Saṃgha knows of the situation and does not return it, both the individual and the Saṃgha incur offenses.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one seeks to collect a debt, one should examine the deceased person [to determine the status of the claim]."

One who maintains the precepts and is trustworthy should not be given [the task] along with one who is untrustworthy; if there is a trustworthy person to serve as a witness, it should be granted, but otherwise it is not permitted.
Seventh, regarding the rewarding of labor: this Vinaya has two sets of five virtues (*pañca-guṇa*). Of these, the first set of five virtues concerns the difficulty of attending to a patient.
The virtues of one who attends to the sick are fulfilled when there are five faults: first, the patient eats what they should not eat and refuses to take medicine;
second, the caregiver possesses a sincere heart but does not speak the truth; third, the caregiver fails to remain where they ought to stay and so forth;
fourth, the caregiver has physical pain but cannot endure it; fifth, the caregiver is physically capable but does not act, suppresses others from acting, or is unable to remain composed.
The second set of five virtues for one who sits to pacify the inner mind concerns the qualities of the attending physician’s own conduct:
first, knowing what the patient may eat and what they may not eat, and providing what is permissible; second, not loathing the patient’s excrement, urine, saliva, or vomit;
third, possessing a compassionate heart and attending to the patient not for the sake of food or clothing; fourth, being able to manage and prepare medicinal decoctions.
Even until the patient’s life comes to an end, there are five [qualities] by which one may preach the Dharma to the patient so as to bring them joy;
furthermore, if one’s own merit in the wholesome dharmas increases, there are two sets of five virtues by which one should be granted clothing and requisites for the patient.

If one tends to the sick only slightly or lacks a sincere heart, the Buddha ruled that they shall not be granted [rewards]. The *Saṃghāṭi-vibhaṅga* states that there are four types of those who tend to the sick who do not deserve a reward.
1. To look at an object for only a brief moment without harboring a long-term intention; 2. To look while being assigned by turn according to the monastic order; 3.
To look out of a desire for one's own merit and fortune rather than out of compassion; 4. To look with a wrong livelihood, seeking only gain and offerings—none of these are permissible.

If, however, one intends to benefit the patient and desires their swift recovery—even down to lighting a single lamp and watching until the end of their life—one should be permitted to do so according to this Vinaya.
One should not inquire as to the superiority or inferiority of their virtue when providing robes for the caregiver;

however, if one does not know which are the robes for a caregiver, one should assess whether the patient is of superior, middling, or inferior condition. If the patient is in extremely good health, one should provide the three superior robes;

if the condition is middling or inferior, one should provide the three middling or inferior robes. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, one first asks the caregiver what robes and bowl they themselves maintain.
If there is one who asks separately but either does not know or does not believe, one should grant them the six items of middle rank. According to this Vinaya, the six items for rewarding labor are:
the three robes as three, the alms bowl as four, the sitting mat as five, and the needle case as six.

(For nuns, the addition of the *saṃkakṣikā*—the shoulder-covering garment—would make eight according to the *Mahāsāṃghika*). Furthermore, the text adds ten items; regarding the "containers for clothing," the "clothing container" is simply that which holds the robes.

"Bag" and "five-robed garment pouch" refer to the bowl bag and its case, etc.; these all generally fall under the category of rewards for service. By principle, this is based on two factors: the object and the virtue. 1.

When both the object and the virtue are present, one is fully rewarded. 2. When the object is present but the virtue is not, one is not fully rewarded. 3. When the virtue is present but the object is not, one is not fully rewarded. 4. When neither the object nor the virtue is present, one is not rewarded. However, in the case of nursing the sick, [the situation differs].

Even if the object is not present, if the virtue is present, it is still considered a reward. Furthermore, even if the virtue is not present, if the object is present, it is also considered a reward. Only when both are absent is there no reward. Thus, the nursing of the sick is distinct from other cases.
If one who is suffering wishes to provide for others, they should assemble those present and, after the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is completed, evaluate their relative merits and virtues;

then, after three proclamations, the Saṃgha shall grant rewards according to the degree of merit. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, when a bhikṣu is ill, the seven classes of followers should attend to him;

two classes are entitled to receive the robe-offering, namely the bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras. When a bhikṣuṇī is ill, three classes are entitled to receive the robe-offering, namely the bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and śrāmaṇerīs.
Even if one’s parents, brothers, or others look after a *bhikṣuṇī*, one should not give [them] labor, for it would fail to fulfill their merit. The *Vinaya-śāstra* (Gā-lùn) states:

"If a layperson looks after her, one should give them a small amount. By this principle, if many *bhikṣuṇīs*, *śikṣamāṇās*, or *śrāmaṇerīs* are looking after the patient, they should be given until the task is finished.
If they finish together, it should be given to one person; then, in a private place, one should distribute [the remainder], according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
If a caregiver goes out on behalf of a patient to beg for robes or medicine and succeeds in obtaining the three robes, they should set them aside and wait until the patient returns to give them back;
alternatively, they may include them in the current distribution by chanting and assigning them, which is also permissible.
If monks from other locations come to visit the patient, they should also be given a reward (the same applies to *bhikṣuṇīs*).
Regarding the eighth period: the *Saṃghīti* states that if a sick person dies, one should not immediately open their door.

If there is a disciple who maintains the precepts and is trustworthy, they should be given the door-bolt. If such a person is not available, the door-bolt should be entrusted to a monastery official (*karmadāna*).
Once the śarīra has first been honored and the funeral arrangements completed, the disciple who maintains the precepts and is trustworthy shall be sent out.
If the robes are not to be trusted, one should have a steward take out the robes before the Sangha distributes them.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, they were distributed near the corpse; when the corpse rose up to protect the robes, the Buddha said: "Wait until the corpse has departed or is in another location, then you should distribute them.

(In the present day, when a monk or nun first passes away, the doors are closed from beginning to end while the robes are divided inside. This is because they fear that visiting nuns might obtain them; it is not merely that the distribution of the robes is invalid, but it is also improper for those residing outside to be excluded.)

Regarding the ninth section on the distribution of property (*dharmabhāga*), this chapter has three parts: first, formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*); second, face-to-face procedure (*pratyekamukha*); and third, mental recollection (*manasikāra*).
In the first part, regarding formal ritual action, a group of five persons may perform the *karmavācanā* for the distribution of robes as a reward for service;

if there are only four persons, they may only distribute the robes but cannot perform the *karmavācanā* for the reward because the quorum of the Saṃgha is not met. It would be better, therefore, to perform the *karmavācanā* first and subsequently take possession of the robes.

Regarding the harmonious verbal acknowledgment of labor, the *Mātṛkā* states that among four persons, if one is designated to enter the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*), the remaining three do not constitute a *saṃgha*.
Therefore, the current established rule is that the attendant of the dying person shall bring both the light and heavy articles into the midst of the *saṃgha*.
As for heavy items, they cannot be lifted; once the number of those that can be counted has been determined, it is permissible to pay them directly into the *saṃgha* treasury during the day.

It is even better to perform the ritual during the day; one must not close the doors or restrict access for visiting nuns, for the principle of the ten directions is that there should be no private bias.
The *P'o-lun* (Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra) states: "If one closes the doors during the day and does not strike the bell or drum before eating, it is called the offense of stealing the Sangha's food.
Furthermore, although this distribution of robes may not be formally completed, these items belong to every individual, as each person has a share in them and possesses a mind [regarding them].
Regarding those who limit their invitations [to specific monks], each incurs a number of *sthūlātyaya* offenses equal to the number of atoms [in the world].

Thus, the *Śāṅshēng jīng* (Sūtra on Good Birth) states: "As for one who steals the robes and belongings of a deceased bhikṣu: if the *karman* has not yet been performed, one incurs an offense with respect to the Saṃgha of the ten directions;

if the *karman* has already been performed, one incurs a *pārājika* offense if the value reaches five [units] with respect to the Saṃgha that performed the same *karman*, and a *sthūlātyaya* if it does not reach five. (This is mentioned in the commentary because this evil practice is observed in various monasteries. [Next is the section on] Attending to the Sick.

A person should kneel for a long time beside the object, grasp it, and set it aside; if there is no *upadhivārikā* (superintendent) or *karmadāna* (steward) nun to do so, she may set it aside herself.
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen! A certain bhikṣuṇī has passed away at a certain residence. Whatever [belongings] she possessed, whether robes or..."
This is not clothing; it is the property of the resident Saṃgha that should be divided. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], now relinquish this to the Saṃgha (having spoken thus once).
The one among the assembly who is learned in the Vinaya shall then adjudicate, saying: "First, let us ask within the Saṃgha who knows whether the deceased person owed anything to the Three Jewels."
If there are other persons present, who knows of the deceased’s belongings? One must interrogate each individual regarding the existence or non-existence of the items.

Only after this is determined should one decide on the gravity of the matter: heavy items are placed in one location and light items in another, while also questioning the attendant as to whether they brought the deceased’s light or heavy items to the funeral.
If the attendant claims to have taken the light items, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) shall be performed for their restitution.

Regarding the division of heavy property: if it was brought to the Saṃgha with the original intent to steal, it is improper to seek a share of the remainder, as the act of theft has already been completed.
However, if it was borrowed for temporary use or done without a mind of theft, one should seek a share, as the act of theft is not established.

One must inquire thoroughly; having first [ascertained the facts], one then measures merit and rewards labor. If the five virtues are not possessed, then it is improper to grant a reward. Those who perform the rites nowadays simply...
When asked by a monk whether one possesses the requisite qualities, if one answers that they do not possess them, it is extremely base and evil;

if one does possess them, one deserves to receive [the reward]. Since there is labor involved, one ought to obtain it. Knowing this to be the case, those who have rendered service in caring for the sick deserve to be rewarded.

As the Vinaya Master said: "Sister, you have indeed performed meritorious labor in caring for the sick. The Buddha commanded that you be generously rewarded. If you are not so rewarded, you would be contravening the Sage."
"Venerable Sister, you should follow the instruction and accept it. The nun who was nursing the patient then stated that she lacked virtue, and the monks likewise urged her to accept.
In this manner, they yielded to one another so that both parties might cultivate goodness; not only was their own conduct exemplary, but the communal ritual also generated merit.
Having understood this matter, he then questioned [the patient].
“Sangha, being now in harmony, what shall we do? [The response was: “We shall perform the *karmavācanā* for rewarding labor.

‘Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen! The bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has passed away. Her robes, bowl, sitting mat, needle-case, and clothing-storage vessels are to be divided by the present Sangha of this residence.
If it is the time for the Sangha and the Sangha is willing to grant permission, let the Sangha now—’”
[This is] the formal announcement for the bhikṣuṇī [Name], who attended to the sick:

"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, please listen. The bhikṣuṇī [Name] has passed away. All her robes, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and containers for storing clothes are to be divided by the present Saṃgha.
They are now being given to the bhikṣuṇī [Name], who attended to the sick. Which of you, Venerable Sisters..."
The Sangha consents. To the nun [Name], who attended to the sick, the Sangha gives her robes, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and clothing storage container.
Those who consent remain silent; whoever does not consent may speak. The Sangha has consented and grants [these items] to the nun [Name], who attended to the sick.
The robes, bowl, sitting mat, needle-case, and containers for storing clothing are now complete. Because the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

The meaning is that one should recite according to the number of items; one must not recite the text in its entirety as a whole, for it is feared that there may be items not accounted for in the formal motion (*karmavācanā*).
A *karmavācanā* (formal act) that is performed contrary to the Dharma is called a "defective *karmavācanā*"; although it is technically accomplished, one still incurs a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*).

For example, if two *śrāmaṇeras* receive the precepts at the same time—one with obstacles and one without—the one without obstacles may validly complete the ordination without hindrance, yet he still incurs a minor offense. The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"If one seeks the three robes from another location and intends to offer them as a reward here, if this requisite virtue is not fulfilled, then [the robes] shall be distributed according to their respective shares. If one relies upon...
In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) for when a śrāmaṇera dies should be stated as follows:
"The life of the śrāmaṇerī so-and-so has ended; all her inner and outer robes, as well as non-robes, should be divided.
The remaining wording is the same as that for the Saṃgha. Next, the ritual method for dividing light garments is explained; the master of the ritual asks:
The Saṃgha is now in harmony. What is to be done? Answer: The distribution of the light belongings of the deceased bhikṣuṇī by means of a formal act (karmavācanā).
Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen! The bhikṣuṇī [Name] has passed away. Whatever robes or non-robes she possessed should be divided by the present Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent. The Saṃgha now takes these robes and articles and bestows them upon the bhikṣuṇīs.
"Such-and-such a bhikṣuṇī, [name], shall return this to the Saṃgha.
It is announced thus: 'Venerable sisters of the Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣuṇī, [name], has passed away. Whatever robes or non-robes she possessed should be divided by the present Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha now takes these robes and articles and gives them to the bhikṣuṇī, [name]. The bhikṣuṇī, [name], [accepts them]. "
It should be returned to the Saṃgha. Which of you, Venerable Sisters, approves? This Bhikṣuṇī [Name] has passed away;
her robes and personal effects should be divided by the present Saṃgha. The Saṃgha now takes these robes and gives them to the Bhikṣuṇī [Name], who shall return them to the Saṃgha.
Those who approve, remain silent. Those who do not approve, speak. The Saṃgha has approved; it takes these robes...
This object is given to the nun [Name] and the nun [Name]. They shall return it to the Saṃgha.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If the robes are insufficient for all, the Sangha shall give one set to a monk who has no robes (the same applies to a nun).

If there is one particularly high-quality robe, according to the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it should be distributed sequentially from the top; those who need it receive it directly, and there is no need to proceed to the bottom.

(According to this rule, it is also permissible to distribute them by breaking the order. Question: After the *karmavācanā* has been performed, may the Sangha collectively request [the laity] to perform funeral rites for the deceased?

Question: Can one obtain merit through these [offerings]? Answer: For those who have left the household life, wisdom and virtue should reside within their hearts; they do not take the cultivation of merit as their primary vocation.

According to the judgment of the Vinaya, for such persons to enter the Sangha is most excellent. However, if one generates wholesome thoughts toward external objects and internally abandons the mind of greed, then performing meritorious acts on behalf of the deceased—whether small or great—will benefit both the living and the dead.
This is because both practices will bring benefit. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

If one seeks clothing or medicine on behalf of a sick person, or performs laborious tasks for the sake of the Saṃgha, even if they are not present at that time, they should still receive a share (provided they are those with good intentions and virtuous conduct).
Question: Should śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇerīs, family members, and pure attendants (karmadāna) receive a share?
Answer: This Vinaya states: "If the Saṃgha is in harmony, a share should be given to the śrāmaṇeras and others; if they are not in harmony, then..."
If [the property] is divided into four parts, one part is given to the *kappiyakāraka* (pure person); if it is divided into five parts, one part is given to them.
If they cannot be obtained, one should not divide [the property]. If one divides it [without them], one incurs an offense. The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states:

"If five persons live together and one dies, the three remaining persons shall collectively appraise the robes, bowl, and other items and give one portion to the nurse; the other four persons may only perform a direct division."
Regarding the *karmavācanā*, it is not necessary to divide the items by passing them around;

rather, one should announce the distribution of the rewards for nursing services, saying: "Sisters, please bear this in mind. I now take these robes, bowl, sitting mat, and other belongings of the deceased nun [Name], to reward the nursing nun [Name].

(Recite this three times, naming the specific items according to their quantity; do not recite them all at once. If there are two recipients, simply say: "Sisters," and for those beyond the two, proceed as before.)
The *jñapti-karman* for direct distribution states:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen! A certain bhikṣuṇī has passed away. Whatever robes or non-robes she possessed shall be distributed by the present Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: the Saṃgha now distributes these robes and articles. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*)."
Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen. A certain bhikṣuṇī has passed away. Whatever robes or non-robes she possessed, these should be divided by the present Sangha.
Venerable Sisters who consent to the Sangha now dividing these robes and articles, remain silent. Whoever does not consent, please speak. The Sangha has consented;
the Sangha has finished dividing these robes and articles. Because the Sangha consents and remains silent, this matter is so settled.
This is the holding [of the precepts].

Regarding the second case of addressing one another (*pratimukha*), the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "When four persons live together and one dies, the remaining three should speak to one another in turn, saying:"
"Two elder sisters, remember: this object should belong to me. (The other two likewise say this to one another, and thus it becomes a shared distribution of the clothing.
When three people live together and one dies, those remaining face one another and say: "We speak to each other mutually... [and so forth].
"Sister, remember this: these items should belong to me (the same applies to the later nun).
If there is someone who has provided nursing care and deserves a reward for their labor, it is also permissible to jointly entrust the robes and bowl to those two people."

Regarding the third [method], the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "As for the 'single formal act of correspondence' (*ekasamvāsa-vijñapti*), when two persons are living together and one dies, the survivor performs a mental reflection and speaks these words:

'This property of the deceased bhikṣuṇī should belong to me. (Having performed this face-to-face mental reflection and recited it three times, they both take hold of the robe; subsequently arriving guest bhikṣuṇīs are not entitled to a share)."
This Vinaya states: "If one person receives a gift, they should mentally reflect and verbally declare:
'This is my portion. The same applies to deceased property. Regarding the tenth section on miscellaneous rules:
if a nun dies in a monastery estate or a private monastery, she should be dealt with according to the rules for a temple.

Regarding this, what is meant by a "private ārāma"? It refers to a single courtyard constructed by laypeople in a village or settlement for the common use of the Three Jewels alone, where white-robed householders are not permitted to reside;
furthermore, it is surrounded by fences, walls, and the like—it is called an ārāma even without having been formally demarcated by boundary-setting (sīmā-bandha).
If there is a nun tending to the sick, her heavy belongings may enter the nuns' [quarters].
Light items belonging to this temple that have entered another temple must be divided by means of a *karmavācanā* if four or more people witness the deceased’s property.

If no boundary has previously been established, the division is performed through a formal ritual (*dharma-karman*); if there are three or fewer people, it is divided through face-to-face consultation (*pratyakṣa-vibhāga*), as this differs from the case of death in a layperson’s household.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if a bhikṣu’s robes and bowl are deposited in a bhikṣuṇī temple, they shall be returned.
If a bhikṣu claims a share of a bhikṣuṇī’s deposited robes and bowl, the same rule applies to the monastic community.
If there is no one to guard or maintain them, the matter is treated according to the household laws of laypeople. Therefore, this Vinaya states:

"If a bhikṣuṇī dies in a layperson's house where there is no residence for nuns, a faithful donor (dānapati) should take charge of these items. If there are members of the five groups of renunciants present first..."
If someone arrives, one should give it to them; if no one arrives, one should deliver it to a nearby monastery.

The meaning is that even if one knows of deceased property in a layperson's house, one must physically grasp it and witness it with one's own eyes while forming the intention that it belongs to oneself before one may obtain this object;
otherwise, it is not accomplished. If a nun arrives later, she should share it equally. If a layperson has already taken possession of it as their own, it constitutes the theft of property.
One who has attained realization (Arthasiddhi) may not reclaim property that has been lost. However, if a layperson, out of fear of the law, returns it to a nun, she may take it.
If monks and nuns both see the lost property at the same time, if it belongs to a nun who has died, it belongs to the nuns; if it belongs to a monk who has died, it belongs to the monks.
They may not be held jointly, because each is a person who knows the Dharma. There is no need for a formal ritual; if one simply takes possession according to one's own intent, it is acquired.
Regarding Bi Zhuang Temple: because it was secluded and remote, it was necessary to establish a formal procedure.
If monks or nuns arrive before or after one another, they shall belong to whoever arrived first, and those who arrived later may take them in together with the former.
○ *Za yao pian*, Chapter Thirty.
This chapter has eight main sections: 1. Monastic Property; 2. Begging for Food; 3. Ascending the Seat; 4.
Engaging in the Dharma; 5. Pure Grounds; 6. Encountering Robbers; 7. Saving Living Beings; 8. Miscellaneous Matters.
Regarding the first category, the property of the Saṃgha: this section has five parts. First is the property of the Saṃgha of the four quarters;
this refers to all heavy items, from Arhats above down to Śrāmaṇeras below, all of whom have a share in them. These may not be sold, traded, or diverted for private use by the assembled community.
This is designated as such based on its universal scope. Second is the property of the resident Saṃgha; this refers to items that must remain permanently at this location and cannot be moved.
1. *Cāturdiśa-saṃgha* (literally "the Saṃgha of the four directions"): This refers to the use [of property] by the Saṃgha coming from the four directions at this very location;

it is named after its function. 2. *Jātidhārmika-vastu* (formerly called *zhāotí sēngwù*, "property of the Saṃgha of the four directions"): This refers to when laypeople, on separate plots of land, each construct private dwellings for the *pratyutpanna-saṃgha* (the Saṃgha present there).
When members of the *cāturdiśa-saṃgha* arrive, they erect rooms and provide all necessary supplies; it is named after the location. 5. *Saṃgha-mālya* (the Saṃgha’s garland/ornament).
"Objects" refers to the flowers, fruits, and goods obtained from a garden; it is named after the *mālā* (garland) because they are brought here from that source.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The Saṃgha has five kinds of property that cannot be sold and cannot be divided: first, land; second, buildings; third, necessary utensils; fourth, fruit trees;
and fifth, flowers and fruits. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If the Saṃgha plants fruit trees on its land, there is merit; if [there is] one tree..."
If one listens to [the rules regarding] a garden, when one cannot take both [types of produce] at once, one may take one branch per year; once all branches have been taken, one must stop.

If it concerns planting melons or vegetables, one may listen to [the rule] of taking one shearing. If a bhikṣu builds a house on land belonging to the Saṃgha and the Elder (sthavira) arrives, he shall not give [it to him];
he should take the grass and wood and go elsewhere.

The second point regarding the practice of begging for food (*piṇḍapāta*) states that the *Śāstra* explains: "To beg for alms" means to solicit food. The noble ones (*ārya*) of the Three Vehicles all practice begging for food.

According to this Vinaya, if a bhikṣu enters a village to beg for food, he should wash his hands at dawn, put on his seven-strip robe (*saptaka-cīvara*), drape the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) over his shoulder, hold a staff (*khakkhara*) in his hand, and while walking along the road, constantly contemplate wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*).
If one sees people, one should first greet them, saying, "Welcome. When approaching a village, one should put on the outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) and go to the village gate.

One should observe the streets and lanes, noting the characteristics of the first and seventh gates. Holding a staff in the right hand and a bowl in the left, one should walk along the side of the road and beg for food in due order.
If a layperson brings food, one must not go out to meet and receive it, except when summoned to do so.

If one cannot obtain food by forceful begging, one should stand waiting; once food has been obtained, one may leave the village, place the bowl on the ground, and fold up the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) as before, then depart.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, when begging for food, one must not say, "Give me food;
you shall become very wealthy," but should stand silently in the presence [of the donor]. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, when begging for food, one enters [the village].
When one reaches the middle courtyard through the three gates, one must snap the fingers three times; if permission is not granted, one must depart.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that when Kāśyapa made a vow to beg for food, he first gave whatever he obtained to monks and nuns, and only thereafter ate it himself. The *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* says: "Whenever one obtains food by begging, divide it into four parts:

one part to give to fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring life; one part to give to the poor and those who do not beg; [the second part for oneself]; and the third part to offer to the Three Jewels."
One-third [of the food] is given to the various ghosts and spirits; the fourth part is for one's own sustenance.

One should only keep in mind the cultivation of the Path, giving rise to no heart of greedy attachment toward that food. When begging for alms, one should maintain mindfulness of dignified deportment, never being frivolous or rash, looking straight ahead at a distance of no more than one fathom, and begging in successive order.

Regarding the third point concerning ascending the seat: the *Sāhasrika-vinaya* (Three Thousand Dignified Manners Sūtra) states that when the senior monk (*sthavira*) recites the sūtras, he first pays homage to the Buddha, then to the Dharma of the sūtras, and finally to the senior monks present.
Once he is seated upright upon the seat and the sound of the *ghanṭā* has ceased, he should first recite verses of praise and chant according to the Dharma.
According to this Vinaya, two persons must not occupy the same high seat to preach the Dharma, lest they fall into mutual contention.

Because they sought out each other's faults, the *Wu-bai wen shi* (Five Hundred Questions) states: "If one preaches the Dharma in the midst of the Saṃgha while seated on a high seat, one must not lean against a desk or grasp a *cūḍāmaṇi* (dust-whisk) unless one is ill;
to do so constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. However, one who possesses a whisk made of non-hair materials may keep it.

This Vinaya permits the keeping of a *cūḍāmaṇi* whisk. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "A *cūḍāmaṇi* whisk made of yak-tail hair may be used to sweep a Buddha-stūpa; therefore, it is permitted for the Saṃgha to receive [such a whisk]."
Ghoṣaka said: "From this day forward, it is permitted to grasp a whisk made of thread, split wool, tree bark, and so forth;
however, except for those with handles of yak-tail hair, horse-tail hair, gold, or silver, everything else is forbidden to be grasped. If it is white, it must be dyed to change its appearance;

one must not grasp it or use it to put on airs or affective gestures like a courtesan, for that is called 'unlawful. If it is used for the purpose of spreading [a seat] for a Vinaya-master or a Dharma-master..."

When scattering flowers upon a lion throne, one must not sit on it until they have been swept away; the *Pó lùn* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra) states that one must not place flowers, incense, necklaces, or other ornaments upon the body of the Buddha.
It is likewise permissible to scatter them on the ground as an offering to the Saṃgha, yet one must not place flowers or incense upon the gruel, food, or drink as an offering to the Saṃgha.
Fourth, regarding the one who preaches the Dharma: this Vinaya permits preaching the Dharma for lay donors (*dānapati*). One may preach the *Sūtras* and explain their meanings;

however, it is not permissible to recite the full text word-for-word. The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "If a great assembly has gathered and the text is extensive, there is a fear that weariness and distaste may arise.

In such cases, it is permitted for the bhikṣus to cite essential passages and elegant phrases from within the Sūtras to directly reveal the meaning; thus, they do not commit an offense. Furthermore, according to the Buddha-dharma...

In the middle [of the discourse], one does not prize flowery and ornate language; though the words may be plain and simple, they do not lose their meaning and are easy for others to understand—this is the establishment of the intent (*abhiprāya*).
The *Pañcavastuka* states: "If the assembly delights in the shallow and does not delight in the profound, it does not benefit those who came before and is called 'evil exposition' (*durākhyāta*);
the opposite of this is called 'good exposition' (*sukhākhyāta*). Furthermore, one should eliminate the mind of greed, the mind of self-deprecation, and the mind of disparaging the great assembly.
One should establish a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of sympathetic joy, a mind of beneficial intent, and an unshakable mind;
by establishing such minds even for the duration of a single four-line verse, one causes the person before one to understand according to reality, bringing them peace and happiness for a long night.

Furthermore, monks, there were those who invited precept-breakers and those lacking the roots of virtue to preach the Dharma, whereby these evil persons gained power and brought disgrace upon the Sangha. The Buddha said: "I permit you to invite a Dharma Master."

The Tripiṭaka master states that the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "If a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma for the sake of gain and offerings, and his followers likewise imitate their teacher, such a person destroys his own assembly.

The *Five Hundred Questions on Matters* states: "If one reads scriptures or preaches the Dharma with a heart of expectation for material gain, one commits an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*);
if there is no heart of greed, there is no offense. One may accept miscellaneous items if one has no robes."
The *Āgama Sūtras* state that a single bhikṣu may receive the instruction and preaching of up to sixty newly ordained bhikṣus.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "If there are those who uphold, recite, transcribe, or proclaim [the teachings], they must not do so at an improper time or in an unsuitable country, nor preach without being requested.

They must not speak with a frivolous mind or with contempt for others, nor praise themselves; they must not preach indiscriminately in every place, even to the point of causing the extinction of the Buddha-dharma."

One who measures others and causes them to fall into hell is an evil friend (*pāpamitra*) to sentient beings. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that there are five kinds of persons to whom one should not explain the *vinaya* when questioned:

those who ask out of a desire to test [the teacher], those who do not have doubts, those who do not ask for the sake of repenting their transgressions, those who ask without accepting the words [of the teaching], and those who ask for the sake of refutation;
in all these cases, one must not answer. The *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* states that one should not instruct a donor.
Regarding the *Buddha-nature Vinaya*, this bhikṣu acts like a thief and dwells like a thief; his wearing of robes, eating, sitting, and lying down are all those of a thief.

Fifth, concerning the "Pure Ground" (*śuddhasthāna*), the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "If one were to sweep a single monastic cell in Jambudvīpa, it would not equal sweeping [the ground] before the Buddha."
The *Ekottarikāgama-sūtra* (compiled by one hand) states that sweeping the ground yields five merits: first, one removes the defilements of one's own mind; second, one eliminates arrogance;
third, one subdues the mind; fourth, one increases merit; and fifth, one attains rebirth in a favorable realm.
The *Śrāmaṇera-ācāra-sūtra* states that there are five rules for sweeping the ground: first, one must not sweep with one's back turned toward others; second, one must not sweep against the grain.
Third, one must ensure it is clean; fourth, there must be no visible tracks [left behind]; fifth, one should discard it immediately.

The *Wugou Qingjing Nüwen Jing* (Sutra of the Stainless Pure Woman’s Questions) states that sweeping the ground where the Buddha dwells yields five blessings: first, one’s own mind becomes pure, and others who see this will also give rise to a pure mind;

second, one will be loved by others; third, the devas will rejoice in their hearts; fourth, one accumulates the karma for physical excellence; and fifth, at the end of life, one will be reborn in a good realm.
Regarding the section on the heavens:
Sixth, concerning the encounter with bandits—when a bhikṣu under this Vinaya is stripped of his robes and cannot walk about uncovered, he incurs an offense.
He should cover his body with soft grass or tree leaves, take a long robe (*prāvaraṇa*) and wear it, and seek a robe from among his friends within the Saṃgha by begging for one.
Once it has been obtained, should one return it to its original place? Regarding this, the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states that one should cause the thief to depart by making a hollow sound oneself.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If a thief asks, "Where is the property of the Saṃgha? one must not point out the actual location. Furthermore, one must not speak falsely;

rather, one should indicate the rooms, beds, and so forth [as belonging to the Saṃgha], and point to the offerings near the stūpa as being the property of the Buddha. If there is [property] while traveling on the road...
Liu instructed that young monks should be placed in front; if there is danger from bandits or wild beasts, the elder monks should remain in the center.
However, if one wishes to arouse a mind of compassion in the bandits, the elder monks should go in front.
Seventh, regarding the salvation of animals: according to the Vinaya, one should act with a compassionate heart to release dogs that have been tied up or piglets that have been drowned.

Regarding the case of thieves tethering oxen at an *araṇya* (hermitage) site, there is no offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one possesses supernatural power (*ṛddhi-bala*) and seizes those who plunder people from thieves, releasing various birds and beasts, it is an act of compassion;
there is no offense. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one dismantles nets out of compassion or breaks down prisons, one commits only a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense).
The *Pañcaśata-praśna* states: "When traveling, if one stays overnight in a house belonging to ghosts or spirits, one must not remain there."
To disturb or cause offense against the mind constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the eighth miscellaneous matter, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that there are seven disadvantages to lighting fires: first, it impairs the eyes; second, it impairs the complexion;

third, it causes physical weakness; fourth, it soils the robes; fifth, it damages bedding and furniture; sixth, it creates conditions for the arising of transgressions of the precepts; and seventh, it increases worldly attachments.
The *Wǔbǎi wèn shì* (Five Hundred Questions) states: "To continue the Buddha’s radiance, one must not extinguish the lamp during the day;

for the Buddha has no darkness of ignorance, as he is eternally free from verbal thought and conceptual limits, extinguishing [the lamp] would be a transgression. The Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of the Great Tang stated:

"Regarding the lamp before the Buddha, one may take it up from the side using an object so as not to damage the light. The *Saṃghīti-vinaya* states: "One must not suddenly carry a lamp into the hall."

One should announce: "Venerable sirs, the lamp is about to enter [extinction]," and so on until it is extinguished; likewise, one should prevent it with the hand and not allow it to be blown out by mouth.
Instead, one should fan it with the corner of one's robe; when fanning, the head should be tilted, and the flame will be extinguished.

The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states that those who have left the household life should abandon the five kinds of stinginess: first, stinginess regarding material wealth; second, stinginess regarding the Dharma; third, stinginess regarding dwellings; fourth, stinginess regarding... [the text continues].
Dwelling in stinginess, one praises stinginess and is stained by attachment to kinsmen and the delight in one’s dwelling;

therefore, one falls into birth among the *kālaṅka* and other hungry ghosts (*preta*). The *Āgama-sūtra* states that the four objects of gratitude are the parents, the teacher, the monastic community, and the king and donor.
The four classes refer to devas, nāgas, humans, and spirits. This Vinaya states that if there is urine where it is not a place for walking or coming and going, and...

When washing one’s hands and feet, it is permitted to wear sandals; furthermore, one must not go to the toilet naked. The *Sāhasrika-vaipulya-sūtra* (Three Thousand Rules of Dignified Conduct) states:
"If one has not washed the areas used for defecation or urination, one must not sit upon the monastic sitting mat (*saṃghāṭī*).

When the senior monk (*sthavira*) prostrates before the Triple Gem, if there is no merit [in doing so while impure], he should remove his *kāṣāya*. During defecation or urination, one must not wash [the area]; having defecated or urinated, one must wash."
If one lies down upon the bedding used by a monk while lying or sitting upon it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. This Vinaya states that there are five faults in not chewing a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*):

first, the breath becomes foul; second, one cannot distinguish flavors; third, undigested heat remains in the body; fourth, one cannot distinguish between foods; and fifth, the eyes lose their clarity.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that after chewing, one should rinse it and discard it, lest insects eat it and die. Furthermore, there are those who lack forbearance.
The five faults are: first, being fierce and intolerant; second, giving rise to regret later; third, being disliked by many people;

fourth, the spread of an evil reputation; and fifth, falling into the evil realms after death. This Vinaya states that walking meditation (caṅkrama) has five benefits: first, the ability to travel long distances;

second, the capacity for contemplation; third, having little illness; fourth, the digestion of food and drink; and fifth, the attainment of long-abiding concentration. The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* says: "To go..."
There is no fault in giving alms to those who beg at monasteries—such as those without food, infants, prisoners, and pregnant women.
The *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* states that if one has lustful thoughts while performing music as an offering to the Buddha, one must immediately depart.

The *Ekottarika-āgama* states that after King Ajātaśatru developed faith, he did not allow the households serving the Buddha to provide transport for his processions. The *Pañcaśata-praśna-vastu* states: [text follows].

If one gives military weapons, they need not accept them. The *Abhidharmakośa-mūla-śāstra* states that if one acts as a teacher for laypeople and performs meritorious deeds through their conversion, there are five matters to observe:
first, one should not reside in the donor's house; second, one should not harbor thoughts of greed for profit;

third, one should preach the Dharma to them individually, such as on generosity, ethical discipline, and the eightfold precepts; fourth, one should not engage in entertainment with them; and fifth, one should maintain focused mindfulness.
Craving gain, they constantly desire to see one another. Furthermore, there are five matters by which one becomes a respected and honored donor (*dānapati*):

first, not visiting places where one has no prior acquaintance; second, not seeking to use one's influence to manage the household affairs of the donor; third, not engaging in secret conversations that might cause suspicion within the family;
fourth, not instructing [the donor] on auspicious times or days for sacrificing to spirits; and fifth, not being excessive.
There are five faults in frequently visiting the homes of laypeople when seeking this Vinaya: first, one frequently sees men; second, having seen them, one becomes intimate with them;
third, they become close friends; fourth, one gives rise to lustful thoughts; fifth, because of those lustful thoughts, one may suffer the pain of death or near-death.
The *Dharaṇīdhara-sūtra* states: "If one sees sentient beings, one should immediately greet them with a serene countenance."

First, one should speak with a level gaze, a harmonious expression, and maintain right mindfulness before oneself. According to this Vinaya, if a layperson sneezes, one should offer the blessing of long life.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that one is permitted to keep bricks or tiles for the purpose of scrubbing the feet. The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states that in cold places, one is permitted to wear the boots of laypeople.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that when making boots or leather footwear, they should not be made too deep; they are permitted to reach up to above the ankles. The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* asks: "How does one remove the leather?"
If one walks around the Buddha wearing sandals, laypeople will reproach them, giving rise to feelings of aversion and arrogance;

therefore, this Vinaya ordains that the Saṃgha shall keep measures such as *dō* (dou), *ke* (sheng), *watsu* (he), and *gō* (liti), as well as scales. If a room becomes malodorous, one should apply fragrant mud or even hang incense at the four corners.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that when bathing, it is not a fault for a non-ill person to scrub another. The *Mātṛkā-vinaya* states that when bathing... [text ends]
For the sake of adorning the body and maintaining cleanliness, one should merely remove the wind and cold from within the body so as to attain peace and proceed on the path.

One should cultivate a sense of revulsion toward the phenomena of the body and subdue the phenomena of the mind, giving rise to a heart of loving-kindness in order to attain few desires and contentment.
Therefore, according to this Vinaya, if a person managing affairs constructs a dwelling that is completed, adorned, perfumed, and fully equipped with all necessities, it shall be granted [to him].

One may occupy a room for ninety days before moving; one must not accept another room. If there is someone capable of maintaining the rooms, they should be granted [the privilege] via a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one announcement).

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If the monthly supervisor or the food overseer wishes to know whether the food is cooked or raw, sour or salty, they may place it in the palm of their hand and taste it.
The *Sūtra on the Dharma of the Uposatha* says that tasting is not permitted, meaning that tasting with a greedy mind is forbidden. This is the fifth major point.

The *Sūtra on Turbidity* states that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there shall be five corruptions: first, bhikṣus of the future will learn the Dharma from laypeople—this is the first corruption of the world;
second, laypeople will sit in the places of bhikṣus while the bhikṣus sit below them—this is the second corruption of the world;
third, bhikṣus will not practice or uphold the preaching of the Dharma, but instead take the preaching of laypeople as supreme—this is the [third corruption of the world]...

The fourth of the three corruptions is when bhikṣus of Māra’s faction arise in the present world and take what they themselves do not understand to be the Truth of the Path, falsely pretending to have faith;

this is the first of the four corruptions of the world. The fifth is that bhikṣus of the future will maintain wives and children, slaves and servants, engage in livelihoods such as trade and commerce, and involve themselves in disputes and litigation;
they will not uphold the Buddha’s teachings. This is the fifth corruption of the world, whereby they shall not be permitted to reside in stūpas or monasteries.
Regarding "internal defilement," [the *Jian lun*] says that one who practices *dhūta* shakes off [defilements].

The *Zhidu lun* states that taking the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) constitutes *dhūta*. When a Bodhisattva dwells amidst afflictions yet contemplates the supreme patience regarding phenomena, this is the superior *dhūta*.
Some sutras state that *dhu* means few desires and *ta* means contentment. Xuanzang says it refers to an *araṇya* (wilderness retreat).
The *Śūnyatā-vihāra-sūtra* (East) states: "The *Miśraka-hṛdaya-śāstra* says that contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*) pertains to the present, while having few desires (*alpecchatā*) pertains to future rebirths;
it is easy to attain *nirvāṇa* [through these]. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Not giving rise to greed for wealth not yet obtained is called having few desires;
not giving rise to greed for wealth already obtained is called contentment. Contentment refers to the present, while having few desires refers to the future."
Coming again, there is little desire, yet there remains desire; with contentment, there is no further desire.
*The Fourth-Part Vinaya Bhikṣuṇī Yao*, Scroll Lower of the Lower Section (End).
I prostrate to the Buddhas of the ten directions, possessors of all-knowledge, and to the True Dharma Wheel of the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
To the noble masters of the fruits of the Three Vehicles, I now offer this general confession of my dedication:
I contemplate myself submerged in the ocean of suffering within birth and death, Following along with ignorance and craving, drowning in the long river;
Desiring to escape, yet unable to leave, I rely upon the distant compassion of the Sages to rescue me from this sinking and drowning.
Having briefly stilled the sufferings of the four torrents and gained admission to the life of a renunciant to serve the Triple Gem,
and further having been granted permission by the power of the king and my parents to follow and study the various Dharma gates,
I do not know how I shall repay this debt of gratitude; therefore, I praise and extol [the Buddha] to requite his kindness.
This compendium of the sublime words is mostly composed as praise; I prostrate and repent, praying for your compassionate regard.
Produced in the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, I have drafted this for my own recitation; how could it compare to others?
Should there be anyone who peers even at a single phrase herein, May we all together rejoice in the source of ultimate truth.
Although the printing blocks for this commentary were produced during the Song Dynasty, they had not yet been carved in Japan; thus, the labor required for transcription was great.

Therefore, the Bhikṣuṇī Qinyuan, in order to broaden its dissemination, universally exhorted the fourfold assembly to respectfully open these six volumes and present them as a gift to the Vinaya Library of Donglin, so that students might copy them by folding the pages. By this merit, may it reach all beings.
This is a record respectfully inscribed on the final day of the fifth month in the year of *kōshin* (1289), by the late master Enkū,
a preeminent lineage holder who early on attained the highest rebirth and swiftly investigated each stage of realization to its ultimate advancement.
Postscript to the *Biqiuni chao*:
Now, since the Buddhist teachings have flourished, one must understand the distinct paths of the monks and nuns;

therefore, our Great Master [Daoxuan] composed the three great treatises, such as the *Seng shishi chao*, for the sake of the monks, and he composed this work in three fascicles for the sake of the nuns. Thus, regarding the Vinaya...
Once the lamp has burned brightly, those who raise its flame in future generations will stand towering within the world; such is the preservation of the ancestral instructions.
Nevertheless, had I not beheld this book, the faith of the nuns in the oil would have led to a leakage that caused the light of their precepts to diminish accordingly.
Since my youth, I have traveled through the Vinaya collections, and upon first seeing this book present there, I received it with joy and reverence, spreading it out upon my desk.
The upper volume has suffered much from insect damage, and its beginning and end are incomplete.

During my recent days of ritual recitation, I have examined the texts of this great work to supplement and correct them, while also adding harmonious translations for the convenience of beginners. I request that readers study these with meticulous care;
the distinct practices for monks and nuns are now clearly and easily accessible. This edition is now being carved into woodblocks at the bookstore of Mr. [Name] to propagate it widely.

I transmit this with the sincere wish that those who open this volume and raise their eyes may enter directly into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) and continue the Buddha’s life-force of wisdom without end;
thus shall my own aspiration be fulfilled. Some may say that this *Commentary on the Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya of the Four-Part Vinaya* was composed by the Tang dynasty Vinaya Master Daoshi;
this is not so, for while he knew the title was the same, he did not know the difference in the number of fascicles.
On the anniversary of the Buddha’s birth in the first year of the Jōkyō era (the year of the Rat), the junior bhikṣu Shōben Eiga,
a late follower from Mount Ōyama, took up his brush at the Mitsu-gon Ritsu-an in northern Kyoto.
